chapters.title: Bimala: Vermilion and Mother's Blessing
paragraphs: Mother, today I remember the vermilion in the parting of your hair, that red-bordered sari, those two eyes of yours—calm, gentle, deep. I see them now on the sky of my mind like the crimson streaks of dawn. The day of my life set out on its journey with that golden provision. And after that? Did dark clouds come racing down the path like bandits? Did they leave not a single particle of my light behind? Yet, that gift of the dawn, given in the Brahma-moment of life by the chaste morning-star—though it may be covered in calamity, can it ever be destroyed?

In our country, we call one beautiful whose complexion is fair. But the sky that gives us light is blue. My mother’s complexion was dusky, her radiance was of virtue. Her beauty would put the pride of beauty itself to shame.

Everyone says I look like my mother. As a child, I once became angry at the mirror because of this. It felt as though my entire being was somehow unjust—my complexion, as if it were not truly mine, as if it belonged to someone else, a complete and utter mistake.

I am not beautiful, but I wished with all my heart before the gods that, like my mother, I might gain the reputation of a chaste and virtuous woman. When my marriage was being arranged, an astrologer from my in-laws’ side came and, after reading my palm, declared, “This girl is blessed with good fortune; she will be a devoted and virtuous wife.” All the women said, “Of course she will—Bimala looks just like her mother.”

I was married into a royal house. Their honor dates back to the times of ancient emperors. In my childhood, I had heard tales of princes in fairy stories—since then, I had painted an image in my mind: the son of a royal house, his body fashioned from jasmine petals, his face slowly shaped by the single-minded prayers of countless maidens who, through the ages, had worshipped Shiva. What eyes, what a nose! The line of his youthful moustache like the wings of a bumblebee—dark and delicate.

When I saw my husband, he did not quite match that image. In fact, his complexion was just like mine. The self-consciousness I had always felt about my own lack of beauty was somewhat eased, but that...

Along with it came a long sigh. For my own shame, perhaps I could have died, but why did I never get to see, even once, with my own eyes, that prince who lived in my heart? Yet, perhaps it is better when beauty, slipping past the watchful eyes, reveals itself hidden within. Then it stands in the immortal realm of devotion—there, it needs no adornment to arrive. Everything becomes beautiful in the beauty of devotion itself. I saw this in my childhood. When Mother, especially for Father, would peel the fruit and arrange the breakfast on a white marble tray, when she would set aside the betel leaves for him, carefully wrapping them in a piece of cloth sprinkled with kewra water, when she would gently fan away the flies with a palm-leaf fan as he sat down to eat—her loving hands, the stream of nectar from her heart, into what ocean of wondrous beauty did it plunge? Even in my childhood, I could sense this in my mind.

Was not that note of devotion present in my heart? It was. Not argument, not the discernment of good and bad, but only a melody. If there is any fulfillment in making one’s whole life a hymn sung in the temple courtyard of the Giver of Life, then that morning melody had already begun its work.
I remember, in the early morning, when I would rise very carefully—

When I used to take the dust of my husband's feet, it seemed to me that the vermilion in the parting of my hair shone like a starfish. One day, suddenly waking up and laughing, he said, "Oh Bimala, what are you doing?" I shall never be able to forget that shame. Perhaps he thought I was secretly performing some pious act. But no, no, it was not my piety—it was the heart of a woman in me, whose love desires to worship of its own accord.

My husband's family is bound by the old customs. Some of their manners and rules are Mughal-Pathan, some of their regulations are from Manu and Parashara. But my husband is entirely different. He is the first in this family to have received a proper education, to have passed his M.A. His two elder brothers drank themselves to death at a young age—they left no children. My husband does not drink, there is no restlessness in his character—in this family, this is so out of place that not everyone likes it; they think that those who have no Lakshmi in their house are the ones who ought to be so utterly pure; "There is no broad space for blemish among the stars, only in the moon."

It has been many years since my father-in-law and mother-in-law passed away. My elder aunt-in-law is the mistress of the house. My husband is the necklace on her breast, the jewel of her eye. Even from birth, my husband had the courage to step beyond the bounds of custom. That is why, when he appointed Miss Gilby as my companion and teacher...

Then, all the flavors of home and the world turned to poison, yet my husband's resolve remained unshaken. At that time, he had passed his B.A. and was studying for his M.A. He had to stay in Calcutta to attend college. Almost every day, he would write me a letter—his words were few, his language plain, and those rounded, gentle letters of his handwriting seemed to gaze softly at my face.

I kept his letters in a sandalwood box, and every day I would pick flowers from the garden to cover them. By then, my fairy-tale prince had faded away in the light of dawn like the moon. On that day, my true prince had taken his seat upon the throne of my heart. I was his queen, I could sit beside him; but greater than that joy—my true place was at his feet.

I have been educated, so now I am familiar with the language of this present age. Even to myself, these words of mine today sound like poetry. Had I not encountered this poetry, I would have thought of my feelings of those days as simple prose—just as I knew that being born a woman was not of my own making, so too it seemed natural that a woman would melt her love into devotion—there was nothing extraordinary in it—

Whether there is any extraordinary poetic beauty in it or not, I do not need to pause even for a moment to consider. But from that boyhood until now, having barely reached the midpoint of youth, I find myself in another era. What was once as effortless as breathing, now comes with advice to shape it into an art, like poetry. The thinkers of today speak daily, in ever more melodious tones, of the unparalleled poetry in a wife’s chastity and a widow’s celibacy. From this, it is clear how, at this point in life, truth and beauty have become separated. Now, can truth be regained merely by invoking the name of beauty?

I do not believe that all women’s minds are cast in the same mold. But I do know this much: within my own mind was that very thing my mother possessed—the eagerness to worship, to devote. That this was my natural state I now clearly understand, now that it is no longer simple from the outside.

Such is my fate: my husband did not wish to grant me the opportunity for that worship. That was his greatness. The greedy priests at the holy places quarrel over worship, because they are not truly worthy of it; in this world, only cowards demand the worship of women. In that, both the worshipper and the worshipped are utterly humiliated.

But why so much care for me? Through adornments, servants, and all manner of things, it was as if his affection overflowed both my shores in a flood. Amidst all this, through what opening could I offer myself in return? I needed the opportunity to give far more than the opportunity to receive. Love is by nature an ascetic; it scatters its countless blossoms on the dust by the wayside, not in the porcelain vases of the drawing room to display its riches.

My husband could not entirely do away with all the old customs that prevailed in our inner quarters. I could not meet him freely at any time of day, whenever I wished. I knew exactly when he would come—so our meetings could not happen haphazardly, in disorder. Our union was like the union of poetry—it came through rhythm, through pause. After finishing the day’s tasks, bathing, carefully binding my hair, marking my forehead with vermilion, draping the pleated sari, gathering my scattered body and mind from the whole household, I would offer myself to him alone, on the golden platter of a particular hour. That time was brief, but within that brevity lay the infinite.
My husband has always said that husband and wife have equal rights toward each other, and therefore an equal relationship of love. I have never argued with him about this.

But my heart tells me, devotion does not hinder people from becoming equals. Devotion seeks to lift a person upwards, to make them equal. That is why, in the joy of becoming equal, there is always fulfillment—never does it run dry and turn into something to be neglected. On the plate of love, the worship of devotion is like the light of the arati lamp—its radiance falls equally upon both the worshipper and the one who is worshipped. Today I know for certain: a woman's love is worshipped only when it worships—otherwise, it is a thing to be scorned! When the lamp of our love is lit, its flame rises upward—the burnt oil of the lamp alone can trickle down.

Beloved, you never sought my worship, and that is your greatness, but had you accepted it, it would have been good. You have loved me by adorning me, by teaching me, by giving me what I desired, by giving me even what I did not desire—you have loved me in every way. I have seen that my love never brought a shadow upon your eyes, I have seen that my love only brought a secret sigh upon your breath; you have loved my body as if it were the heavenly parijat blossom, you have loved my nature as if it were your own good fortune. (This fills me with pride, I feel it is my own wealth that has drawn you so eagerly to my door. Then, seated on the queen’s throne, I claim my right to honor—a claim that is only...

It keeps growing, never finding satisfaction anywhere. Is a woman's happiness truly in the thought that she holds the power to subdue a man, or is her welfare in that very thing? Only by immersing that pride in devotion can it be preserved. Shankar stood at the door of Annapurna as a beggar, but could Annapurna have borne the fierce austerity of his begging if she had not performed penance for Shiva?

Today I remember how, on that fortunate day of mine, so many hearts in the household burned with the slow fire of envy. And why shouldn't they have? I had received so much, and so easily—almost by cheating. But deceit cannot last forever; the price must be paid, or fate will not tolerate it. For a long time, day after day, one must repay the debt of fortune before true ownership is secured. God may grant us gifts, but we must earn them by our own merit. Even what is given, we do not truly receive—such is our ill-starred fate!

Because of my good fortune, how many fathers of daughters heaved long sighs! Was I so beautiful, so gifted, was I truly worthy of this house? Such questions were whispered from neighborhood to neighborhood, from house to house. My elder aunt-in-law, my mother-in-law, all were famed for their extraordinary beauty. My two widowed sisters-in-law—such beauty is rarely seen. But when, one after another, misfortune befell both of them, my elder aunt-in-law resolved firmly that her one—

For the sake of the one remaining grandson, she would no longer search for a beauty. It was solely by the strength of my good fortune that I was able to enter this household—otherwise, I had no claim here at all.

In our house, in this world of indulgence, very few wives have truly received the honor due to a wife. Yet, that is said to be the custom here; thus, even though all the tears of their lives were drowned beneath the froth of wine and the tinkling of the dancer’s anklets, they clung only to the pride of being the mistress of the great house, keeping their heads afloat above it all. But my husband never even touched wine, nor did he, driven by lust for women’s flesh, squander his humanity at the doors of sinful markets. Is this due to my own virtue? What incantation did the Creator grant me, that I could subdue the wild, frenzied mind of a man? It is nothing but fate—nothing else! And in the case of those other women, was the wretched Creator not in his senses? Every letter of their fate was crooked! No sooner had evening fallen than their festival of pleasure was over—the lamps of beauty and youth kept burning all night in empty halls, in vain. There was no music anywhere, only the burning.
My husband’s two aunts pretended to scorn his manliness. To entrust the boat of such a proud household to the sail of a single wife’s sari? At every opportunity...

How much I have been mocked by them! It is as if I am stealthily stealing my husband’s affection. Nothing but deception, all of it artificial; the shamelessness of modern women! My husband has adorned me in the latest fashions—seeing all those colorful jackets, saris, chemises, and petticoats, they would burn with envy. No beauty, only the display of beauty! Turning the body into a veritable shop window—do you not feel ashamed?

My husband knew everything. But his heart overflowed with compassion for women. He would tell me again and again, “Do not be angry!”—I remember once I said to him, “Women’s minds are so small, so twisted.” He replied, “Just as the feet of Chinese women are small, and twisted! All of society presses in from every side, squeezing and bending the minds of our women.” Fate gambles with their lives—the outcome depends entirely on the roll of the dice; what rights do they truly possess?

My sisters-in-law would demand whatever they wished from their younger brother, and he would grant it. He never judged whether their demands were just or unjust. My heart would burn within me when I saw that they were not even a little grateful for this. Even my eldest sister-in-law, who was so fearsome in her austerity, always fasting, immersed in prayer and penance, with such an air of renunciation on her face—

What was spent for the mind was hardly a quarter of an anna, nothing remained—she would repeatedly tell me that her lawyer brother had said, if she filed a case in court, then she—oh, so many things, what more can I write? I had promised my husband that, under no circumstances, would I ever respond to their words, and so my irritation became even more unbearable; I would feel that there is a limit to being good—if one crosses that, somehow it seems to diminish one’s manliness. My husband would say that neither the law nor society is on the side of his sisters-in-law, but what is most difficult is that, what they once took for granted as their own by right of marriage, today they must beg for, seeking favor from others like mendicants—such humiliation is hard to bear. And on top of that, to demand gratitude as well? To be beaten and then to offer thanks? Shall I speak the truth? Many times I have thought, my husband ought to have had a little more of the spirit to be just a bit less good.

My middle sister-in-law was of a different sort. She was younger—she did not pretend to be virtuous. Rather, her words and laughter always had a touch of mischief. The young maidservants she kept with her were of questionable character. No one objected to that—because that was the custom in this house. I understood that my...

The enthusiasm for depositing money surged greatly among the villagers, because the interest rate was very high. But for the very reason that people’s enthusiasm kept increasing, through that gaping hole of high interest, the bank eventually sank. Witnessing all these events, his old retainers became extremely irritated and anxious, while the opposing faction mocked and ridiculed him. One day, my elder sister-in-law, making sure I could hear, said that her renowned lawyer cousin had told her that if an appeal could be made to the judge, perhaps there was still a way to save the honor, prestige, and property of this aristocratic family from the hands of this madman.

In the entire family, only my grandaunt-in-law’s mind remained untroubled. She called me over and rebuked me many times, saying, “Why do all of you keep bothering him? Worried about property? In my lifetime, I have seen this estate go into receivership three times. Are men like women? They are reckless, they only know how to soar. Granddaughter-in-law, your fortune is good that he himself is not flying away with you. You don’t remember your sorrows simply because you haven’t suffered.”

My husband’s list of donations was very long. Whether it was a weaving mill, or a rice-husking machine, or any such endeavor that anyone tried to start, he supported them to the very end, even to their final failure. Competing with British companies—

A Swadeshi company was formed to run steamers for the Puri pilgrimage; not a single one of their ships ever sailed, but many of my husband’s company shares have sunk. What annoyed me most was when Sandipbabu, under various pretexts of serving the country, would drain my husband’s money. He would run a newspaper, go about propagating Swadeshi ideals, or, on a doctor’s advice, would need to travel to some distant place for a while—my husband would unhesitatingly provide for all his expenses. Besides this, there was a regular monthly allowance for his household needs. Yet, what was astonishing was that my husband did not even share his views. My husband would say that just as the country remains poor if we cannot extract the products from its mines, so too, if we cannot discover and acknowledge the treasures of strength within the country’s soul, that poverty is even more grievous. One day, in anger, I told him, “They are all deceiving you”— He laughed and said, “I have no special abilities, yet by giving only money I am becoming a partner in their abilities—so it is I who am profiting by deception.” I have recounted something of this earlier era, for without it, the drama of this new age cannot be clearly understood. As soon as the storm of this age touched my blood, the first thing I said to my husband was, “All my belongings made of foreign things—”

I will burn the clothes. My husband said, “Why will you burn them? As long as you wish, you can simply not use them.” What are you saying—‘as long as I wish’? In this life, I have never— Well then, in this life, you may choose not to use them. But if you do not burn them with ceremony! Why do you object to this? I am saying, give all your strength to the work of building up; do not waste even a quarter of it in the excitement of needless destruction. It is this very excitement that helps in building up. If that is what you say, then I must say—without setting the house on fire, one cannot light up the house. I am willing to endure a thousand troubles to light a lamp, but I am not willing to set the house on fire for quick convenience. That may look like heroism, but in truth, it is a patchwork of weakness. My husband said, “Look, I know you do not understand my words today, yet I am telling you this—think it over. Just as a mother adorns each of her daughters with her own jewelry, so today has come a time when the whole world is adorning each country with its own ornaments. Today, our food, clothing, movement, thoughts—everything— is connected with the whole world. That is why I think—”
This is an age of fortune for every nation—there is no heroism in denying this good fortune.”

Then there was another commotion. When Miss Gilby first came into our inner quarters, there was quite an uproar for some days about it. Later, as people grew accustomed, it subsided. Now, everything was stirred up again. For a long time, I had not even thought whether Miss Gilby was English or Bengali—but now the thought began to arise. I told my husband, “Miss Gilby must be dismissed.” My husband remained silent. That day I said whatever came to my lips; he left with a pale face. I wept for quite a while. After crying, when my heart had softened a little, he came to me at night and said, “Look, I cannot see Miss Gilby merely as an Englishwoman, through a clouded lens. Even after all these years of acquaintance, will the barrier of that name never dissolve? She loves you.”
I felt a little ashamed, yet, keeping a slight edge of my pride, I said, “All right, let her stay, who is telling her to go?”

Miss Gilby remained. One day, while on her way to church, one of our distant relatives—a young boy—threw a stone at her and insulted her. My husband had, until then, been supporting that boy—he dismissed him. This caused quite a stir.

Whatever that boy said, everyone believed. People said that Miss Gilby had insulted him and had spread false stories about him. I, too, felt that it was not impossible. The boy had no mother; his uncle came and pleaded with me. I tried a lot on his behalf, but nothing came of it.

No one could forgive my husband's conduct on the day of the expulsion. Nor could I. In my heart, I condemned him. This time, Miss Gilby left on her own. As she departed, tears fell from her eyes—but my heart did not go out to her. Alas, why did she ruin the boy so utterly with a lie? And such a boy! In his Swadeshi enthusiasm, he had no time even to eat or bathe—my husband took Miss Gilby to the station in his own carriage and saw her off onto the train. That seemed to me a great excess. When this incident became the subject of gossip in society, growing branches and leaves in every direction, I felt that this punishment was his due.

Previously, I had often been anxious for my husband, but never until now had I felt ashamed of him, not even for a single day. This time, I did feel shame. I do not know whether Noren wronged Miss Gilby or not, but in these times, even to attempt impartial judgment on such a matter is itself a shameful thing. From the very sentiment that led Noren to show arrogance towards the Englishwoman...

I have not been able to suppress him, nor do I wish to suppress him in any way— this was something my husband absolutely refused to understand. It seemed to me that this was a lack of manliness in him. That thought brought me shame.

But that was not all. What pierced my heart most deeply was that I had been forced to admit defeat. My pride only burned me, but it did not make my husband shine. This, then, was the insult to my chastity.

And yet, it was not that my husband had no connection with the Swadeshi movement, nor that he was opposed to it. But he could not fully accept the mantra of "Bande Mataram" as the ultimate truth. He would say, I am willing to serve my country, but the One whom I worship is far above this. If I worship the country, it will only bring about its ruin.

At such a time, Sandip Babu arrived at our place with his followers to campaign for Swadeshi. In the afternoon, there was to be a meeting in our natmandir. We women sat on one side of the building, screened by a curtain. The lion’s roar of "Bande Mataram" was drawing nearer and nearer, and my heart was trembling within me. Suddenly...

A group of young men and boys, their heads wrapped in turbans and clad in saffron robes, barefoot, surged into our vast courtyard like the first saffron flood of the monsoon in a dead river. The place filled up with people. Through that crowd, a dozen or so boys carried Sandipbabu on their shoulders, seated on a large chair. Bande Mataram, Bande Mataram, Bande Mataram! It seemed as though the sky itself would split and come crashing down in pieces.

I had already seen a photograph of Sandipbabu. At that time, I cannot say I liked him very much. He was not ugly to look at; in fact, he was rather handsome. Yet, I do not know why, it seemed to me that, though there was a certain brilliance, his features were mixed with something base—there was something in his eyes and on his lips that was not quite genuine.

That is why, when my husband fulfilled all his demands without hesitation, I did not like it. I could tolerate extravagance, but I kept feeling that, though he called himself a friend, this man was deceiving my husband. For his manner was not that of an ascetic, nor of a poor man, but rather of a gentleman of leisure. There was a hidden craving for comfort within him—and so on; many such thoughts arose in my mind. Today, all those thoughts come back to me—but let them be.
But that day, when Sandipbabu began to speak—

The heart of this vast assembly swelled and surged, overflowing its banks, ready to be swept away. It was then that I beheld that wondrous figure of his. Especially at one moment, when the sun, slowly descending, cast its rays beneath the roof and suddenly lit up his face, it seemed to me that he was a being from the immortal realms, and that day the gods themselves revealed this truth before all men and women.

From the very first word of his speech to the last, every utterance was like a gust of stormy wind. There was no end to his courage. The thin veil before my eyes—I could no longer endure it. I do not remember whether, unconsciously, I had drawn the curtain aside a little and exposed my face, gazing at his countenance. In that entire assembly, there was not a single person with leisure enough to notice my face. Only once did I see, like the twin stars of the constellation of Time, Sandip Babu’s bright eyes fall upon me. But I was not aware of myself then. Was I, at that moment, the queen of the Rajbari? No—I was the sole representative of all the women of Bengal, and he was Bengal’s hero. Just as the sunlight from the sky fell upon his brow, so too was needed the anointing of the heart of the women of the land. Otherwise, how would the auspiciousness of his march to battle be complete?
I felt clearly that, from the moment his eyes met my face, the fire in his words blazed even more fiercely.

Then Indra’s Uchchaihshravas would no longer heed the reins— Thunder upon thunder’s roar, lightning upon lightning’s flash. My mind said it was the flame of my own eyes that set this fire ablaze. Are we only Lakshmi, are we not also Bharati?

That day, I returned home with an extraordinary joy and a radiance of pride. Inside, a storm of fire’s force dragged me in an instant from one center to another. I longed to cut my hair like the heroines of Greece, to make a bowstring for that hero’s bow—my hair that falls down to my knees. If the ornaments outside were truly joined to the spirit within, then my necklace, my garland, my armlets would have rained down in that assembly like a shower of meteors, falling and scattering everywhere. Only if I could inflict some great loss upon myself, it seemed, could I bear the torrent of that joyous enthusiasm.

In the evening, when my husband came home, I began to fear lest he say anything discordant with the deep, burning melody of that day’s speech, lest his love of truth should prompt him to express even the slightest dissent—if he had, that day I could have openly scorned him.
But he said nothing to me at all. That, too...

I did not feel pleased. He should have said, “Today, after listening to Sandip, I have become awakened; many of my long-held misconceptions about these matters have been dispelled.” Instead, I felt as though he was merely being obstinate and keeping silent, as if he was forcing himself to show enthusiasm.
I asked, “How many more days will Sandipbabu be staying here?”
My husband replied, “He will leave for Rangpur tomorrow morning.”
Tomorrow morning?
“Yes, the time for his speech there has already been fixed.”
I remained silent for a while. Then I said, “Couldn’t he possibly stay just one more day?”
“That is not possible. But why do you ask?”
I wish to serve him a meal myself, in person.
Hearing this, my husband was astonished. Many times before, over many days, he had urged me to come out and meet his friends. I had never agreed.
My husband looked at my face intently, in a way I could not quite understand. Suddenly, I felt a strange sense of embarrassment within. I said, “No, no, that won’t do.”
He said, “And why won’t it do? I— Sandip—”
I said, “If by any means it is possible, then let him stay tomorrow.”
I saw that it became possible.

I will speak the truth. That day I wondered, why did God not make me astonishingly beautiful? Not so that I could captivate anyone’s heart. But beauty is a kind of glory. On this great day, let the men of the country see, in the women of the country, Jagaddhatri herself. But if there is no outer beauty, their eyes cannot see the goddess within.
Can Sandipbabu see in me that awakened power of the nation? Or does he simply think, “She is an ordinary woman, merely the mistress of his friend’s house”?

That morning, after washing my hair, I had carefully tied my long, loose hair with a red silk ribbon. There was an invitation to lunch, so there was no time to tie up my damp hair in a bun. I wore a white Madras sari with a gold border, and a sleeveless jacket edged with a little gold trim.

I had decided this was a very restrained attire—nothing could be simpler than this. Just then, my second sister-in-law came and ran her eyes over me from head to toe. Then she pressed her lips tightly and smiled a little.
I asked, “Didi, why are you smiling?”
He said, “I see you’ve dressed up.”
I felt a surge of irritation within and replied, “Is this what you call dressing up?”
He smiled again, a little crookedly, and said, “Not bad, little queen, it’s quite nice! Only, I was thinking, if you wore that low-cut blouse from your English shop, the look would be complete.”
Saying this, he didn’t just smile with his face and eyes—his entire body, from head to toe, seemed to be filled with laughter as he left the room.

I was furious and felt like throwing everything aside and putting on a plain, thick, everyday sari. But I don’t know why, in the end, I couldn’t bring myself to do it. Inwardly I told myself, “If I don’t dress properly and go before Sandip Babu, my husband will be annoyed—after all, women are the ornament of society.”

I had thought I would only appear before Sandip Babu when he sat down to eat. The act of serving food would help ease the awkwardness of our first meeting. But today, the meal was delayed; it was almost one o’clock. So my husband sent for me to join them for conversation.
When I entered the room, at first I felt terribly shy to look at his face. Somehow, forcing myself, I managed to say, “You’re late for your meal today.”
He came without hesitation and sat down on the bench beside me, saying,
“Look, food is served every day in the same way, but Annapurna remains hidden. Now that Annapurna has appeared, let the food remain concealed if it must.”

There was as much force in his manner as in his speech. Not a trace of hesitation. It seemed to be his habit to claim his place everywhere at once. If anyone should take offense at this, that was not his concern. He seemed to possess a natural right to intimacy, so if anyone found fault with it, the fault lay with them.

I began to feel ashamed, lest Sandip Babu think me nothing more than a hopelessly old-fashioned, inert creature. I had hoped my words would shine brightly, flow freely, that he would be inwardly astonished at each of my replies—but none of this came to pass. Inside, I felt a deep distress—I rebuked myself a thousand times, thinking, “Why did I have to appear before him so suddenly?”

As soon as the meal was somehow over, I was hurrying away—when, just as unselfconsciously, he came to the door, blocked my path, and said, “Don’t spread the rumor that I am a glutton; I haven’t come here out of greed for food. My only desire is that you have called me. If you run away immediately after the meal, you will be cheating your guest.”

Unless such things are said very simply and very emphatically, they become terribly awkward. My husband is his dearest friend, and I am like his own sister. When I was struggling within myself, trying to rise to the high plane of intimacy that Sandipbabu offered, my husband, noticing my confusion, said to me, “Well then, finish your meal and come along.”
Sandipbabu said, “But promise you won’t break your word.”
I smiled a little and said, “I’ll come right away.”

He said, “Shall I tell you why I don’t believe you? It’s been nine years since Nikhilesh’s marriage. All these nine years, you have been breaking your word to me. If you do it for another nine years, we shall never meet again.”
I, too, began to speak with familiarity, and in a gentle voice I said, “Why, why should we never meet again?”
He replied, “It’s written in my horoscope that I will die young. None of my forefathers lived past their thirties. I’ve just turned twenty-seven.”

He knew that this would touch my heart. And it did. Perhaps now, in my gentle voice, there was a hint of pathos. I said, “With the blessings of the whole country, your misfortune will surely be averted.”
He said, “The blessings of the country must come from the lips of the country’s Lakshmis. That is why I have been so eager to ask you to come. Then, from today, my Swastyayan will begin.”

Even if the water of a stream is muddy, it can still be used without difficulty. Everything about Sandipbabu moves with such rapidity that what might not be tolerated from another’s lips, from his, there is hardly a chance to object. Smiling, he said, “Look, I am leaving your husband here as surety. If you do not come, then he, too, will not be released.”
As I was about to leave, he called out again, “I have one more small request.”
I stopped and turned back. He said, “Do not be afraid, just a glass of water. You have noticed, I do not drink water during my meals—I take it a little while after eating.”
After this, I could not help but ask anxiously, “Why, tell me?”

Then came the story of when he had suffered from a severe and chronic indigestion. I heard how, for nearly seven months, he had endured unbearable suffering. He recounted how he had run the gauntlet of allopathic and homeopathic doctors, and finally, after all their troubles, how he had found astonishing results from the treatment of a kabiraj. Finishing his tale, he laughed and said, “Even my illnesses, by God’s grace, are just like this—”
“They have become so accustomed to it that, unless they receive their little piece of Swadeshi sweet in hand, they are unwilling to leave.”
After a while, my husband said, “And those bottles of foreign medicine, too—they are just as reluctant to leave your protection for even a moment. The three shelves in your storeroom are completely—”

Do you know what those are? Like punitive police. Not that they have come out of necessity—under the rule of modern times, they descend upon our shoulders—one must only administer punishment, and I am not spared from their prodding either.

My husband cannot tolerate exaggeration. But exaggeration itself is not the creation of the Divine, but of man, for all ornamentation is exaggeration. Once, in the course of justifying one of my own little lies, I told my husband, “Trees, plants, birds, and beasts are truthful through and through—they simply lack the power to lie. This is where man’s superiority over beasts lies, and again, where women’s superiority over men lies—women can wear much more ornament, and many more lies suit them as well.”
When I stepped outside the room, I saw my second sister-in-law standing on the veranda, holding the window shutter slightly ajar.
I asked, “Why are you here?”—She whispered in reply, “I was eavesdropping.”
When I returned, Sandip Babu said, in a plaintive voice, “It seems you have hardly eaten anything today.”

Hearing this, I felt deeply embarrassed. I had returned a little too soon. I had not given as much time to eating as is proper for a genteel meal. If one were to calculate, the part of my meal that was left uneaten today would surely outweigh what I actually ate—any reckoning of time would make that clear. But it never occurred to me that anyone else was keeping such account.

It seemed Sandipbabu noticed my embarrassment—that made me even more ashamed. He said, “Like a doe of the forest, you seemed eager to flee, yet you endured so much to uphold the truth—surely that is no small reward for me.”

I could not manage a proper reply; blushing and sweating, I sank into a corner of the sofa. The way I had imagined myself, like the very embodiment of the country’s womanly power—emerging before Sandipbabu without hesitation or shame, and by the mere act of appearing before him, crowning his brow with a garland of victory—none of that came to pass.

It was by Sandipbabu’s own wish that he provoked a debate with my husband. He knows that in argument, the keen edge of his mind flashes forth in all its brilliance. Even so, I have always noticed that whenever I am present, he never lets slip even the slightest opportunity for a debate.
Referring to my husband’s views on the ‘Bande Mataram’ mantra, he said, “In the service of the country,
“Don’t you acknowledge, Nikhil, that there is a realm for the imagination in man?”

I do admit there is such a realm, but I do not admit that it is everywhere. I wish to know my country as a reality, in the truest sense, within my own mind, and I want others to know it as well. When it comes to something so great, I am both afraid and ashamed to use any spell of enchantment to beguile the mind.

What you call a spell of illusion, I call truth itself. I truly accept the country as a deity. I am a worshipper of Narayana in man—God’s true manifestation is in humanity, and likewise, in the country.
If you truly believe this, then for you there can be no distinction between one person and another, and thus, no distinction between one country and another.
That is true, but my strength is limited; therefore, it is through the worship of my own country that I worship the Narayana of all nations.
I do not forbid you to worship, but how can that worship be fulfilled if, in doing so, you harbor hatred toward the Narayana present in other countries?

Hatred is also a part of worship. Arjuna gained his boon by fighting with Shiva disguised as a Kirata. One day, we too will strike down the Lord from one side, and in that very act, He will be pleased.
If that is so, then those who are harming the country and those who—

Both are serving the country, both are worshipping it—then what special need is there to propagate patriotism further! As for oneself, that is a different matter—there, within the heart, the altar of worship is clearly set. Then why only one’s own country? There is an even clearer commandment concerning one’s own self. The mantra of worshipping the Narayana within oneself resounds louder than any other, in any land! Nikhilesh, all these arguments you make are but the dry logic of intellect. Will you not acknowledge that there is such a thing as the heart? I tell you truly, Sandip, when you make the country into a deity and try to pass off injustice as duty, unrighteousness as virtue, it wounds my heart, and I cannot remain unmoved. If I steal for my own gain, do I not strike at the very root of my true love for myself? Is it because I have reason that I cannot steal? No, it is because I have respect for myself. Inside, I was growing angry; I could not restrain myself any longer. I burst out, “English, French, German, Russian—is there any civilized nation whose history is not a history of theft for the sake of their own country?”
They must answer for that theft, and even now, they are being held to account! History has not yet come to an end.

Sandip Babu said, “Well then, so shall we. First, we’ll fill our house with stolen goods, and then, at our leisure, over a long period, we too shall answer for them. But let me ask you—when you say they are still being held to account, where do you see that?”

When Rome was answering for its own sins, no one could see it. At that time, its wealth knew no bounds. When the day of reckoning comes for the great robbers of civilization, it cannot be seen from the outside. But can you not see one thing—their politics, filled to the brim with lies, deceit, betrayal, espionage, the sacrifice of justice and truth for the sake of prestige—are they not carrying this burden of sin? And does this not, every day, suck the very blood from the heart of their civilization? Those who do not honor religion in their own land, I say, do not honor their country either.
I have never heard my husband argue with outsiders—he has debated with me, but his compassion for me is so deep that it would pain him to defeat me. Today, I saw him wield his weapons.
My mind could not, in any way, agree with my husband’s words. I kept feeling that there must be a fitting reply to this.
It was there, but at the moment, it was not coming to my mind.

The difficulty is that when one invokes the name of religion, one must fall silent— It is hard to say, but I am not willing to accept religion to that extent. I had resolved that I would write a proper answer to this argument and hand it to Sandipbabu. That is why, as soon as I returned home, I made notes of today's conversation.
At one point, Sandipbabu looked at me and said, “What do you say?”

I replied, “I do not wish to go into subtleties; I will speak plainly. I am human, I have desires, I will desire for my country—I want something that I will seize and gather; I have anger, I will be angry for my country, I want someone upon whom I can vent my long-standing humiliation; I have fascination, I will be enchanted with my country, I want such a tangible form of my country that I can call her Mother, call her Goddess, call her Durga; to whom I will offer sacrificial animals and flood her with blood. I am human, I am not a god.”
Sandipbabu rose from his chair, flung his right hand towards the sky, and exclaimed, “Hurrah, hurrah!”— Then, correcting himself, he said, “Bande Mataram, Bande Mataram!”
A deep sorrow in my husband's heart cast a shadow across his face and passed away. In a very gentle voice he said,
"I am not a god either, I am a man, and that is why I said, whatever is evil in me, I shall never give it to my country—never, never, never."

Sandip Babu said, "Look, Nikhil, the truth is mingled with life itself in women, it is entirely one with them. In us, truth has no color, no flavor, no life—only logic. A woman's heart is like a lotus of blood-red petals, upon which truth sits enthroned in form; it is not formless, as it is in our arguments. That is why women alone know how to be truly cruel, men do not know it so well, for the sense of righteousness weakens men; women can bring utter ruin with ease, men can too, but hesitation of thought comes into their minds; women can commit injustice like a storm, and that injustice is terribly beautiful, while a man's injustice is ugly, for within it there is the torment of conscience. That is why I tell you, on this day, it is our women who will save our country. Today is not the day for religion, for duty, for judgment or conscience; today we must become pitiless, indifferent, and cruel, we must commit injustice, today we must welcome sin, garlanded with the red sandalwood of blood, into the hands of the women of our country. Do you not remember what our poet has said?—"

Come, sin, come, O beautiful one! Let the wine-fire of your kiss course again through my blood! Let the conch of misfortune sound, Smear my forehead with infamy, Place upon my breast the shameless, black mire of corruption, O destroyer, bring it upon me! Today, shame upon that virtue which knows not How to bring utter ruin with its own hands!

With these words, he stamped twice, hard, upon the floor—startling a cloud of sleeping dust from the carpet, which rose and settled in the air. All that mankind, in every land and every age, has revered as great—he, in a single instant, insulted it, and stood with such pride, his head thrown back, that looking upon his face, my whole body shivered with gooseflesh.

Again, he suddenly roared, “The fire that burns the home, the fire that sets the world ablaze—I see clearly now, you are the beautiful deity of that fire, you give us today the irresistible energy to be destroyed, you make our injustice beautiful!”

Those last words—whom he addressed them to, was not entirely clear. One might have thought he spoke to the one he worships as Bande Mataram, or perhaps to the woman of the nation, the representative of that Lakshmi of the land, who was then present there.

It could be thought that, just as the poet Valmiki, struck by compassion against sinful intent, suddenly uttered his first Anushtubh verse in a single moment, so too did Sandipbabu, struck by a blow of pitilessness against religious conscience, suddenly speak these words; or perhaps, in his lifelong trade of captivating the minds of the public, he gave here a remarkable display of his consummate skill in performance.
He might have said more, but just then my husband rose, gently placed his hand on Sandip’s shoulder, and said softly, “Sandip, Chandranath Babu has arrived.”

The spell was suddenly broken. I turned to see the serene figure of an elderly man standing by the door, hesitating whether to enter the room. Like the setting sun at dusk, the radiance of his face was suffused with gentleness.
My husband came to me and said, “This is my master. I have spoken to you of him many times. Offer him your respects.”
I took the dust of his feet and bowed to him.
He blessed me, saying, “Daughter, may God always protect you.”
At that very moment, I felt the need for that blessing.
chapters.summary: Bimala reflects on her mother's virtue, her own devotion as a wife, and her evolving relationship with her progressive husband, questioning tradition, love.

chapters.title: Nikhilesh: The Thorn of Doubt
paragraphs: Once, I believed that whatever God would give me, I would be able to accept. Until now, that faith had not been tested. Perhaps the time has come.

When I examined my mind in solitude, I imagined many sorrows. Sometimes I thought of poverty, sometimes of prison, sometimes of dishonor, sometimes of death. Even, at times, I tried to imagine Bimala’s death. Whenever I said that I would bow and accept all these upon my head, I do not think I was lying.
Only one thing—I could never even imagine in my mind. Today, I have sat the whole day pondering that very thing. Will I be able to bear this too?

Somewhere deep within, a thorn is lodged. I go about my work, but the pain does not cease. Perhaps, even when I sleep, that ache gnaws at my ribs. As soon as I awake in the morning, I find the radiance of daylight has withered away. What is this? What has happened? What is this darkness? Through which crack has this shadow come to fall upon my full, bright moon?

Suddenly, my mind’s faculty of perception has grown so terrifyingly acute that the sorrow which, in the past, had hidden itself deep within my heart under the guise of happiness, now tears at my very nerves, exposing all its falsehoods. And the shame, the grief, that has gathered around me—however desperately it tries to draw its veil tighter before my heart, the more its covering slips away.
My entire heart is filled with vision—things not meant to be seen, things I do not wish to see, yet I sit and watch them all.

All these years I had sat, a beggar, within the hollow of prosperity, and that truth, which I had managed to forget for so long, now suddenly, day after day, moment after moment, word after word, glance after glance, comes forth, bit by bit, revealing the misfortune of my deceived life. Why has this day come?

For these nine years of youth, I have paid rent to illusion; now, until the last moment of my life, truth will demand its dues, with interest, down to the last coin. The one whose means of repayment are utterly exhausted must bear the heaviest burden of debt. Yet, even so, may I be able to say with all my might: O Truth, victory be yours.

Yesterday, my cousin Munu’s husband, Gopal, came to seek help for his daughter’s marriage. He looked at the furnishings of my house and thought to himself that there was no one in the world as fortunate as I. I said, “Gopal,

Tell Munu that tomorrow I will go to eat at her place.” Munu has turned the poor little house into heaven with the nectar of her heart. Today, my entire being longs to taste, just once, the food prepared by that blessed hand. The very wants and lacks of her home have become her ornaments. Let me go and see her today— O pure one, the sacred dust of your feet has not yet vanished entirely from this world.

What will I achieve by forcing myself, by being proud? Let me bow my head and admit—I lack certain virtues. Perhaps I do not possess that strength which women seek most in men. But is strength only bravado, only caprice? Is strength merely this unhesitating trampling underfoot— But why argue all this? No one gains worthiness by quarreling! Unworthy, unworthy, unworthy! Let it be so— But love demands its own price— It can make even unworthiness fruitful. There are many rewards in this world for the worthy— For the unworthy, the Creator has left only this little light of love.

One day I told Bimala, You must step outside. Bimala was within my home— She was the Bimala shaped by the household, Formed by the narrow rules of small duties and a small space. The love I received from her, regularly, Was it truly the product of the deep springs of her heart, or—
Is it like the daily ration of water allotted by the steam-driven pressure of a municipal corporation?

Am I greedy? Did I desire much more than what I had received? No, I am not greedy, I am a lover. That is why I did not want the treasures locked away in an iron chest—I wanted only that which cannot be possessed unless it is given freely. I did not wish to decorate my home with paper flowers cut from the pages of the scriptures of memory; I longed to see Bimala fully blossomed in knowledge, in strength, in love, in the world.

There is one thing I did not consider then: if one wishes to see a person in their complete, liberated, and true form, one must relinquish all hope of having an absolute claim over them. Why did I not think of this? Was it the pride of a husband's perpetual possession over his wife?—No, it was not that. It was because I had absolute faith in love. I had the arrogance to believe that I could endure the wholly unveiled form of truth. Today, that is being put to the test. Whether I live or die, I shall pass this trial—this pride I still hold within me.

Until now, there is one thing Bimala has never been able to understand about me. I have always regarded force as a sign of weakness. The weak do not dare to act justly;—evading the responsibility of fairness, they hasten to injustice.

She wants to reap the fruit. After patience, Bimala has no more patience left. Within a man, she loves to see the fierce, the angry, even the unjust. Along with reverence, there seems to be a longing for fear in her heart. I had thought that, coming to a larger world, when she would see life in a broader way, she would be freed from this fascination with tyranny. But today I see that it is a part of Bimala’s very nature. Her heart’s love is drawn to the extreme. She wants to take all the simple, straightforward flavors of life and, with the fire of chili, set them ablaze from the tip of the tongue to the depths of the stomach—she almost scorns every other taste. In the same way, I have resolved that I will not, intoxicated by the harsh wine of excitement, throw myself madly into the work of the country. I would rather tolerate faults in work than beat or abuse a servant; if I am suddenly angry with someone, to say or do anything in a fit of rage causes a deep discomfort throughout my body and mind. I know Bimala inwardly disrespects this restraint of mine, calling it weakness—and today, for the same reason, she is secretly angry with me when she sees that I do not go about shouting ‘Bande Mataram’ and doing whatever I please all around. Today, in the country’s orgy of frenzy, with the cup of wine in hand, I—

Because I did not join, I have become unpopular with everyone. The people of the country think I desire a title, or that I am afraid of the police; the police think that I must have some secret plot within, and that is why I present myself as such a virtuous man outwardly. Yet, I have chosen to walk this very path of distrust and humiliation.

For I say this: those who cannot serve their country simply and truthfully, knowing it as their country, who cannot respect people simply as people, but instead shout incantations, calling the country “Mother” and “Goddess”—those who only require enchantment—their love for the country is not true love, but rather like an addiction. The effort to keep some illusion stronger than truth itself is a sign of our ingrained servility. Once the mind is set free, we lose our strength. Unless we seat some fantasy, or some person, or the system of Bhatpara itself, upon the back of our numb consciousness, it refuses to stir. As long as we do not find delight in simple truth, as long as we need such illusions, we must understand that we do not yet have the strength to possess our country in freedom. Until then, whatever our condition may be, some imaginary ghost, or some real exorcist, or both together, will continue to torment us.
That day, Sandip said to me, “You have many other virtues—”
“It may be, but you lack the faculty of imagination;—that is why you cannot see this divine image of the motherland as real.”

I saw that Bimala agreed with him. I did not reply further. There is no happiness in winning an argument. For this is not a difference of intellect, but a difference of nature. Within the narrow bounds of a small household, this difference appears in a minor form, so the harmony of union is not broken. In the larger world, the waves of this difference are greater—there, these waves do not merely make a pleasant sound, they strike and hurt.

No faculty of imagination? That is to say, in the lamp of my mind there may be oil and a wick, but the flame is lacking! I would say, rather, that the lack is yours. You are like flint, without light; that is why you must strike so hard, make so much noise, before a few sparks appear—and those scattered sparks only increase your pride, not your vision.

I have noticed for a long time that there is a certain coarseness of desire in Sandip’s nature. It is this fleshy attachment that creates his fascination with religion and drives him toward tyranny in the service of the country. His nature is coarse, but his intellect is sharp; thus, he adorns his instincts with grand names. For him, the immediate satisfaction of hatred is as urgently necessary as the gratification of pleasure.

Bimala has told me many times before that Sandip has a certain greed for money. It is not that I did not understand this, but I could never bring myself to be miserly with Sandip when it came to money. I would feel ashamed even to think that he might be deceiving me. I was afraid that my financial assistance to him might appear in an unseemly light, and so I never wished to raise any complaint about him. But today, it will be difficult to make Bimala understand that so much of Sandip’s patriotic fervor is but a transformation of that same greed. Bimala worships Sandip in her heart; thus, to say anything to her against Sandip makes my own heart shrink, as if perhaps some jealousy within me might be stirred, or perhaps I might go too far. The image of Sandip that rises in my mind may well be warped by the intense heat of my pain. Still, it is better to write it down than to let it fester in memory.

My master, Chandranath Babu—I have watched him now for nearly thirty years of my life. He fears neither slander, nor loss, nor death. In the house where I was born, no advice could have protected me—but that man, with his peace, his truth, his pure presence, entered the very center of my life.
He has established his life—because of that, I have found welfare to be so real, so tangible.
That very Chandranath Babu came to me the other day and said, “Is there any need for Sandip to stay here any longer?”

Whenever the slightest breeze of misfortune stirs anywhere, it strikes his heart—how he senses it, I do not know. He does not become agitated easily, but that day he seemed to see the shadow of a great danger before him. I know how much he loves me.
At the tea table, I said to Sandip, “Aren’t you going to Rangpur? I’ve received a letter from there—they think it’s I who have forcibly kept you here.”
Bimala was pouring tea from the teapot. In an instant, her face turned pale. She cast a fleeting glance at Sandip’s face.

Sandip said, “We have been going around everywhere, spreading the message of Swadeshi, but on reflection, I feel this is merely a wasteful expenditure of energy. It seems to me that if we work by making one place a center, our work could become much more lasting.”
Saying this, he looked at Bimala’s face and asked, “Don’t you think so too?”
At first, Bimala could not decide what answer to give. For a moment—

Later he said, “There are two ways to serve the country. One can go around working everywhere, or one can sit in one place and work—one must choose according to one’s own wish or nature. The way of working that your heart desires, that alone is your path.”

Sandip said, “Then let me speak the truth. All this time I believed that my task was to roam from place to place, stirring the whole country. But I misunderstood myself. The reason for my mistake was that I never found, in any one place, a source of power that could keep my soul always full. So I had to go from land to land, rousing new hearts, and from that excitement draw the vigor of my own life. But today, you yourself are the message of the country to me. This fire—I have never seen it in any man till now. Shame on me for having been so proud of my own strength all these days. I no longer keep the pride of being a leader of the nation. I can boldly say, I am but an instrument, and by remaining here, in the blaze of your energy, I can set the whole country alight. No, no, you must not be embarrassed—your place is far above false modesty, hesitation, or humility. You are the queen bee of our hive—we shall work around you on all sides—but the power of that work is yours alone—so your...
If we move away from it, our work will become aimless, joyless. Please, accept our worship without hesitation.
Bimala’s face flushed with both embarrassment and pride, and as she poured tea into the cups, her hand began to tremble.
One day, Chandranath Babu came again and said, “Why don’t you two go to Darjeeling for a few days? Looking at your face, I feel your health is not well. Perhaps you’re not sleeping properly?”
In the evening, I asked Bimala, “Bimala, would you like to go to Darjeeling for a trip?”
I know Bimala has always longed to see the Himalayas in Darjeeling. But that day she replied, “No, not now.”
She feared it might harm the country.
I will not lose faith, I will wait!

The road from a small place to a larger one is a stormy path;—the arrangements within the four walls of the home, within which Bimala’s life had built its nest, are not enough when she suddenly steps outside. When the unfamiliar outside becomes familiar, when an understanding is firmly established, then I will see where my place is. If I see that this

If I no longer fit anywhere within the great order of life, then I shall know that all I had embraced until now was but a deception. There is no need for such deception. If that day comes, I shall not quarrel; I shall quietly take my leave. Force, compulsion—what for? Can force ever prevail against truth?
chapters.summary: Nikhilesh grapples with growing doubts about his marriage and ideals, reflecting on Bimala's changing affections, Sandip's influence.

chapters.title: Sandip: The Marauder's Creed
paragraphs: Only that which has fallen to my share is truly mine—this is what the powerless say, and the weak listen to it. That which I can snatch away and make my own, that alone is truly mine—this is the lesson taught by the whole world.
Just because I happened to be born in this country does not make it mine—only on the day when I can seize the country by force and make it my own, will it truly become mine.

Desire is natural because the right to gain is natural. Nowhere in nature is there a command that I must be deprived of something for any reason. What the mind desires within, must be attained without—this is the contract of nature, the truth of within and without. That truth, the lesson which does not teach it, we call morality; and for this reason, mankind has never been able to truly accept morality.
There are some half-dead people in this world—those who do not know how to snatch, who cannot hold on, whose grip loosens at the slightest touch; for them, morality is a consolation—let them have it.
But those who can desire with all their heart, who can strive with all their life—

Those who know how to enjoy, who have no hesitation, they are the true favorites of Nature! For them, Nature has arranged everything beautiful, everything precious. They are the ones who will swim across rivers, scale walls, kick down doors, and snatch away what is worth having. In this lies true joy, here lies the value of precious things. Nature will surrender herself—but only to the marauder. For she loves the force of desire, the force of taking, the force of possessing—she does not wish to place the garland of her springtime bridal on the half-dead ascetic’s bony, protruding neck.

The orchestra is playing in the music room—the auspicious hour passes by, and my mind grows restless. Who is the bridegroom? He who can come with a torch in hand and claim the seat of the bridegroom, it is his. Nature’s bridegroom arrives uninvited.

Shame? No, I do not feel shame. What I need, I ask for, and even what I do not ask for, I take. Those who, out of shame, do not take what is theirs by right, they give that shame a grand name only to cover up the sorrow of their own denial. Here we are, come to this world—this is the world of reality. Those who, deceiving themselves with lofty words, leave this marketplace of things with empty stomachs and empty hands—why were they born into this solid, earthly world at all? From the pious gentlemen’s club, who would play the flute in the flowery groves of the sky, weaving sweet phrases in the air—

Did they ever beg and plead for it? I have no need for the tune of that flute, nor will my hunger be sated by those sky-flowers. What I desire, I desire with all my being. I will crush it in both hands, trample it beneath both feet, smear it over my whole body, devour it until my belly is full. I feel no shame in wanting, no hesitation in taking. Those who have grown thin and pale from fasting on principle, who have become as wan and white as the bedbugs in long-abandoned cots, their shrill-voiced reproaches will not reach my ears.

I do not wish to play at hiding, for there is cowardice in that; but if, when necessary, I cannot hide, that too is cowardice. What you desire, you wish to wall in; therefore, what I desire, I wish to tunnel out and seize. You are greedy, so you build walls; I am greedy, so I dig through them. If you use force, I will use cunning. These are the true facts of nature. Upon these truths, the kingdoms and empires of the world, the great affairs of the earth, are built and maintained. And those avatars who descend from heaven and speak in the language of that other realm—their words are not real. That is why, for all their loud proclamations, such words find place only in the corners of the weak. Those who are strong and rule the world cannot abide by them. For to abide by them is to lose strength; because—

These words are not true. Those who do not hesitate to understand this, who do not feel ashamed to admit it, they are the ones who succeed; but the unfortunate ones who, caught between nature on one side and the pressure of the Avatar on the other, set foot on two boats—one real, one unreal—sway and perish, unable to move forward, unable to survive!

There are some people who are born into this world with a vow not to live. Like the sky at sunset, there is a certain beauty in dying; they gaze at it, enchanted. Our Nikhilesh belongs to that breed—one must call him lifeless.

About four years ago, I had a heated argument with him over this very matter. He said to me, “I admit that nothing can be gained without strength, but what do you call strength, and in which direction should it be applied—that is the question. My strength lies in renunciation.”
I replied, “In other words, you are utterly intoxicated with the idea of loss.”

Nikhilesh said, “Yes, just as a bird inside an egg becomes desperate to break its shell at any cost. The shell is indeed something real, but in exchange for it, the bird gets air, gets light—in your view, perhaps, it is cheated.”
Nikhilesh speaks in such metaphors, and then—ah, it is so difficult to make him understand that even so, these are only words, not the truth; but yes, he continues with such metaphors—

Let them live in happiness if they can—we are the carnivores of the world, we have teeth, we have claws, we can run, we can seize, we can tear apart—we cannot spend our days, like cattle, grazing in the morning and ruminating till dusk; therefore, the arrangements for our sustenance in this world— if you, the keepers of fairy tales, stand guard at its doors, we shall not survive. We shall have to steal, or else rob! Otherwise, our very lives will not be spared—we are not enchanted by the love of death, ready to lie upon a lotus leaf and, in the tenth stage, surrender our breath—no matter how much our Vaishnav babajis may grieve over it!

Everyone will say of my words—oh, that is just your opinion. But the truth is, those who walk this earth do so by these very laws, yet they speak otherwise. That is why they do not know that this law itself is morality. I know it. My words are not mere theory; they have been tested in life. By the path I walk, it does not take me long to win over the hearts of women. They are creatures of the real world; unlike men, they do not ride empty balloons of ideas, wandering among the clouds. In my body, mind, words, and thoughts, they perceive a powerful will— a will that is not dried up by any asceticism, not turned away by any argument, but is utterly overflowing—

Desire, with its constant want, its insatiable hunger, has surged forth like a flood in the rainy season. Women know from within themselves that this indomitable desire is life itself. That life, because it refuses to acknowledge anyone but itself, is triumphant on all sides. Time and again I have seen women surrender themselves to this desire of mine, losing all awareness of whether they will live or die. The force by which these women are won is the very force of the hero—the power to possess the real world. Those who imagine that there is another world to be attained, let them divert the current of their desire from the earth towards the sky—let us see how high their fountain rises, and how long it endures. Women were not created for these subtle, idea-dwelling, ethereal beings.

“Affinity!” Providence has paired and matched, sending each woman and each man into the world as special counterparts, their union purer than the union of incantations—such words I have uttered in many places, as needed, at the right time. The reason is that people wish to accept nature, but unless they hide behind some phrase, they cannot be happy. Thus the world has become filled with falsehoods! Why should there be only one affinity? There are a thousand affinities. For the sake of one affinity, must all other affinities be dismissed and left aside? There is no such contract with nature. In my life I have found many affinities—
Even so, another path to attainment has not been closed. I can see it clearly—that affinity too has revealed itself to me. And after that? After that, if I cannot conquer, then I am a coward!
chapters.summary: Sandip passionately defends his creed of desire and conquest, contrasting his own aggressive philosophy with Nikhilesh’s ideals of renunciation, while reflecting on power, morality.

chapters.title: Bimala: Shame Lost and Found
paragraphs: I wonder where my sense of shame had gone.
I had not a moment to look at myself—my days and nights were whirling around me like a storm. So, in those days, shame found not the slightest gap to enter my mind.

One day, right in front of me, my elder sister-in-law, laughing, said to my husband, “Dear brother-in-law, all these years in your house it has always been the women who have wept; now it is the men’s turn, now we shall make you cry. What do you say, little queen? You have donned your battle attire, warrior maiden—now strike the man’s heart with your arrow!”

Saying this, she let her eyes travel over me from head to toe. In my dress and adornment, in my manner and movement, some new hue was shining forth from within, and not the slightest trace of it escaped my sister-in-law’s gaze. Today, I feel ashamed to write of it, but in those days I felt no shame at all. For then, my entire nature was acting from within itself—I did nothing with calculation or design.

I know that day I had dressed up a little more than usual. But it was as if absentmindedly. I could always clearly understand which of my adornments Sandipbabu especially liked. Besides, there was no need to guess; Sandipbabu would discuss it openly in front of everyone. One day, right before me, he said to my husband:

“Nikhil, the day I first saw our queen bee—sitting quietly, draped in that sari with the golden border, her eyes gazing into the infinite like two lost stars—as if, in search of something, waiting for someone, she had been looking out across the shoreless darkness for thousands upon thousands of years—then, something trembled within my heart. It seemed as though the flames of her inner fire were entwined around her, flickering along the edges of her sari. This is the fire I desire—this living, visible fire. Queen bee, I have only one request: grant us another vision of you, adorned once more in that fiery radiance.”

All these days, I had been like a small river in a village—my own rhythm, my own language. But one day, without warning, the tide of the sea swept in—my breast swelled, my banks overflowed, and to the beat of the sea’s drum, the music of my own current began to resound and surge; within the depths of my own blood
I could not grasp the true meaning of that sound at all.

Where had I gone? Suddenly, from where did this wave of beauty surge and foam within me? Sandipbabu’s two unsatisfied eyes seemed to blaze like worship lamps toward my beauty. That I am wondrous in beauty and in strength—this truth began to ring out in all of Sandipbabu’s looks and words, like the temple bells shattering the sky. That day, all other sounds of the world were drowned beneath it.

Did the Creator fashion me anew today? Did He repay, in a single stroke, all the neglect of so many years? She who was not beautiful became beautiful. She who was ordinary felt within herself the living pride of all Bengal. For Sandipbabu is not merely one man—he is like the confluence of the hearts of millions in this land. Thus, when he called me the queen bee of the hive, it was as if I was anointed that day by the chorus of all the country’s servants.

After that, the silent disdain of my elder sister-in-law in the corner of our house, and the outspoken mockery of my middle sister-in-law, could not touch me at all. My relationship with the entire world had changed.
Sandipbabu made me feel as if the whole country had urgent need of me. That day, I believed it.

There was no obstacle to doing it. I can do it, I can do everything—within me has come a divine power—something so extraordinary, something I had never felt before, something beyond my past. This sudden surge of immense emotion in my heart—what is this thing? I had no time for doubt to arise in my mind;—it seems to be mine, and yet not mine, as if it comes from outside me, as if it belongs to the whole country. It is like the floodwaters, for which no little courtyard pond is answerable.

Sandipbabu would consult me on every small matter concerning the country. At first, I felt terribly shy, but that soon passed. Whatever I said would astonish Sandipbabu. He would always say, “We men can only think, but you women can understand; you do not need to think. The Creator has made women from His mind, but men He has fashioned with His hands, hammering them into shape.” Hearing this again and again, I began to believe that within me there was a natural wisdom, a natural power, so simple that I myself had not seen it all these days.
Letters would come to Sandipbabu from all around the country, bringing various news, and I would read them all. None of them would be answered without first taking my opinion. In between...

Sometimes, on certain days, Sandipbabu would not agree with me at all. I did not argue with him. But then, after two days, it was as if he would wake up in the morning and see a light, and immediately call for me and say, “Look, what you said the other day was the truth; all my arguments were wrong.” On other days he would say, “It is exactly because I did not take your advice that I have been deceived. Well, can you explain this mystery to me?”

Gradually, I began to believe with certainty that, at the root of all the work being done in the country at that time, was Sandipbabu—and at the root of Sandipbabu, the simple wisdom of an ordinary woman. My heart swelled with the pride of such a great responsibility.

In all these discussions and counsels, my husband had no place. Just as an elder brother dearly loves his younger brother but does not trust his judgment in matters of work, Sandipbabu would express a similar attitude towards my husband. That my husband was utterly childish in these matters, that his judgment was completely contrary—Sandipbabu would say this with a deep, affectionate smile. There was such a comic flavor in all my husband’s strange opinions and reversals of judgment that it seemed as if, for this very reason, Sandipbabu...
He loved even more. That is why, with utmost affection, my mother-in-law had completely relieved my husband of all the responsibilities of the household.

In the medicine chest of Nature, there are many remedies to numb pain. When the cord of a deep relationship begins to be severed, no one knows when, deep within, those numbing medicines are supplied—until one day, upon awakening, one finds that a great dissection has already taken place.

When the knife was slicing through the greatest bond of my life, my mind was so thoroughly enveloped in the fumes of a violent emotion that I did not even realize what a cruel event was unfolding. Perhaps this is the nature of women—when their hearts are powerfully aroused in one direction, they become numb to everything else. That is why we are cataclysmic; we bring about destruction not merely with our intellect, but with our blind nature. We are like rivers: when we flow within our banks, we nurture with our whole being; but when we overflow, we destroy with that same entirety.
chapters.summary: Bimala reflects on how Sandip’s admiration transforms her sense of self, as she becomes swept up in a tide of passion and pride.

chapters.title: Sandip: Crossing the Inner Threshold
paragraphs: I can sense that some confusion has arisen. The other day, I caught a glimpse of it.

Since my arrival, Nikhilesh’s drawing room had become a sort of amphibious entity, blending the outer and the inner worlds. From the outside, I had my rights there; from the inside, Bimala faced no restrictions.

If only we had enjoyed these rights with some restraint, holding ourselves a little in check, perhaps people would have grown accustomed to it in their own way. But when a dam first breaks, the rush of water is always at its strongest. Our gatherings in the drawing room began to proceed with such intensity that all other thoughts were swept away.

When Bimala comes to the drawing room from her own quarters, I sense it in a particular way. There is the faint sound of bangles, the occasional clink of this or that. I think she opens the door with a touch more force than necessary. Then, the glass pane of the bookcase is a bit stiff; when she pulls it open, it makes a considerable noise. When I enter the drawing room, I see Bimala standing with her back to the door, at the shelf—
She is extremely particular about selecting books to her liking. Whenever I offer to help her in this difficult task, she starts in alarm and objects—then the conversation shifts to another topic.

That day, on Thursday morning, I set out from my room, prompted by the familiar sounds. Halfway along the corridor, I saw a doorman standing guard. Without paying him any heed, I proceeded—when suddenly he blocked my way and said, “Babu, you must not go that way.”
Must not go? Why?
Ranimā is in the sitting room.
Very well, go and inform your Ranimā that Sandip Babu wishes to see her.
No, that will not do, I have no orders.
I grew quite angry, raised my voice a little and said, “I am ordering you—go and ask her.”

Seeing my manner, the doorman hesitated for a moment. Then I pushed him aside and advanced towards the room. When I had almost reached the door, he, eager to fulfill his duty, rushed up, seized my hand, and said, “Babu, you must not go.”
What? Lay hands on me! I snatched my hand free and gave him a slap across the face. At that moment, Mokshi...
As soon as I stepped out of the room, I saw the doorman was about to insult me.

I shall never forget that sight. My discovery is that Makhhi is beautiful. In our country, most people would not even glance at her. Tall and slender in build—what our connoisseurs of beauty disparagingly call “lanky.” Yet it is that very tall figure that captivates me—as if a fountain of life, surging upwards with force from the secret heart of the Creator. Her complexion is dusky—but dusky like a blade of steel—what brilliance, what sharpness! That brilliance flashed across her entire face and eyes that day. Standing on the threshold, raising her forefinger, Rani said, “Nakku, go away!”
I said, “Please do not be angry—since it is forbidden, I myself will leave!”
Makhhi said in a trembling voice, “No, you will not go—come inside.”
This was no request, it was a command. I came inside, sat on a couch, and began to fan myself with a hand fan.
Makhhi wrote something with a pencil on a scrap of paper, called Behara, and said, “Take this to Babu.”
I said, “Forgive me, I could not restrain myself—I struck the doorman.”
Makhi said, “You did the right thing.”
But the poor fellow is not to blame—he was only doing his duty.
At that moment, Nikhil entered the room. I quickly rose from the couch and, turning my back to him, went and stood by the window.
Makhi said to Nikhil, “Today, Nanku the doorkeeper insulted Sandip-babu.”

Nikhil, in his usual gentle way, asked in astonishment, “Why?”—at which I could bear it no longer. I turned my face and looked straight at him. I thought, the pride of a virtuous man’s truthfulness does not stand before his wife, if the wife is of a certain kind.
Makhi said, “Sandip-babu was coming into the drawing room, and the doorkeeper blocked his way and said, ‘There is no permission.’”
Nikhil asked, “Whose permission is lacking?”
Makhi replied, “How can I say?”
In anger and distress, tears rolled down Makhi’s cheeks.
