Nikhil called for the doorkeeper. He said, “Huzoor, I am not at fault. I only obeyed orders.”
Whose orders?
The elder Rani-ma, the younger Rani-ma—they called me and gave the instructions.
For a moment, we all remained silent.
When the doorman had left, Makshi said, “We must have Noku released.”

Nikhil remained silent. I understood that his sense of justice was troubled. There was no end to his scruples. But it was a difficult problem! She was no ordinary girl. The opportunity to have Noku released was being used as a means to avenge the insult to the women.
Nikhil stayed silent. Then, from Makshi’s eyes, sparks of anger began to fly. Her hatred for Nikhil’s goodness knew no bounds.
Without a word, Nikhil got up and left the room.
The next day, the doorman was nowhere to be seen. Upon making inquiries, I learned that Nikhil had assigned him to some work in the suburbs—Doormanjii had gained rather than lost by it.
Within this brief span, how many storms had raged behind the scenes—I could sense it in hints. Again and again, only one thought comes to mind: Nikhil is a strange man, utterly unlike any other!
As a result, for some days after this, Makshi would come daily to the drawing room, have the servant call me in, and begin to converse with me—without even the pretense of necessity or accident.

In this way, through gestures and attitudes, gradually, in hints and suggestions, the unformed takes on shape, the indistinct gathers into clarity. This is the wife of the home, to the man from outside she is a being from a world of stars, utterly unattainable. Here, there is no set path.

Through this pathless void, slowly and inexorably, the pull and the knowing, the invisible currents, sweep away, one after another, the veils of custom, until at some unknown moment, they find themselves standing naked in the midst of pure nature—such is the wondrous triumphal march of truth.

Is it not truth, after all! The attraction that draws man and woman together is a real thing; from the speck of dust to the stars in the sky, the whole universe is on its side. And yet, man tries to hide it behind a few words, to claim it as his own by building walls of rules and prohibitions, to make it a possession of his household. As if one could melt down the solar system and forge a watch-chain for a son-in-law! But when the real thing awakens at the call of its own, it sweeps away all the subterfuges of man’s words in a moment, burns them to ashes, and takes its rightful place. Then, can the power of religion, the strength of faith—can any of these hold it back? Then come reproaches, lamentations, commands—but can one quarrel with a storm using only words? The storm does not answer, it only shakes; it is reality itself.

That is why I find such exquisite delight in witnessing this direct manifestation of truth before my very eyes. How much shame, how much fear, how much hesitation—if these did not exist, what flavor would remain in truth? This trembling of the feet, this turning away of the face again and again—how sweet it is! And this deception, not only towards others, but towards oneself as well. When reality must battle with unreality, deception becomes its chief weapon. For the enemy side shames the real thing, saying, “You are base.” So it must either remain hidden, or go about cloaked in illusion. In such circumstances, it cannot boldly declare, “Yes, I am base, for I am truth, I am flesh, I am instinct, I am hunger—shameless, pitiless—like that relentless stone which, swept by the torrent of rain, comes rolling down from the mountain and crashes upon the dwellings below, regardless of who may live or die thereafter!

I see everything. See how the veil is fluttering and falling; see how the ornaments of the drama are being carried along the path of destruction; see that little strip of red ribbon, so small, barely visible amidst the masses of tousled hair—a glimpse, like the greedy tongue of the nor’wester, crimsoned by the secret arousal of desire; see that subtle gesture of the border, that faint suggestion of the jacket—I can distinctly feel its heat. Yet all these arrangements are, for the most part, concealed from view.
It is happening, and it remains hidden; even the one who is doing it does not fully know.

Why does he not know? The reason is, man has always covered up reality—layer upon layer—destroying, by his own hand, the means to know and accept reality clearly. Man is ashamed of reality. Therefore, reality must work in secret, slipping through the countless veils that man himself has woven—so we cannot trace its movements, and at last, when it suddenly falls upon us, right at our neck, there is no way left to deny it. Man has tried to banish it, calling it the devil; that is why, taking the form of a serpent, it slipped into Eden, and by whispering in the ear, it opened the eyes of man's beloved and made her a rebel; from then on, there was no more peace, and after that—what else but death!

I am materialism. Naked reality today is breaking out of the prison of contemplation and coming forth into the light, and at every step my joy swells. What I desire will come very near, I will grasp it thick and whole, I will hold it tight, I will not let it go for anything—whatever lies in between will be shattered, crushed to dust, scattered in the wind—this is joy, this is joy indeed, this is the frenzied dance of reality—and after that, life or death, good or bad, happiness or sorrow, all are trivial, trivial, trivial!

My queen bee is still moving in a dreamlike trance—she does not know which path she is treading. It is not safe to suddenly awaken her and make her aware before the time is ripe. It is best that she believes I have noticed nothing. That day, as I was eating, my queen bee was gazing at my face in a certain way, as if she had entirely forgotten the meaning of such a gaze. Suddenly, when I lifted my eyes to hers, her face flushed red, and she turned her gaze away. I said, “You seem utterly astonished, watching me eat. I can hide many things, but this greed of mine is exposed at every step. See, since I myself feel no shame in it, you need not feel embarrassed on my behalf.”
She turned her head away, blushing even deeper, and began to say, “No, no, you—”

I said, “I know women love a greedy man—for it is through that very greed that women conquer them. I am greedy, and so, always pampered by women, I have reached such a state that I no longer feel the slightest trace of shame. Therefore, you may gaze in wonder as I eat; I do not care in the least. Each of these stalks I will chew until they are utterly drained and only then will I let them go—that is my nature.”

Some days ago, I was reading an English book of the present times, in which there were very clear and realistic discussions about the principles of union between man and woman. I had left that book in their sitting room. One afternoon, for some reason, as soon as I entered that room, I saw the Queen Bee sitting with that book in her hand, reading it—hearing my footsteps, she hastily covered it with another book and got up. The book she used to cover it was a volume of Longfellow’s poems.

I said, “I really don’t understand why you people feel embarrassed to read poetry books. It is the men who ought to be ashamed—after all, some of us are attorneys, some engineers; if we must read poetry, it should be at midnight, with the door shut. But you, from beginning to end, are in harmony with poetry. The Creator who made you is himself a lyric poet—Jayadeva sat at His feet and practiced his art in the ‘Lalita Lavanga Lata’.”
The Queen Bee gave no reply, only smiled and made to leave. I said, “No, that won’t do—you must sit and read. I’m just here to retrieve a book I left behind.”
I picked up my book from the table. I said, “Luckily, this book didn’t fall into your hands, or else you might have come to kill me.”
Makhi asked, “Why?”

I replied, “Why not? This is not a book of poetry. What it contains is the plain truth of human life, spoken in the simplest of terms, without any artifice. I very much wished that Nikhil would read this book.”
Makhi frowned slightly and said, “Why, tell me?”

I said, “Because he is a man, one of our own group. He always wants to see this world of the school through a haze, and that’s why I end up quarreling with him. You have seen for yourself how he treats our Swadeshi movement as if it were a poem by Longfellow—as though every word must be measured and sweetly rhythmic, that is his intention. But we go about wielding the mace of prose; we are the breakers of rhythm.”
Makhi asked, “What connection does this book have with Swadeshi?”

I replied, “You will understand once you read it. Whether it is Swadeshi or any other matter, Nikhil always wants to proceed with preconceived notions, and so at every step he clashes with the true nature of people. Then he starts blaming that very nature—he simply refuses to accept that, long before words were formed, our nature was already shaped, and long after words have ceased, our nature will still survive.”
Makhi remained silent for a while, then, in a grave tone,
He said, “Isn’t it our very nature to want to rise above our nature?”

I laughed inwardly—O Queen, this is not your own thought, this is something you have learned from Nikhilesh. You are a perfectly healthy, sensible person, savoring the essence of your own nature with delight; the moment you hear its call, your whole being—blood and flesh—responds at once. How could the spell cast upon you all these days by those whispered mantras hope to hold you fast in its web? Do I not know how the fire of life burns in every vein of yours? How much longer can the damp towel of saintly tales be wrapped around you to keep you cool?

I said, “The weak are always the majority in this world; to save themselves, they keep chanting such mantras into the world’s ear day and night, corrupting even the ears of the strong. Those whom nature has deprived and made feeble are the very ones who advise others to weaken their own natures.”
Mokhshi said, “We women are weak too; we must join in the conspiracy of the weak.”

I laughed and said, “Who says you are weak? Men, by praising you as helpless and virtuous, have shamed you into weakness. I believe it is you who are truly strong. You can break down the fortresses built by men’s mantras and become fearsome—”

…will attain liberation, I am writing this down for you. Men may shout and make noise outside, but you see their inner selves—they are, in truth, most confined beings. Until today, it is they who have forged their own scriptures with their own hands and bound themselves; with their own breath and fire, they have fashioned golden chains out of women and entwined themselves, inside and out. If men did not possess this strange power to bind themselves in their own traps, who could have held them in check till now? The very snares of their own making are the greatest objects of worship for men. They have painted them in many colors, adorned them in many guises, worshipped them by many names.
But women? You, with your bodies and your minds, have sought the reality of flesh and blood in this world, have given birth to reality, have nurtured reality.”
Mokhi is an educated woman; she does not easily give up an argument. She said, “If that were true, then could men ever truly desire women?”

I replied, “Women know well the danger—they know that men, by nature, love deception; that is why women borrow words from men themselves and, donning the mask of illusion, try to beguile them. They know that men, intoxicated by nature, are drawn more to wine than to food; so, by various means and gestures, they try to pass themselves off as wine, while concealing as much as possible the fact that they are, in truth, sustenance.”
Women are materialists, in truth; they do not require any apparatus of illusion—the various arrangements of enchantment are all for men. Women have become enchantresses only out of necessity.”
Makhi said, “Then why do you wish to break this enchantment?”

I replied, “Because I desire freedom—freedom for my country, and freedom in my relationships with people. My country is intensely real to me, so I cannot allow any haze of moralistic rhetoric to obscure it, even slightly. I am intensely real to myself, you are intensely real to me, and therefore I do not at all like the business of scattering mere words in between, making people remote and incomprehensible to one another.”

I felt that it is nothing to startle a man who is walking in his sleep. But my nature is untamable; moving slowly and cautiously is not my way. I know that the manner and tone in which I spoke that day were bold—perhaps too bold. I know the first blow of such words can be hard to bear—but with women, it is the bold who win. Men love the smoke, while women love the substance—that is why men run to worship the incarnations of their own ideals, and women bring all their offerings and lay them at the feet of the strong.

Just as our conversation was beginning to heat up, Nikhilesh’s childhood tutor, Chandranath Babu, appeared in our room. On the whole, the world is quite a pleasant place, but the nuisance of these tutors makes one wish to pack up and leave it altogether. People like Nikhilesh want to turn this whole existence into a school until their dying day. He has grown older, yet the school still follows him doggedly; when he enters the world, the school enters with him. Truly, at the time of death, one ought to drag the schoolmaster along to the funeral pyre.

That day, in the midst of our conversation, that embodiment of the school appeared at an inopportune moment. I suppose, in all of us, there remains somewhere within a little corner where a student still resides. Even I, such a hardened rogue as I am, was suddenly brought up short. And our queen bee—at the very sight of him, it seemed she instantly became the best student in the class, sitting up straight in the front row, grave and attentive—as if she suddenly remembered her duty to pass the tests of this world.
Certain people are like railway pointsmen, sitting by the tracks; they can, with a casual motion, switch the train of thought from one line to another.
Chandranath Babu, upon entering the room, seemed hesitant and tried to withdraw—"Forgive me, I—" he began, but before he could finish, our queen bee bowed at his feet in respectful greeting.

And then he said, “Mastermoshai, don’t go, please stay.”— It was as if he had fallen into deep water, seeking refuge with Mastermoshai. Coward! Or perhaps I am misunderstanding. Perhaps there is some cunning within this. A desire to increase his own worth. Perhaps he wants to ostentatiously let me know: you think you have overwhelmed me! But I respect Chandranathbabu far more than I do you! Don’t do that. One must, after all, respect people like Mastermoshai. But I am not a Mastermoshai—I do not crave empty reverence. I have already said, empty words will not fill my stomach;—I recognize substance.

Chandranathbabu brought up the topic of the Swadeshi movement. I wanted to let him speak on uninterrupted, without offering any reply. It is best to let old men talk—then they feel as if they themselves are turning the wheels of the world—poor souls, they do not realize that while their tongues move in one direction, the world moves far away from them. At first, I remained silent for a while—but even his worst enemies could not accuse Sandipchandra of possessing patience. When Chandranathbabu said, “Look, we have never farmed, and if we now expect to reap a harvest immediately—”
I could not restrain myself—I said, “We do not seek the harvest. We say, ‘Ma phaleshu kadachana.’”
Chandranath Babu was astonished—he said, “Then what do you all want?”
I said, “Thorn bushes—plants that require no expense to cultivate.”
Mastermoshai said, “Thorn bushes not only block others’ paths, they also litter your own.”

I replied, “That is a maxim for teaching in schools. We are not writing proverbs on the board with chalk in hand. Our hearts are burning now—that is what matters most. Now, we will plant thorns on the path, keeping in mind the soles of others’ feet—later, when they prick our own feet, we can calmly repent. Is that really too much? When the time comes to die, there will be time to cool down; but when it is the age of burning, then restlessness is only fitting.”

Chandranath Babu smiled slightly and said, “If you wish to be restless, then be so, but do not think of that as heroism or achievement and thus try to save yourself. The nations that have saved your own did not fidget—they acted. Those who have always seen work as a tiger, when they suddenly wake from sleep, imagine that by rushing down the wrong path of inaction, they will quickly cross the world.”
Just as I was girding myself to give a sharp reply, Nikhil entered. Chandranath Babu rose and the Mukhi—
Looking around, he said, “I must go now, mother, I have work to do.”
As soon as he left, I showed Nikhil that English book of mine and said, “I was telling the Queen Bee about this book.”

One has to deceive fifteen and a half annas out of sixteen of the world’s people with lies, but this eternal schoolmaster’s pupil is most easily deceived by the truth. Only when you let Nikhil be deceived knowingly does he truly get deceived. That is why the game of hide-and-seek is the best game to play with him.
Nikhil read the title of the book and remained silent.

I said, “Man has made this world of his own habitation so obscure with so many words, and these writers, with broom in hand, sweep away the dust from above to reveal the substance within more clearly; that is why I said, it would be good to read this book.”
Nikhil said, “I have read it.”
I asked, “What do you think?”
Nikhil replied, “For those who wish to seek the truth with books like this, it is good—for those who wish to deceive, it is poison.”
I asked, “What do you mean by that?”
Nikhil said, “Look, in today’s society, the man who—”

If someone says that no person has an absolute right to their own property, such words suit only the lips of one who is truly free from greed—but if by nature he is a thief, then those words from his mouth are utter falsehood. If the instinct is strong, then the real meaning of these books will never be grasped.

I said, “Instinct is like nature’s gas lamp, by whose light we find our way along these streets. Those who call instinct false are like people who gouge out their own eyes in the vain hope of gaining divine sight.”

Nikhil said, “I only accept instinct as truth when, at the same time, I also accept restraint as truth. If you try to see something by pressing it into your eye, you destroy the eye itself, and see nothing. Those who wish to see everything solely through the lens of instinct distort instinct itself, and cannot see the truth either.”

I said, “Look, Nikhil, viewing life through the gold-rimmed spectacles of morality is just a kind of mental snobbery for you—that’s why, when it comes to action, you see reality blurred, and you can never do anything with real force.”
Nikhil replied, “I do not call it ‘action’ merely to do something with force.”
Then what?
What is the use of arguing over falsehoods? If one goes on discussing such matters in vain, their beauty is lost.

I had wished that Makhi would join in our debate. Until now, she had sat silently without uttering a single word. Perhaps today I have stirred her heart a little more than usual. That is why a hesitation has arisen within her—she feels the urge to clarify her lesson with the schoolmaster.

Who knows if today’s lesson has been somewhat excessive. But it is necessary to give a good shake. That which the mind has always considered immovable and has rested assured in, it is essential to know from the beginning that it can indeed be shaken.
I said to Nikhil, “It is good that I spoke with you. I was almost about to let the Queen of the Bees read this book.”

Nikhil replied, “What harm is there in that? If I have read the book, why should not Bimala read it as well? I only have one thing to explain. Nowadays, in Europe, people are examining everything from the perspective of science—discussions proceed as if man is merely a subject of physiology, or biology, or psychology, or at most sociology—but do not forget, for heaven’s sake, that man is not a mere theory, that man, surpassing all theories, stretches himself toward the infinite. You tell me,
I am the schoolmaster’s pupil—not I, but you all are. You want to understand people through the science master’s eyes— not through the voice of your own soul.”
I said, “Nikhil, why are you so agitated these days?”
He replied, “Because I can clearly see that you are belittling people, insulting them.”
Where do you see this?
In the air, in my pain. The one who is greatest among men, the ascetic, the beautiful—him you wish to make weep to death!
What nonsense is this, your madness!

Nikhilesh suddenly stood up and said, “Listen, Sandip, I firmly believe that man will suffer mortal sorrow, but still will not die. That is why I am prepared to endure everything—knowingly, consciously, with full understanding.”
Saying this, he left the room and went out.

I was watching his behavior in astonishment when suddenly, at the sound of something, I saw two or three books fall from the table onto the floor, and the Queen Bee, with swift steps, walked past me at a little distance.
Strange man, that Nikhilesh—he understands well enough that a danger is gathering within his home, yet still he forces me—

Why doesn’t she just say goodbye and be done with it? I know she is waiting, waiting to see what Bimala will do. Only if Bimala tells her, “There is no bond between us,” will she lower her head and softly say, “Then it seems there has been a mistake.” But to admit a mistake as a mistake is the greatest mistake of all—she does not have the strength to understand this. How feeble an idea can make a person—Nikhil is a direct example of that. I have never seen another man like him—he is truly a whim of nature. You cannot even spin a story or a play around someone like him, let alone build a home.

And then there is Makshi—it seems today her trance has broken. She has suddenly realized which current she has been swept away by. Now, knowingly, she must either return or go forward. But no, from now on she will sometimes advance, sometimes retreat. That does not concern me.

When a cloth catches fire, the more you run about in fear, the more fiercely the fire blazes. It is the shock of fear that makes the heart’s passion burn even stronger. I have seen this before. Remember that widow Kusum, who, trembling with fear, finally surrendered herself to me? And that English girl who lived near our hostel—she would get angry with me; some days it seemed she would tear me apart in her rage. I still remember that day—

I remember well the day she screamed at me, shouting “Go, go!” and forcibly drove me out of the room. But no sooner had I set foot across the threshold than she rushed to me, clung to my feet, and, weeping, began to beat her head on the floor until she fell unconscious. I know their kind very well—call it anger, fear, shame, or hatred—all of these only serve as fuel to fan the fire in their hearts, until it burns itself to ashes. The only thing that can control this fire is the Ideal. Women have no such thing. They perform rituals, go on pilgrimages, prostrate themselves at the feet of their gurus—just as we go to the office—but they never approach the Ideal. I will not say much to her directly—not now. I will give her some English books of the present age to read. Gradually, she will come to understand, more and more clearly, that to acknowledge and respect instinct as reality is what is modern. To be ashamed of instinct, to value restraint above all—that is not modern. If she can take refuge in this word “modern,” then she will gain strength—for they need pilgrimages, they need gurus, they need fixed customs—only the Ideal is empty to them.
Anyway, let this drama play out to the fifth act. I cannot boastfully declare that I am merely a spectator, sitting in the royal seat above, occasionally only—

I am applauding. There is a pull within my chest, now and then the veins throb with pain. At night, when I turn off the lamp and lie down on the bed, the slightest touch, the faintest desire, the smallest word fills the darkness and keeps circling round and round. In the morning, upon waking, a thrill shimmers within my mind—it seems as if, along with my blood, a stream of melody is flowing through my whole being.

On the photo-stand atop this table, beside Nikhilesh’s photograph, there used to be a picture of Makshi. I had removed that photograph. Yesterday, showing Makshi that empty space, I said, “It is the miser’s fault that theft occurs; therefore, the sin of this theft should rightly be shared between the miser and the thief. What do you say?”
Makshi smiled a little and said, “That photograph wasn’t very good, anyway.”
I replied, “What can be done? A photograph can never be better than the image itself. We must be content with what we have.”
Makshi opened a book and began turning its pages. I said, “If you are angry, I will somehow fill up that empty space.”
Today, I have filled that space. This photograph of mine is from my younger days—the face in it is still unformed, the mind was like that too.

In those days, I used to believe in many things—of this world and the next. Faith may deceive, it is true, but it has one great virtue: it lends a certain grace to the mind. Beside Nikhilesh’s portrait, my own remained—two friends, side by side.
chapters.summary: Sandip navigates the tense boundaries of Nikhilesh’s home, clashing with servants and customs, while growing increasingly captivated by Bimala.

chapters.title: Nikhilesh: The Weight of Marriage
paragraphs: Never before have I thought about myself. Now, quite often, I find myself observing myself from the outside. I try to see myself through Bimala’s eyes—how does she perceive me? I am deeply serious by nature—it is my habit to view everything with excessive gravity.

But truly, is it not better to laugh away life than to drown it in tears? That is how it goes on. All the sorrow scattered throughout the world, within and without the home, we so easily brush aside in our minds, like shadows, like illusions, and thus we dance and feast without care. If, for even a single moment, I could hold that sorrow as real, could look upon it as truth—would I still have an appetite for food, would sleep remain in my eyes?

Only myself—I cannot see myself among those who so easily let things drift away. It seems to me that my sorrow alone has settled upon the world’s heart as an eternal burden. That is why I am so grave—why, when I look within, my chest is flooded with tears...
O wretched one, stand once in the open court of the world and measure yourself against all others. There, across the ages...

In the vast fair, amidst the crowd of millions, Bimala—who is she to you? She is your wife! Whom do you call your wife? That very word, which you have been inflating with your own breath, tending it day and night—do you know, if a single pin pricks it from outside, in a moment all the air will escape and it will collapse entirely!

My wife—therefore she is mine! But if she wishes to say, no, I am my own self—then at once I protest, how can that be, you are my wife! Wife! Is that an argument, is that a truth? Can a living person be locked up, sealed away, from head to toe, within that single word?

Wife! Into this word I have poured all that is sweet in my life, all that is sacred, and made it human within my heart; never, not for a single day, have I cast her down into the dust. How much incense of worship, how many notes of the Sahana flute, how many bakul blossoms of spring, how many shefali flowers of autumn have I offered to that name! If today, like a paper boat, she suddenly sinks into the muddy water of the gutter, then with her—there, you see, again this gravity! Whom do you call gutter, whom do you call muddy water? Those are words of anger. Just because you are angry, the world will not change. If Bimala is not yours, then she is not yours—no matter how much you press or rage, the more you do so, the more that very truth will be proven. The heart may break—let it. But by that, the world—

It will not go bankrupt, not even you will go bankrupt. Whatever a person loses in life, he himself is far greater than all of it—there is a shore even beyond the ocean of all tears—that is why he weeps; otherwise, he would not weep at all.

But from the perspective of society—let society’s thinkers ponder such matters, let them do what must be done. I am weeping my own tears, not the tears of society. If Bimala says she is not my wife, then let my social wife remain wherever she may; I take my leave.

Sorrow, of course, is there. But one sorrow would be a great falsehood, and I shall save myself from it however I can. Like a coward, I cannot think that my life’s worth has diminished because I am unloved. My life has value—by that value I have not come merely to purchase the inner chambers of my own house. My greater enterprise—this can never go bankrupt, and today is the day to think upon this truth with utmost seriousness.

Today, just as I must see myself, so too must I see Bimala entirely from the outside. All these days, I had adorned Bimala with some precious ideals of my own mind. In the world, Bimala did not always fit with the image I had crafted in my heart, yet still I worshipped her within my imagination.

That is not my virtue, it is my greatest flaw. I am greedy—I wished to enjoy, in my mind, that ideal woman, that Tilottama of my imagination—the outer Bimala merely became the occasion for it. Bimala is what she is—there is no necessity that, for my sake, she must become Tilottama. Is Vishwakarma to labor solely at my command?

Therefore, today I must see everything clearly, once and for all. All those variegated images I have painted in the colors of illusion—I will now wipe them away, firmly and completely. For so long, there were many things I saw and yet refused to see. Today, I have understood plainly that in Bimala’s life, I am but an accident; the one with whom Bimala’s entire nature can truly unite is Sandip. This much knowledge is enough for me.

For today, even before myself, there is no room for false humility. There are many qualities in Sandip that are alluring, and by those very qualities he has drawn me too, all this while. But, even if I speak with the utmost restraint, I must confess to myself today that, on the whole, he is not greater than I. If, in this assembly of self-choice, the garland is not placed around my neck, if Sandip is the one to receive it, then in this neglect let the deity who bestowed the garland be the judge—not I. Today, this is not a matter of pride for me. Today, unless I know and accept my own worth in the deepest truth within myself—
If I must accept today’s blow as the ultimate humiliation of my human existence, then I shall fall like refuse into the dust-heap of the world, and nothing more will ever be accomplished through me.

Therefore, even amidst all this unbearable sorrow, let a joy of liberation awaken within my heart. Now I have come to know—both the outer world and my own inner self. Having settled all gains and losses, what remains is myself. And that self is not a crippled me, not a poverty-stricken me; not the me made feeble by the sickroom diet of the inner quarters, but the me forged by the strong hand of the Creator. What was to happen has happened; now nothing can destroy it.
Just now, Mastermoshai came to me, placed his hand on my shoulder, and said, “Nikhil, go to bed, it’s one o’clock.”

It is very difficult for me to go to bed unless Bimala has fallen into a deep sleep late at night. During the day, we meet and speak as usual—but in the silent solitude of the night, what can I say to her? My whole body and mind are overcome with shame.
I asked Mastermoshai, “Why haven’t you gone to sleep yet?”
He smiled a little and said, “My time for sleep is past; now is the time to be awake.”

I had written up to this point and was about to go to bed, when suddenly, in the sky outside my window, the monsoon clouds parted at one spot—and through that opening, a great star began to shine, bright and clear. It seemed to say to me: So many relationships are being woven and unwoven like dreams—but I remain steadfast; I am the eternal lamp of the bridal chamber, the everlasting kiss of the night of union.

In that moment, my whole heart filled to the brim, and I felt—behind the veil of this worldly existence, my beloved of eternity sits waiting, unmoving. Through so many births, in so many mirrors, I have glimpsed her image—mirrors broken, mirrors warped, mirrors clouded with dust. Whenever I say, “Let me claim this mirror as my own, let me lock it away in a box,” at that very instant, the image slips away. Let it be—what matter if it is my mirror, or the image itself! Beloved, your faith remains unbroken, your smile will not fade, the line of vermilion you have drawn at your hair parting for me is made radiant by the dawn of each new day.

In a corner of the darkness, a devil stands and says, “These are just tales to fool children.” Well, let it be so—children must be lulled, after all—countless children, millions of children, one after another...

Children—how many children, how many tears! Can so many children be pacified with falsehoods? My beloved will not deceive me—that is true, that is true—this is why I have looked at her again and again, and will look at her again and again—even through mistakes I have seen her, even through the thick mist of tears she could be seen. In the crowd of the marketplace of life I have seen her, lost her, and seen her again; even after passing through the tunnel of death, I will see her again. O cruel one, mock me no more—on the path where your footprints have fallen, in the air filled with the scent of your loose hair, if now I have lost my way, then do not let that mistake make me weep forever. That unveiled star tells me, no, no, do not fear, what is meant to remain forever, remains forever.

Now let me go and see my Bimala—she is lying on the bed, asleep. Without waking her, I leave a kiss on her forehead. That kiss is my offering of worship. I believe that after death I will forget everything else, all mistakes, all tears—but the vibration of the memory of this kiss will remain somewhere—for, birth after birth, the garland of these kisses is being strung together to be placed around the neck of that beloved.
At such a moment, into my room came my middle sister-in-law and—
It struck two o’clock. At that moment, our watchman’s clock sounded with a resonant “dong, dong”—two times.
“Thakurpo, what are you doing? Dear brother, go to bed—don’t torment yourself like this. I cannot bear to see what has become of your face!”
As she spoke, tears began to fall, drop by drop, from her eyes.
Without saying a word, I bowed to her, touched the dust of her feet, and went to bed.
chapters.summary: Nikhilesh reflects on his identity and the meaning of marriage, grappling with his sorrow over Bimala's emotional distance.

chapters.title: Bimala: Ecstasy of Ruin
paragraphs: At first, I suspected nothing, feared nothing; I believed I was surrendering myself to the country. What an overwhelming ecstasy there is in complete surrender! That day, for the first time, I discovered that the greatest joy lies in one’s own ruin.

I do not know—perhaps, in this way, through a vague emotion, this intoxication might have faded away by itself one day. But Sandipbabu could not let that happen; he made himself so vivid, so unmistakably present. The cadence of his words seemed to touch me, to brush against me; the gaze of his eyes seemed to beg at my feet. Yet within all this, there was such a terrible force of will, as if he were a ruthless bandit, seizing me by the hair and dragging me away.

I will speak the truth: this tempestuous incarnation of desire pulled at my heart day and night. It began to seem so alluring—to utterly destroy myself! How much shame, how much fear there was in it, yet how piercingly sweet!
And there was no end to my curiosity—about a man I did not truly know, a man I could not be certain of, a man whose...

Power is immense—the mystery of the turbulent desire of a man whose youth blazes with a thousand flames—how fierce, how vast it is! I could never have imagined it. The sea that was once far away, whose name I had only heard on the pages of books—now, in a ravenous flood, crossing all barriers in between, it surged and crashed at my very feet, where I wash dishes and draw water at the back steps, spilling its foam before me, laying its infinity at my feet!

At first, I began to revere Sandipbabu, but that reverence was swept away—I do not respect him, in fact, I even feel a kind of disrespect for him. I have understood very clearly that he cannot be compared to my husband. And this too, if not at first, then gradually I have come to know—that what seems like manliness in Sandip is nothing but restlessness.

Yet, this veena of mine, fashioned from my own flesh and blood, my thoughts and feelings, began to play in his hands. I want to hate that hand, and this veena as well—but the veena played on. And when my days and nights became filled with that music, then compassion and mercy deserted me. In the depths of that melody, my every nerve, every wave of my blood, told me: you too must be swept away, and let everything that is yours be swept away as well.
There is no longer any doubt in my mind that there is something within me—what shall I call it!—for which I feel it would be better if I were dead.

Whenever Mastermoshai finds a little time, he comes and sits with me. He has a certain power; he can place the mind upon such a peak that, from there, I can see the entire circumference of my life enlarged in an instant—what I had always thought to be a boundary, I see then is no boundary at all.

But what of it! I do not even wish to see things in that way. The intoxication that has seized me—I cannot truly wish for it to leave me. Let the sorrows of the world come, let the truth within me wither and die moment by moment in darkness, but this intoxication of mine—may it remain forever—this wish I cannot relinquish in any way. When my sister-in-law Monu’s husband used to beat her after drinking, then, overcome with remorse, would weep and wail, swear he would never touch liquor again, yet the very next evening would return with drink in hand—I used to burn with anger and disgust at the sight.

Now I see that my own drunkenness is even more terrible—this is not a drink that must be bought, not something to be poured into a glass—it is something that arises on its own from within my blood. What am I to do! Is life to pass in this way?

At times I startle and look at myself, wondering if I am nothing but a nightmare from beginning to end—perhaps, suddenly, I shall discover that this “I” is not real. How terribly incoherent this is, how the end bears no resemblance to the beginning—like a magician’s illusion, where dark stains are painted over in the colors of the rainbow. What has happened to me, how did it happen—I cannot understand any of it.

One day, my second sister-in-law came and laughed, saying, “Our little queen has her own talents! Such care for the guest, though she never wants to stir an inch from the house. In our time, too, there was a guest room, but never so much pampering for the guest—back then, it was customary to look after the husband as well. Poor brother-in-law, he was simply born in the wrong age, that’s why he’s been cheated. He should have come to this house as a guest; then perhaps he could have lasted a little longer—but now, I doubt it very much. Little ogress, have you ever looked at his face to see what state it’s in?”

Once, such words would have shamed me; back then, I thought they simply could not understand the vow I had taken. There was an aura of purpose around me then—I believed I was sacrificing my life for my country, that I had no need for shame or modesty.
For some days now, talk of the country has ceased. Now—

Discussions, the relationships between men and women in modern times, and a thousand other topics. Amidst all this, there was the introduction of English poetry and Vaishnava songs—woven through all these poems ran a certain strain, a note struck on a very thick string. I had never tasted this note in my own home before—it seemed to me, this was the note of manliness, the note of strength.

But today, there was no more concealment—why Sandipbabu spent day after day here without any apparent reason, why I, too, found myself conversing with him at all hours without any real necessity, there was no longer any answer to these questions.
So that day, in anger at myself, at my middle sister-in-law, at the entire arrangement of the world, I declared, "No, I will not go to the outer rooms anymore—not even if I die."

For two days, I did not go outside. In those two days, for the first time, I clearly understood how far I had come. It seemed as though the very taste of life had vanished. I felt an urge to throw everything away, to push it all aside. It seemed as if someone was waiting for me—from the hair on my head to the nails on my toes—as if all the blood in my body was listening, with its ear pressed to the outside world.
I tried very hard to keep myself busy with work. My

The floor of the bedroom was quite clean—yet I stood there myself, pouring jar after jar of water to have it scrubbed again. The things inside the almirah were arranged in a certain way, but I took everything out, dusted and shook them, and rearranged them differently for no reason at all. That day, it was two o’clock before I managed to bathe.

That afternoon, I did not even have time to do my hair; somehow, I twisted my loose hair into a knot, and then set the household staff into a flurry, making them tidy up the storeroom. I discovered, in the meantime, that much had already been stolen from the pantry—but I did not dare to rebuke anyone, lest someone, even in their heart, should retort, “Where have your eyes been all this time?”

That day passed in such a frenzy, as if possessed by a ghost. The next day, I tried to read a book. I cannot recall what I read, but time and again I found myself, absentmindedly, wandering about with the book in my hand, standing silently by the window that opened onto the path leading from the inner quarters to the outside. From there, I could see the row of outer rooms on the north side of the courtyard. Among them, one room seemed to have drifted away to the far shore of the ocean of my life. No boat would ever ferry me there again. I gazed and gazed, unable to look away. It felt as if I were the ghost of my former self from bygone days—present in all those places, and yet not there at all.
At one point, I saw Sandip with a newspaper in his hand...

Taking it in his hand, he stepped out from the room onto the verandah. I could clearly see a strange agitation on his face. At times, it seemed as if he was growing angry at the courtyard, at the railings of the verandah themselves. He flung the newspaper away—as if, had he been able, he would have torn away a piece of the sky itself. His resolve could not hold. Just as I was about to go towards the drawing room, suddenly I saw—standing behind me was my second sister-in-law! “Oh, you startled me!”—saying this, she walked away. I did not go outside.
The next morning, Govinda’s mother came and said, “Choto-ranima, it’s time to give out the provisions.”

I replied, “Tell them to bring Harimoti out.” Saying this, I tossed the bunch of keys aside and sat by the window, beginning to work on my English embroidery. Just then, a servant came and handed me a letter, saying, “Sandip Babu sent this.”—There is no end to his audacity;—what must the servant have thought? My heart began to tremble as I opened the letter and saw there was no salutation, only these few words—“Very important. For the country’s work. Sandip.”
My embroidery lay abandoned. I quickly stood before the mirror and straightened my hair a little. The sari remained as it was, but I changed my jacket.
I know that, in her eyes, this jacket carries a particular association with me.

The veranda through which I must go outside—there, as usual, sits my second sister-in-law, slicing betel nuts with her customary precision. Today, I felt no hesitation at all. My second sister-in-law asked, “Well, where are you off to?”
I replied, “To the drawing room.”
“So early in the morning? Is there some family gathering?”
Without answering, I walked away. My second sister-in-law began to sing—
“When my Radha goes away, she swoons and falls! Like the crocodile in the fathomless waters, She knows not the taste of mere sugar!”
chapters.summary: Bimala is swept up in a storm of desire and restlessness as Sandip's presence intensifies her inner conflict, leading her to question her identity.

chapters.title: Bimala: Between Pride and Humility
paragraphs: When I entered the drawing room, I saw Sandip sitting with his back to the door, deeply engrossed in a book—a catalogue of paintings exhibited at the British Academy. Sandip considers himself quite the connoisseur of art. One day, my husband told him that if artists ever needed a guru, as long as Sandip was alive, there would be no shortage of suitable candidates.
It is not my husband’s nature to make such pointed remarks, but lately his temperament has changed a little—he never misses a chance to prick Sandip’s pride.
Sandip said, “Do you think artists no longer need to be made into disciples?”
My husband replied, “People like us will always have to keep learning new lessons from artists about art, because there is no single, fixed lesson in this field.”
Sandip laughed heartily, mocking my husband’s humility. He said, “Nikhil, you think poverty itself is the greatest asset—the more you invest it, the more your wealth will grow. But I say,
He who has no pride is like moss upon the current, drifting aimlessly on all sides.”

My mind was in a strange state. On one hand, I wished that my husband would win the argument, that Sandip’s pride would be humbled a little. Yet, it was precisely Sandip’s unabashed pride that drew me—like the dazzling sparkle of a precious diamond, it could never be shamed; it would not even concede defeat to the sun itself, rather, its defiance would only grow stronger.

I entered the room. I knew Sandip had heard the sound of my footsteps, but he pretended not to, and kept his eyes fixed on the book as if engrossed. I was afraid he might begin to speak of art again. For, under the pretext of art, Sandip loved to discuss with me certain pictures and their meanings, and I had not yet grown accustomed to such conversations without feeling embarrassed. To hide my embarrassment, I had to pretend that there was nothing in it to be ashamed of.
So, for a moment, I thought of turning back—when suddenly Sandip heaved a deep, heavy sigh, raised his face, and, catching sight of me, seemed to start in surprise. He said, “Ah, so you have come!”
In his words, in the tone of his voice, in his eyes, there was a subtle reproach. I was in such a state that I accepted even that reproach. The claim Sandip had come to have over me...
Even my absence for two or three days seems to be a crime!
I know that this grievance of Sandip is, in truth, an insult to me, but where is the strength in me to be angry?

Without giving any reply, I remained silent. Although I was looking away, I could feel clearly that Sandip’s two eyes, full of complaint, were as if sitting right before my face, refusing to move. What a situation this is! Sandip picks up some topic, and I try to hide behind it for a little shelter! Perhaps five or ten minutes passed in this way, when the embarrassment became unbearable, and then I said, “Did you call me for something important?”

Sandip, slightly startled, replied, “Why, must there always be some necessity? Is friendship a crime? Is the greatest thing in the world to be treated with such neglect? Must the worship of the heart be driven away from the door like a stray dog, Queen of the Bees?”

My heart began to tremble within me. Danger is drawing ever closer, and now it cannot be held back. In my mind, both thrill and fear rose up equally. How am I to bear this burden of disaster upon my back? Must I fall, face down, upon the dust of the road?
My hands and feet were trembling. I tried to be very strong
Standing before him, I said, “Sandipbabu, you called me here saying you had some work for the country, so I have left my household duties behind.”

He smiled slightly and said, “That is exactly what I was telling you. Do you know, I have come here for worship? Have I not told you that in you I see the very strength of my country made manifest? A description of geography is not a real thing—can anyone give their life merely remembering that map? It is only when I see you before me that I understand how beautiful, how beloved, how vibrant with energy my country is! Only when you yourself place the mark of victory upon my forehead with your own hand will I know I have received my country’s command. Then, if I fall to the ground pierced by the arrow of death, fighting and remembering that command, I will know that it is not just the soil of a geographical description—it is a piece of cloth, an anchal. Do you know what kind of anchal? The other day, the sari you were wearing—the color of red earth, and its broad border red as a stream of blood—that anchal of that sari—can I ever forget it! These are the things that make life vibrant, that make death beautiful.”
As Sandip spoke, his eyes began to blaze. Whether that fire in his eyes was hunger or worship, I could not tell.

I remembered that day when I first heard his speech. That day, I had forgotten whether he was a man or a flame of fire. With ordinary people, one can interact in ordinary ways—there are many rules and conventions for that; but fire belongs to another kind altogether, it dazzles the eyes in an instant, it makes even destruction appear beautiful. It seems as if the truth, which had been hidden in the neglected, dry wood of daily life, has today assumed its radiant form and is rushing forth in wild laughter to burn up all the misers’ hoarded treasures around it.

After that, I had no strength left to say anything. I was afraid that at any moment Sandip would rush over and seize my hand. For his hands trembled like restless tongues of flame, and his gaze fell upon me like a burning brand.

Sandip exclaimed, “Will you magnify every little rule and restriction? Do you possess such a spirit, that with a mere hint of it, we can make life and death seem trivial—is that to remain hidden behind the veils of the inner quarters? Today, feel no more shame, pay no heed to the whispers of others—today, snap your fingers at all prohibitions and come rushing out into the midst of freedom!”
In this way, as Sandip Babu’s words mingled with the hymns to the country...

My hymn merges and dissolves—then the bonds of shyness can hold no longer, then a dance stirs in my blood. As long as it was all about art and Vaishnava poetry, and the analysis of the relationship between man and woman, and the debate between the real and the unreal, my mind was growing dark with shame. Today, in the blackness of that coal, fire has been kindled once more—that very radiance has dispelled my embarrassment. It seemed to me that being a woman was, in itself, a wondrous, divine glory.

Alas! Why does that glory not shine forth from my hair at this very moment, like a visible flame? Why does no word rise from my lips now, a word that, like a mantra, could instantly initiate the whole country into a baptism of fire?
Just then, wailing loudly, Khema the maid burst into my room. She said, "Pay me my wages, let me go, I cannot stay here another lifetime—howl, howl! Howl, howl!"
What? What is the matter?
The Majorani’s maid, for no reason at all, had picked a quarrel with Khema—she had hurled whatever insults came to her mouth.
No matter how much I said, "All right, I will look into it," Khema’s tears would not stop.

In the morning, the melody of the Dipak raga had gathered such intensity, and now it felt as if water used for washing dishes had been poured over it. A woman is like a lotus in a pond, but now the mud beneath had been stirred up. To quickly cover this up from Sandip, I had to rush at once into the inner quarters. There I saw my middle sister-in-law sitting on the veranda, head bent in concentration, slicing betel nuts—her lips touched by a faint smile, humming softly, “Rai is about to leave me and go”—there was not the slightest sign on her face that any calamity had occurred anywhere.
I said, “Mejorani, why do you let Khema scold you so needlessly?”

She raised her eyebrows in surprise and said, “Oh, really? Is that so? I’ll thrash the wretch and drive her out. Look, look what she’s done, ruining your morning sitting room gathering. And Khema’s sense, too—she knows her mistress is talking a little with the gentleman from outside, and yet she barges right in—completely shameless, sitting there as if nothing’s wrong. But Chotorani, you don’t bother yourself with these household matters, you go outside, I’ll settle everything as best I can.”

How strange is the human mind! In a single moment, the wind in its sails can so utterly change direction! This very morning, leaving aside household affairs, to sit and converse with Sandip in the drawing room—
To go—such an act seemed so utterly out of keeping with the ideals I had always cherished in the seclusion of my inner apartments, that I gave no reply and quietly returned to my room.

I am certain that, at the right moment, Mejo-rani herself had instigated Khema to quarrel, pressing her to do so. But I am in such a precarious state these days that I cannot bring myself to speak of any of this. Only the other day, in the heat of the moment, I quarreled with my husband so insolently over the matter of dismissing Nonu, the gatekeeper—but in the end, it did not last. Soon enough, my own agitation brought a sense of shame upon me. In the midst of this, Mejo-rani came to my husband and said, “Thakurpo, it was my fault. Look, brother, we are old-fashioned people; I simply cannot approve of the ways of your Sandip Babu—so, with the best of intentions, I instructed the gatekeeper. I never imagined this would insult Chhoto-rani; in fact, I thought quite the opposite! Ah, my wretched fate, such is my wisdom!”

In this way, from the perspective of the country, from the perspective of worship, that which I see as so radiant—when it begins to be muddied from below in this manner, at first comes anger, and then a deep sense of shame.
Tonight, I went to the bedroom, closed the door, and sat by the window, trying to attune myself to the world outside, to harmonize with all that surrounded me.

How simple life could truly be, if only we let it! There sits Mejo-rani, at ease on the veranda, slicing betel nuts with a tranquil mind. That effortless posture, that stream of simple work—how unattainable it seems to me today! Every day I ask myself, where is the end of all this? Will I die, will Sandip go away, will all of this, like the delirium of a fevered patient, be forgotten entirely when I recover—or will I be crushed so utterly beneath the weight of disaster that there will be no rescue for me in this life? I could not accept the fortune of life in its simplicity—I have shattered it so completely, but how?

This very bedroom—where, nine years ago, I first set foot as a new bride—now its walls, its ceiling, its floor, all gaze at my face in astonishment. After passing his M.A. examination, my husband brought back from Calcutta a rare and costly orchid from some distant island in the Indian Ocean. Just a handful of leaves, but from them bloomed a long cluster of flowers, as if some goblet of beauty had been upturned and poured out entirely, as if a rainbow had been born as a flower in the lap of those few leaves and was swaying there. Together, the two of us hung that blossoming orchid by the window of our bedroom. It flowered that one time, and never again; still, we hope.

And yet, I still believe that one day the flowers will bloom again. It is strange—habitually, I continue to water this plant every day; it is strange that the binding of these few leaves, tied round and round with that coconut rope, has not loosened—the leaves are still green.

It has been four years since I placed a portrait of my husband, framed in ivory, in that niche. Whenever my eyes happen to fall upon it, I cannot look away. Even six days ago, every morning after my bath, I would pick flowers and place them before that picture, bowing in reverence. How many times this has led to arguments with my husband!
One day he said, “You worship me, raising me higher than I am, and it makes me feel deeply embarrassed.”
I asked, “Why does it embarrass you?”
My husband replied, “It is not just embarrassment, but jealousy.”
I said, “Listen to yourself! Jealousy—of whom?”

He said, “Of that false self of mine. It shows me that you are not satisfied with this ordinary me; you desire someone so extraordinary that he overwhelms your intellect. You have created another me in your mind, and with that you beguile your heart.”
I said, "Hearing these words of yours makes me angry."

He replied, "What use is it to be angry with me? Be angry with your fate. You did not choose me in a swayamvara assembly; you had to accept me as you found me, with your eyes closed. So, you are trying to reform me as much as you can by endowing me with divinity. Damayanti could choose in a swayamvara, and so she could reject the god and accept the man. But since you women could not have a swayamvara, every day you reject the man and place the garland on the god."
That day, I was so angry at these words that tears fell from my eyes. Remembering that, today I cannot lift my eyes towards that niche.

There, in my jewelry box, there is another photograph. The other day, on the occasion of cleaning the outer drawing room, I brought in that photo stand—the one in which, beside my husband's picture, is Sandip's photograph. I do not worship that picture, I cannot offer it my reverence—it lies hidden among my diamonds, rubies, and pearls. Precisely because it is hidden, there is such a thrill in it! I close all the doors of the house before I take it out to look at it. At night, I quietly turn up the kerosene lamp, hold that picture before me, and sit gazing at it in silence. Afterwards, every day I think—

In this kerosene flame, I want to burn it to ashes, to end it forever. Yet, every day, with a long sigh, I slowly lock it away beneath my diamonds, rubies, and pearls. But, destroyer, who gave you these diamonds, rubies, and pearls? How many days’ worth of affection is entwined within them! Where will all that love hide itself today? Only in death is there release!

Sandip once told me that hesitation is not in a woman’s nature. She has no right or left, only forward. He said again and again, when the women of the country awaken, they will declare far more clearly than men, “We want”—and before that wanting, no argument of good or bad, possible or impossible, will stand; they will have only one word: “We want!” This “I want” is the primal utterance of creation—it is that utterance which, without heed to any scripture or judgment, has flared up as fire in the sun and the stars. Its passion is terrifying in its partiality—it has desired man, and for that desire, through ages unending, countless creatures have been sacrificed at its altar. That dreadful “I want” of creation and destruction is now incarnate in women! That is why timid men try to dam and restrain that primal wildness of creation, lest it sweep away their pumpkin trellises with roaring laughter.

Dancing, it goes away. Man believes he has made this dam strong and permanent for all time. The water gathers, it accumulates—today the lake’s waters are calm and grave, today it neither moves nor speaks, silently filling the water jars of the men’s kitchen. But the pressure will not be borne much longer, the dam will break—then the dumb force of all these days will rush forth, roaring, “I want! I want!”

Sandip’s words seem to beat like a drum within my mind. So, when conflict arises within myself, when shame begins to reproach me, Sandip’s words come to me. Then I realize that this shame is only the shame of the world—it takes the form of my second sister-in-law, sitting outside, slicing betel nuts, casting sidelong glances. Why should I care for her! To be able to say “I want” freely, without hesitation, with all my strength, both within and without—that is the full expression of oneself—not to be able to say it is failure.
What are those parasites, what are those niches—what power do they have to mock and insult this awakened self of mine!
Thinking thus, I suddenly wished to throw that parasite outside the window—to take down the picture from the niche—

—Let the shameless nakedness of the force of destruction be revealed. My hand was raised, but it struck into my own breast; tears welled up in my eyes—I flung myself face down upon the floor and began to weep. What will become of me, what will become of me! What is written in my fate!
chapters.summary: Bimala finds herself torn between her admiration for Sandip's passionate pride and her husband's humility.

chapters.title: Sandip: Veiled in Dust and Desire
paragraphs: When I read over the autobiography I have written of myself, I wonder, is this Sandip? Am I made of mere words? Am I a book bound in the flesh and blood of a living body? The world is not a dead thing like the moon; it breathes, Vapors rise from all its rivers and seas— It is wrapped in that vapor, dust swirls all around it, And it is shrouded in that veil of dust. The observer who looks at this world from outside Will see only the light reflected off that vapor and dust. Will he ever truly discern its lands and continents?

Just as the earth is alive, so too is a living man; From his innermost being, ideas rise like breath, And so he is obscured in vapor; Where his inner lands and waters lie, where he is most diverse, There he cannot be seen— He appears only as a sphere of light and shadow.
It seems to me that, like a living planet, I am only sketching the sphere of my ideas. But what I desire, what I think, what I resolve— From beginning to end, am I truly that?

That alone is not all—what I do not love, what I do not desire, yet I am that as well. Even before I was born, my being had already been shaped—I could not choose myself; I must make do with what I have received.

I know well that greatness is cruel. What is just for the common is unjust for the uncommon. The earth’s surface is level from end to end, but a volcanic mountain rises only when the fiery horn of flame pierces it with a terrible thrust. It does not judge all sides equally; its judgment is for itself alone. By the force of all its injustice and unfeigned cruelty, whether man or nation, it has risen to become a lord of millions, a master of the earth. Only by swallowing one with closed eyes can two become two—otherwise, the straight line of one would have continued unbroken.

That is why I preach the asceticism of injustice. I tell everyone that injustice is liberation, injustice is the flame of fire; whenever it fails to burn, it turns to ash. Whenever a nation or a man becomes incapable of injustice, at that very moment, his fate is to be cast into the world’s broken vessel.
Yet, even so, this is my idea, it is not wholly myself. However much I may boast of injustice, there are holes, there are gaps in the wooden hull of my idea; within it...
What emerges from within is raw, exceedingly tender. The reason is, most of what I am has already been shaped before me.

Sometimes, with my followers, I test the limits of cruelty. One day, we had gone to the garden for a picnic. A goat was grazing nearby. I asked everyone, “Who among you can cut off one of its hind legs with this knife?” When all hesitated, I went myself and brought it back, severed. Among us, the one reputed to be the most cruel fainted at the sight. Seeing my calm, unwavering face, everyone took the dust of my feet, calling me a great soul, detached and serene. That day, they all saw only the vaporous aura of my ideal; but where I am, by my own fault or by fate, weak and full of pity, where my heart is breaking within—there, it is better to keep myself hidden.

This chapter of my life that is unfolding with Bimala and Nikhil—much remains concealed within it. It would not have been hidden if there were no trace of the ideal in me. My ideal is molding my life to its own design, but even beyond that design, much of life remains—there is not complete harmony between that and my purpose—therefore...
We try to press it down, to cover it up—otherwise, it turns everything to dust.

The thing called life is indistinct, a sum of so many contradictions that it is impossible to define. We, who are people of ideas, want to cast it into a particular mold, to know it clearly in some definite form—this clarity of life itself is what we call the success of life. From the world-conquering Alexander to today’s American millionaire Rockefeller, all have considered themselves successful only because they have managed to shape themselves firmly into the mold of the sword or of money.

It is here that my argument with our Nikhil begins. I too say, “Know thyself.” He also says, “Know thyself.” But what he means is that not knowing oneself is itself the true knowing. He says, “What you call achievement is actually attaining the fruit by leaving yourself aside. The soul is greater than the fruit.”
I said, “That’s a rather vague statement.”

Nikhil replied, “There is no other way. Life is more indistinct than a machine, but that does not mean that by simply calling life a machine and making it straightforward, you truly know life. Similarly, the soul is more indistinct than the fruit; so to see the soul as ultimate only within the fruit is not to see the soul truly.”
I asked, “Then where do you see the Self? On the tip of which nose, between which brows?”
He replied, “The Self is where it knows itself as infinite, where it moves beyond and leaves behind the fruits.”
“Then what will you say about one’s own country?”

“The same thing. Where, in the name of country, I make myself the object, there one may gain results but lose the Self—where one sees the greatest as truly great above all, there one may lose every fruit, but find oneself.”
“Where do you see examples of this in history?”

“Man is so great that he can disregard results as easily as he can disregard examples. Perhaps there are no examples—just as there is no example of the flower within the seed; but the pain of the flower is within the seed. Still, are there truly no examples at all? Was the striving by which Buddha awakened all of India for centuries a striving for results?”

It is not that I do not understand Nikhil’s words at all. But therein lies my difficulty. I was born in India—the poison of sattvic nature does not wish to die out completely from my blood. However much I may call it madness to walk the path of self-denial, I cannot entirely dismiss it. That is why, in our country nowadays...

A strange thing is happening. I am running both—the cry of religion and the cry of country—at full throttle, side by side. We want both the Bhagavad Gita and Bande Mataram. But in wanting both, neither is becoming clear; it is as if the drums of the fort and the shehnai are being played together. We understand this. The work of my life is to stop this discordant tumult. I will uphold only the drums of the fort—the shehnai has brought us to ruin. The banner of instinctual victory that Mother Nature, Mother Shakti, Mother Mahamaya has placed in our hands and sent us to the battlefield with—we shall not bring shame to that. Instinct is beautiful, instinct is pure, like the wild bhui-champa flower, which does not run at every turn to the bathhouse to lather itself with Vinolia soap.

A question has been circling in my mind for some days now—why am I allowing my life to become entangled with Bimala’s? My life is not a floating raft of banana trunks, drifting wherever it may bump along.

That is what I was saying: when we try to confine life within the mold of a single idea, life overflows it. Again and again, people are flung out, scattered. This time, it seems, I have been flung farther than ever.
I feel no false shame that Bimala has become the object of my desire. I can see clearly that she wants me—that is my rightful due. On the tree, the fruit—

It hangs by its stem—must I accept the claim of that stem as eternal? All its sap, all its sweetness, is meant to fall wholly into my hands—the fulfillment of its being lies in surrendering itself entirely at that moment—that is its true purpose, its dharma, its principle. It is then that I shall pluck it, I shall not let it go to waste.

But my worry is this: I am becoming entangled, it seems Bimala will become a grave burden in my life. I have come into this world to command—to lead people by word and by deed—the crowd itself is my warhorse, my seat is upon its back, its reins in my hands, it knows not its destination—only I know. Thorns will draw blood from its feet, mud will cover its body, I will not let it judge, I will drive it onward.

That very horse of mine now stands at the door, restless, pawing the ground with its hooves, its neighing shakes the very sky today, but what am I doing? Day after day, how am I passing my time? Meanwhile, such auspicious days are passing me by!
I had believed I could rush forward like a storm—I could pluck a flower and cast it aside on the path, yet it would not hinder my progress. But this time—
I am circling around the flower, again and again, just like the bee: not like the storm.

That is why I say, the color with which I paint myself using my own ideas does not always set firmly everywhere; suddenly, I catch sight of that ordinary man. If some inner witness were to write the chronicle of my life, it would surely be seen that there is not much difference between me and that Panchu—or even with that Nikhilesh. Last night, I took up my diary and began to read it. At that time, I had just passed my B.A., my head bursting with philosophy, to say the least. Even then, I had vowed that I would give no place in my life to any illusion, whether crafted by my own hand or by others—I would make my life, from beginning to end, utterly solid and real. But what do I see in the story of my life since then, up to today? Where is that tight weave? It is like a net—the threads run along, but the gaps are at least as great as the threads, if not greater. In fighting against these gaps, I have never been able to defeat them completely. For some time, I managed to go on quite confidently, with some force—but now I see, once again, a great gap.
Now I feel a pain in my heart. “I want, it is within my reach, I will snatch it”—this is a very clear statement, a very short path—those who can walk this path...

They alone attain fulfillment—this I have always believed. But Indra, lord of the gods, did not allow this austerity to remain easy; he sent, from somewhere, the celestial nymph of pain, who clouds the ascetic’s vision with a mist of tears.

I see Bimala struggling like a deer caught in a net; in her large eyes, how much fear, how much pity! In her desperate attempt to break free, her body is wounded and torn—perhaps the hunter delights in this sight. I too have my delight, but there is pain as well. That is why everything is being delayed—I cannot tighten the noose with such force.

I know, once or twice, even thrice, there have come moments when, had I rushed forward, seized Bimala’s hand, drawn her to my breast, she would have been unable to utter a word. She too could sense that something was about to happen—something after which the entire meaning of the world would be utterly changed. Standing before the cave of that supreme uncertainty, her face would grow pale, her eyes shining with both fear and excitement; in that brief span, something would become irrevocably fixed, as if all heaven and earth, holding their breath, stood still for her alone. But I have let those moments pass by—I did not allow the almost-certain to become certain in an instant, with the boldness of utter abandon. From this I understand that all the obstacles that have so long been part of my nature—
Those things that lay hidden within me now stand barring my path.

Even Ravana, whom I revere as the true hero of the Ramayana, met his end in just such a way. He did not bring Sita into his inner chambers but kept her in the Ashoka grove—in the heart of so great a warrior, there lingered a small, tender hesitation in just that one place, and for that very reason the entire episode of Lanka came to naught. Had that hesitation not been there, Sita would have cast off her name as a chaste wife and worshipped Ravana. It was because of just such a hesitation that Ravana, instead of killing Vibhishan as he ought to have done, always treated him with a mixture of pity and contempt—and in the end, Ravana died himself.

Herein lies the tragedy of life. It hides, small and secret, in a corner of the heart, and then in a single moment brings down the great. What a person believes himself to be, he is not; and that is why so many strange things come to pass.

That Nikhilesh is so strange—one might laugh to see it, and yet, deep within, I cannot altogether deny that he is my friend. At first, I did not think much of him, but as the days go by, I find myself feeling ashamed before him, even pained. Some days, I try to talk and argue with him as freely as I used to in the past, but the enthusiasm feels somehow unnatural—even to the extent that I do things I never did before.

I pretend to agree with his opinions, feigning a harmony of thought. But this hypocrisy is something I cannot endure, nor can Nikhil—here, at least, we are alike. Because of this, these days I try to avoid Nikhil, feeling relieved if I can somehow escape seeing him. All this is a sign of weakness. The ghost of guilt, once acknowledged by a man, becomes a tangible reality—no matter how much one tries to disbelieve it, it grips the heart. I want to confess this to Nikhil without hesitation, to see these things clearly, to face them as real and significant. There should be no obstacle to true friendship in the presence of truth! But I can no longer deny that this time I have been made weak. Bimala has not been captivated by my weakness—it was in the fearless fire of my manhood that this moth-like woman burned her wings. When I am enveloped in the intoxication of passion, Bimala’s mind too becomes entranced, but then a revulsion is born within her; though she cannot take back the garland of her self-choice from around my neck, she wishes to close her eyes to the sight of it. But the way back is now closed, for both of us. I do not see within myself the strength to let Bimala go. Yet, for all that, I cannot abandon my own path. My path is the path of the multitude—this inner—

It is not the path through the back gate of the city. I cannot leave my motherland, especially not in these times—today, I shall merge Bimala with my country. The same western storm that has blown away the veil of right and wrong from the face of our nation's Lakshmi shall, in that very tempest, lift the bridal veil from Bimala's face—her unveiling will not bring her dishonor.

The boat will sway upon the waves of the ocean of people, the 'Bande Mataram' victory flag will flutter upon it, all around there will be roaring and foam—that boat will be the cradle of both our strength and our love! There, Bimala will witness such a vast form of liberation that, gazing upon it, all her bonds will, without shame and all at once, slip away from her unawares. Enchanted by this vision of destruction, she will not hesitate for a moment to become ruthless. The ruthlessness that is the innate force of nature—I have seen the embodiment of that supremely beautiful ruthlessness in Bimala. If women were freed from the artificial bonds of men, then on this earth we would behold Kali herself—she, the goddess, is shameless, she is merciless. I am a worshipper of that Kali—in the midst of that cataclysm I shall one day worship Kali with Bimala by my side. Now, let me make preparations for that.
chapters.summary: Sandip reflects on the contradictions within himself, his ideals, and his desires, especially his entanglement with Bimala.

chapters.title: Nikhilesh: The Empty Temple
paragraphs: In the month of Bhadra, the floodwaters ripple all around—the tender sheen of the young paddy fields is like the fresh beauty of a child’s body. The water has reached right up to the bottom of our garden. The morning sunlight burns upon this earth, utterly insufficient, like the love of the blue sky.

Why is it that I cannot sing? The water in the canal shimmers, the leaves on the trees glisten, the paddy fields shudder and flash again and again—in this morning symphony of autumn, I alone am mute. The melody is trapped within me, all the brilliance of the world gets caught inside me, unable to find its way out. When I see this unexpressed, lusterless self of mine, I understand why I am deprived in this world. Who could bear my company, day and night?

Bimala is filled to the brim with the surge of life. That is why, in these nine years, not for a single moment has she grown old to me. But if there is anything within me, it is only a mute depth, not a resonant current. I can only receive, but I cannot give forth.
My company is like a fast for human beings—only now, seeing Bimala today, do I realize what a famine she has endured all these days. Whom shall I blame?
Alas, the monsoon is full, the month of Bhadra, Yet my temple is empty!

My temple was built to remain empty—its doors are closed. The deity I thought resided within has always sat outside the temple; all this time, I did not understand. I believed he had accepted my offerings, that he had bestowed his blessings—but my temple is empty, my temple is empty!

Every year, in the month of Bhadra, when the earth is in the fullness of her youth, the two of us would go boating on the lake at Shyamladaha during the waxing phase of the moon. On Krishna Panchami, when the evening moonlight faded away and sank utterly into darkness, we would return home. I would say to Bimala, “A song must again and again return to its refrain;—in life too, the refrain of the song of union is here, here in this open nature; here, upon the shimmering water where ‘the east wind blows,’ where the green earth, drawing a veil of shadow over her head, listens in silent moonlight along the banks, eavesdropping all night long—here, not within walls, was the first meeting of man and woman, the first union of four eyes;—so here we, too, once more enact that primal union of the earliest age.”

I return amidst the smoke, to that union which is like the union of Shiva and Parvati, in the lotus groves by the waters of Lake Manasarovar on Mount Kailash.
