After my marriage, two years passed in Calcutta amidst the turmoil of examinations—then, for these seven years since, every full moon of the month of Bhadra has come to our watery bridal chamber, beside the blooming kumud flower beds, sounding its silent auspicious conch. Thus, one octave of life has passed. Today, the second octave has begun.

That bright fortnight of Bhadra has come again—I simply cannot forget it. The first three days passed—whether Bimala remembered or not, I do not know, but she did not remind me. Everything has fallen utterly silent, the songs have ceased.
Full monsoon, month of Bhadra, My temple lies empty!

The temple that is emptied by longing still echoes with the sound of the flute—but the temple that is emptied by separation is truly desolate; even the sound of weeping there seems out of tune! Today, my own weeping feels discordant. I must put a stop to these tears. I must not, with these tears, imprison Bimala—may I never become such a coward.
Where love has become utterly false, let not tears seek to bind that falsehood. As long as my...

Until her pain is expressed, Bimala will not be truly free. But I must grant her complete freedom; otherwise, I too shall never be free from the grasp of falsehood. To keep her bound to me now is nothing but to entangle myself further in the web of illusion. There is no good in this for anyone—certainly, there is no happiness. Let there be release, let there be leave—if you can be freed from falsehood, then even sorrow will become the jewel of your heart!

It seems to me that at last I have come to the verge of understanding something. The love between husband and wife—we have all together distilled it, extending its natural rights so far beyond their bounds that now, even in the name of all humanity, I cannot bring it under control. We have turned the lamp of the home into the fire of the home. Now is not the time to indulge it further; the day has come to disregard it. Worshipped again and again by the hands of instinct, it has assumed the form of a goddess; but we shall not accept such worship if it demands that men sacrifice their manhood before her and offer her their blood to drink. The web of adornment and modesty, of song and story, of laughter and tears, which she has woven—this must be torn asunder.

I have always harbored a certain aversion to Kalidasa’s poem, Ritusamhara. All the garlands of flowers in the world, all the baskets of fruit, are laid only at the feet of the beloved, as if by the five arrows of Kama.

The offerings for worship are being gathered—can man truly mar the joyous play of the world in this way? What intoxication is it that has clouded the poet’s eyes? The wine I have drunk all these days was never so red, yet its inebriation was just as intense. Under the sway of this intoxication, since morning I have been humming—
In the month of Bhadra, when the monsoon is full, My temple stands empty!

An empty temple! Do I not feel ashamed to say it? How did such a great temple become empty for you? Because I have recognized a falsehood as false, does it mean that all the truths of life have been swept away?

This morning I went to fetch a book from the shelf in my bedroom. For so many days, I have not entered my bedroom in daylight. Today, as I looked around the room in the light of day, my heart felt a strange pang! In that alcove, Bimala’s folded sari still lies coiled, in one corner her discarded chemise and blouse wait to be washed. On the dressing table, her hairpins, hair oil, comb, a vial of essence, and along with them, the little box of vermilion! Beneath the table, her tiny pair of gold-embroidered slippers—once, when Bimala absolutely refused to wear shoes, it was at that time that I, for her...

Through the help of a Muslim friend from my school days in Lucknow, I had these slippers brought for her. She was so mortified that she could hardly bear to wear them, even just from the bedroom to the verandah. Since then, Bimala has worn out many pairs of shoes, but this particular pair of slippers she has kept with great care. I once teased her, saying, “When I am asleep, you secretly take the dust from my feet and worship me—today, by removing the dust from your feet, I have come to worship my living goddess.” Bimala replied, “Go on, don’t say such things, or I shall never wear those slippers again.”

This bedroom of mine has a familiar scent, one that my whole heart knows—perhaps no one else perceives it. Among all these very small things, my thirsting heart has spread its most delicate roots—never before have I felt this as keenly as I do today. It is not only when the main root is severed that life is set free; even that pair of slippers tries to hold it back. That is why, even after Lakshmi is banished, the mind keeps circling around the scattered petals of her broken lotus.

As I looked around, my eyes suddenly fell upon the niche. There, my portrait remained just as before, and in front of it lay many days’ old, dried, blackened flowers. Even in the face of such neglected worship, the expression on the portrait’s face showed no change.

From this room, these withered black flowers are today my only true offering! The reason they are still here is that there is not even any need to throw them away. In any case, I accept the truth in this very dry, black form—when will I be able to become as indifferent as that picture inside the niche?

At such a moment, suddenly, Bimala entered the room from behind. I quickly turned my eyes away and, moving toward the shelf, said, “I came to get Amiel’s Journal.” I do not know why it was necessary to offer this explanation. But here, I felt like a culprit, an intruder, as if I had come to look upon something hidden, something that deserved to remain concealed. I could not look at Bimala’s face; I hurried out.

Outside, sitting in my own room, when reading became impossible, when everything in life seemed unattainable—when I had no inclination to see or hear, to speak or to act, when all the days of my future seemed to congeal into that one moment, becoming motionless, pressing upon my chest like a stone—at just that time, Panchu came and, placing a basket with a few dried coconuts before me, bowed low in salutation.
I asked, “What is this, Panchu? Why have you brought these?”

Panchu is a tenant of my neighboring landlord, Harish Kundu. I came to know him through Mastermoshai. Not only am I not his landlord, but on top of that, he is desperately poor—I have no right to accept any gift from him. I thought to myself, perhaps the poor fellow, driven by helplessness today, has chosen this way of seeking food under the guise of a gift.
As I was about to take two rupees out of my purse to give him, he folded his hands and said, “No, Huzoor, I cannot take it.”
“What is this, Panchu?”
“No, but let me tell you the truth. Once, during a time of great hardship, I stole a coconut from your government garden. Not knowing when I might die, I have come to repay that debt today.”

Reading Amiel’s Journal today would have done nothing for me—but with this single sentence from Panchu, my heart was suddenly laid bare. Beyond the joys and sorrows of union and separation with a woman, this world stretches far and wide. The vastness of human life; standing in its midst, only then do I seem to measure the worth of my own laughter and tears.

Panchu is a devotee of my Mastermoshai. I know how his household is run. Every morning, he rises at dawn and, carrying a tray, sets out with betel leaves, colored threads, small mirrors, combs, and other tempting trinkets for the village women—

Crossing the water and wading through the marsh, he goes to the neighborhood of the Namasudras; there, in exchange for these goods, he gets paddy from the women. In this, he receives a little more than money. On the days he can return early in the morning, he eats quickly and goes to the batasa-seller’s shop to cut batasa. Returning from there, he sits at home to make conch bangles—by then, it is nearly midnight. Even with such relentless toil, for only a few months in the year can he, with his children, manage two handfuls of food twice a day. His eating habit is such that, as soon as he sits down to eat, he fills his stomach with a pitcher of water, and a large part of his food consists of cheap plantain seeds. For at least four months a year, he cannot manage more than one meal a day.

At one time, I wanted to give him some charity. Mastermoshai said to me, “With your charity, you may ruin a man, but you cannot destroy suffering. In our Bengal, Panchu is not alone. The breasts of the whole country have run dry today. That mother’s milk—you cannot supply it from outside with money in that way!”

These are things to ponder. I had resolved to give my life to such contemplation. That day, I came to Bimala and said, “Bimala, let us devote both our lives to the work of uprooting the country’s suffering.”
Bimala laughed and said, “I see, you are my prince Siddhartha—just don’t float away and leave me behind in the end.”
I replied, “Siddhartha’s asceticism had no wife by his side; in my asceticism, I need my wife.”

Thus, the matter passed over with a smile. In truth, Bimala is, by nature, what one calls a woman. Though she comes from a poor household, she is a queen. She knows that those of the lower classes, their measures of happiness and sorrow, of good and bad, are forever set at a lower standard. They will always have want, but that want is not truly want for them. They are protected by the very fence of their own lowliness—just as the water of a small pond is contained by its own banks. If one tries to cut the banks to make it larger, the water drains away, leaving only mud behind. The pride of caste, which has divided India into so many small fragments, each surrounded by its own little seat of honor, so that even within the narrow bounds of inferiority, one may find a pride of lineage and a sense of distinctness—this pride runs strong in Bimala’s blood. She is indeed a granddaughter of the divine Manu.

In me, perhaps, it is the bloodline of Guhaka and Ekalavya that prevails; those who are now beneath me, I cannot push them far away simply because they are low. My India is not an India only for the gentlemen. I know clearly that those below me—
The more they sink, it is Bharatvarsha that sinks; the more they perish, it is Bharatvarsha that perishes.

I have not found Bimala within my spiritual quest. In my life, I have made Bimala so immense that, in not attaining her, my quest itself has become diminished. I have pushed aside the goal of my life into a corner, thinking I must make room for Bimala. The result has been that I have spent my days and nights adorning her, teaching her, circling her endlessly—so much so that I have not been able to keep in mind, with any clarity, how great a thing a human being is, how noble life itself is.

Yet, even within all this, my Mastermoshai has protected me—as much as he could, he has kept me alive to what is greater, otherwise by now I would have been utterly lost. What a remarkable man he is. I call him remarkable because there is, in him, such a profound difference from the times and the country of mine today. He has seen his own indwelling spirit, and so nothing can delude him. Now, when I reckon up the accounts of my life—what I have gained and lost—on one side there stands a great error, a tremendous loss, but I can still say, with some force, that in my life there is a profit, a sum, that can outweigh that loss.
By the time he had finished teaching me, I had already lost my father and become independent. I said to Mastermoshai, "Please stay with me; do not take up work elsewhere."
He replied, "Look, for what I have given you, I have received my due; if I were to take payment for what I have given you beyond that, it would be as if I were selling my God in the marketplace."

Always, through sun and rain, Chandranath Babu would come from his house to teach me; I could never persuade him to use our carriage or horses. He would say, "My father, all his life, walked from Battala to Lal Dighi to work at his office and raise us; he never once rode even in a shared carriage. We are, by lineage, pedestrians."
I said, "Well then, take up some work related to our estate affairs."
He replied, "No, my boy, do not entangle me in the snare of your high status; I wish to remain free."

His son has now passed his M.A. and is looking for a job. I said, perhaps there could be a position for him here. The son, too, was very eager for this. At first, he mentioned it to his father, but found no encouragement there. Then, secretly, he hinted at it to me. At once, I encouraged him—

I spoke to Chandranathbabu. He said, “No, his work will not be possible here.” By depriving him of such a great opportunity, the son became very angry with his father. In his anger, he left his old, widowed father alone and went off to Rangoon.

He has told me again and again, “Look, Nikhil, I am independent in matters concerning you, and you are independent in matters concerning me—this is the nature of our relationship. If the bond of welfare is made subservient to money, it is an insult to the highest good.”

Now he is the headmaster of the local entrance school. For so long, he would not even stay at our house. Only recently, I have been going to his home almost every evening, spending time in various conversations until nearly eleven at night. Perhaps he thought his small room, in this muggy month of Bhadra, would be uncomfortable for me; that is why he himself has taken shelter here at my place.
It is remarkable—despite being a great man, his compassion remains as boundless as that of the poor; he does not disdain the sorrows of the great any more than those of the humble.

The more closely we look at reality, the more it takes hold of us—when we see the truth only as a hint, then the breeze of freedom brushes our skin. Today, Bimala has made that reality so intensely vivid in my life that truth itself seems to have become shrouded for me. That is why, in this entire universe, I can find no end to my sorrow. That is why...
Today I have scattered the smallest gap within me across the worlds, And through all the autumn morning I have sat singing— This full monsoon, this month of Bhadra, My temple stands empty!

When, through the window of Chandranath Babu’s life, I glimpse the truth, the meaning of that song changes entirely. Then— “Bidyapati asks, how can one live in the village, Day and night, without Hari?” All the sorrow, all the errors—each is born of not finding that truth. How can one spend day and night, a whole life, without taking that truth into one’s being? I can bear it no longer. O Truth, come now, fill my empty temple!
chapters.summary: Nikhilesh reflects on his emotional emptiness and the growing distance from Bimala, haunted by memories and household relics.

chapters.title: Bimala: Bengal Awakens
paragraphs: At that time, I cannot say how suddenly the heart of all Bengal was transformed. It was as if, after the ashes of sixty thousand sons of Sagar, the waters of the Bhagirathi touched them for a moment. For ages upon ages, the ashes had lain buried deep—ashes that would not ignite in any fire, that would not bind together with any moisture—suddenly, those ashes found voice and declared, “Here I am!”

I have read in books that some sculptor-god of Greece, by his boon, infused life into his own creation, but in that transformation from form to life there is a gradual evolution, a striving. But in our land, where was the unity of form amidst the heaps of funeral ash? If it had been something hard and solid, like stone, I could have understood—even Ahalya, turned to stone, became human once more. But this was all scattered, slipping through the Creator’s fingers, drifting away on the wind, lying in heaps, never becoming one. Yet, suddenly, one day, that very thing came near the courtyard of our home and thundered like a cloud, proclaiming, “Ayam aham bhoh!”—“Behold, it is I!”

That is why, on that day, it seemed to us that all this was miraculous. This present moment, like a jewel fallen straight from the crown of some nectar-intoxicated god, had dropped right into our hands; there was no natural continuity between our past and this present. This day was like a medicine we had not sought, had not bought, had not received from any physician, but had won in a dream.

Therefore, it seemed that all our sorrows and all our sufferings would be healed by some incantation. The boundaries between possible and impossible vanished altogether. Again and again, it felt as though, “Now it is done, it is done!”

That day, it seemed to us that history had no vehicle; it came gliding on its own, like the Pushpak chariot—at least, its charioteer required no wages; there was no worry for its fodder, only that, from time to time, its cup of wine must be refilled—and then, suddenly, one would attain heaven in the flesh.

It is not that my husband was unshaken. But, amid all the excitement, a certain melancholy seemed to strike him. Even as he looked at what was before him, he seemed to see something beyond it. I remember, in a debate with Sandip one day, he said, “Fortune—”
Suddenly she comes and calls out at our door, only to show us that we do not have the strength to receive her; we have made no arrangements to invite her in and seat her within our home.”

Sandip said, “Look, Nikhil, you do not honor the goddess, and that is why you speak such atheistic words. We have seen with our own eyes that the goddess of awakening has come to grant us her boon, and yet you refuse to believe it?”

My husband replied, “I do honor the goddess, and that is why I know with certainty in my heart that we have not been able to prepare for her worship. We must possess the strength to receive her boon.”
Such words from my husband would make me terribly angry. I said to him, “You think this enthusiasm in the country is nothing but intoxication. But does not intoxication give strength?”
He replied, “It gives strength, but it does not give weapons.”
I said, “The goddess gives strength—that is the rare thing, and as for weapons, even an ordinary blacksmith can provide those.”
My husband laughed and said, “But the blacksmith does not give them for nothing; one must pay the price.”
Sandip, swelling with pride, declared, “We shall pay the price, oh yes, we shall!”
My husband said, “When you do, then I shall order the feast and the festive seat.”
Sandip said, “We are not sitting here in hope of your bargaining. Our Nikaria festival is not something to be bought with money.”
Saying this, in his broken, rough voice, he began to sing—
“In the garden of delight, the lover of Nikaria-nectar wanders and wanders, On the Nikaria bamboo flute he plays an enchanting tune.”

Looking at me with a smile, he said, “Queen of the bees, when a song wells up in the heart, even a broken voice cannot restrain it—just to prove that, I sang. If one sings with the strength of the voice, the strength of the song becomes light. In our land, a sudden, overflowing song has descended—let Nikhil sit and practice the scales from the beginning, meanwhile, we will intoxicate the world with our broken voices.
My home says, ‘Where will you go? If you go outside, you will lose everything,’— My soul says, ‘Let all you have Fly away, burn away.’
Well, let it be—if utter ruin is to be ours, so be it, I am ready, I am ready for that.
O, if it must go, let it go, let it be lost, Let all be lost with a smiling face, I am setting forth to fill my life With the nectar of humanity.”
The real truth is, Nikhil, our minds have gone astray; we will not be able to remain within the bounds of what is easily attainable—we are about to set forth on the path of the unattainable.

O you, who draw close those who are dear, Who among you knows this rapture? The crooked call of my winding path Has summoned me from afar! Now, let the straight burden Shatter and fall under the pull of the crooked.
It seemed to me my husband had something to say, but he did not speak; slowly, he walked away.

Just as a powerful surge of emotion has suddenly swept over the entire country, so too has something of that nature entered my own life, bringing with it a new melody. The chariot of my fate approaches; from somewhere, the sound of its wheels rumbles day and night within my breast. Every moment, it seems as though some extraordinary wonder has descended upon me—one for which I am in no way responsible. Sin? In the realm where there is sin and virtue, where there is judgment and conscience, where there is compassion and affection—the path to step away from all of that has suddenly opened up before me of its own accord. I never desired this, never waited in expectation for it; looking back over my entire life, I see that I have no claim to it at all.

No accountability! All these days, with a single-minded devotion, I have worshipped him—yet, when the time comes to offer myself, another deity arrives! Just as the entire country has suddenly awakened and, facing forward, cries out, "Bande Mataram"—so too, through every vein and hollow of my being, my soul today resounds with, "I bow—to whom? To the unknown, the unprecedented, to that which transcends all creation!"

What a strange harmony between the music of my life and the song of the nation! On certain nights, very late, I have quietly risen from my bed and stood upon the open terrace. Beyond the wall of our garden lies a field of half-ripened paddy; to the north, through the thick trees of the village, glimmers the river’s water, and farther still, the outline of the forest—all of it, as if within the womb of the vast night, slumbers in a vague, unformed shape, like the embryo of some future creation. Looking ahead, I have seen my country standing there, a woman like myself. She was once in the corner of her own courtyard—today, suddenly, she is called toward the unknown. She had no time to think; she moves forward into the darkness—impatient even to light a lamp. I know how her heart rises and falls in this sleeping night. I know, from that distant place where the flute calls, her whole mind has rushed forth so completely that she feels as if she has already attained, as if she has already found—
We have arrived; now it seems there is no fear even if I walk with my eyes closed.

No, this is not the mother. She does not think of giving her breast to the child, of lighting the lamp in the darkness, of sweeping the dust from the house. She is not mindful of these things. Today, she is the lover on her way to a tryst. This is the land of our Vaishnava songs. She has left her home—forgotten her duties. For her, there is only endless emotion—she moves on, driven by that emotion alone, without a thought for the path or the destination.

I too am the lover venturing out into the dark night. I too have lost my home, lost my way. Both the means and the goal have become utterly blurred before me; there remains only emotion and movement. O you nocturnal wanderer, when the night blushes into dawn, you will not even see a trace of the way back!

But why should I return? I will perish. If the dark night that played its flute brings about my ruin, if it leaves nothing of me, then what is there left for me to worry about? Everything will be lost, not a single particle of me will remain, not even a trace; all my darkness will merge completely into the greater darkness, and after that, where is good, where is evil, where is laughter, where is weeping?

That day, in Bengal, the wheel of time was given a full turn of steam. Thus, what could not easily happen began to happen before our very eyes, swiftly and bewilderingly. In whatever corner of Bengal we lived, nothing could be held back anymore.

Such thoughts began to arise in my mind. All this time, in our part of Bengal, the fervor had been somewhat less than in other regions. The principal reason for this was that my husband did not wish to exert any external pressure on anyone. He would say, “Those who make sacrifices in the name of the country are its true devotees, but those who create disturbances in the name of the country are its enemies; they seek to water the tip of the tree of freedom while cutting at its very root.”

But when Sandip Babu came and settled here, his followers began to gather from all sides, sometimes delivering speeches in the markets and bazaars, and soon the waves began to rise here as well. A group of local youths joined forces with Sandip. Among them were some who had been a disgrace to the village. Yet, under the radiance of enthusiasm, even they became bright both inside and out. It became quite clear that when the air of the country is filled with joy, the distortions in people are naturally healed. It is very difficult for people to be healthy, straightforward, and strong when there is no joy in the land.

At this time, everyone began to notice that foreign salt, foreign sugar, and foreign cloth were still not banished from my husband’s estate. Even my husband’s own officials became restless and ashamed about this. Yet, not long ago, when my husband had introduced swadeshi goods here, the people of this place—

All the boys and old men alike used to laugh about it, both inwardly and openly. When we had no means to compete with foreign goods, we held them in utter contempt, heart and soul. Even now, my husband sharpens his pencil with that native knife, writes with a khāṛā pen, drinks water from a brass pot, and in the evenings, reads and writes by the light of a native lamp set in a shāmādān. Yet, in his extremely pale, faded version of Swadeshi, we found no charm in our hearts. On the contrary, I always felt ashamed of the poverty of furniture in his study, especially when a magistrate or some other English official happened to visit our house. My husband would laugh and say, “Why do you get so agitated over such trifles?”
I would reply, “They will think us uncivilized, mere country bumpkins.”

He would say, “When they think that, I too will remember that their civilization is but a white polish on the surface of their skin, never reaching the red stream of blood within the universal human being.”

On his desk, he would use a simple brass pot as a flower vase. How many times, upon hearing that some English guest was coming, I secretly removed it and arranged flowers in a colored glass vase from England.

My husband used to say, “Look, Bimala, just as the flowers are self-effacing, so too is this little brass pot of mine. But your foreign flower vase is far too conscious of itself—it proclaims loudly that it is a vase. It would be more fitting to keep artificial flowers in it, not those from a living plant.”

At that time, his only enthusiastic supporter in this matter was Mejo-rani. She would come in, quite out of breath, and say, “Thakurpo, I hear that nowadays there’s a new kind of swadeshi soap—well, for us, the days of using soap are long gone. But if it doesn’t have any animal fat in it, then perhaps I could use it. Ever since I started coming to your house, I’ve gotten into the habit. Though I gave it up long ago, even now, if I don’t use soap, it feels as if my bath isn’t quite complete.”

This made my husband very happy. Boxes upon boxes of swadeshi soap began to arrive. But what kind of soap was it? It was nothing but lumps of fuller's earth! Do you think I didn’t know? In her husband’s time, Mejo-rani had always used imported soap, and she still does, without missing a single day; the only thing that changed was that she started washing her clothes with the swadeshi soap.
Another day, she came and said, “Well, Thakurpo, I hear there are swadeshi pens now—I must have some. Get me a whole bundle, and don’t let me rest until you do—”
Thakurpo was thoroughly enthused. Every kind of pen, and every kind of twig used for cleaning teeth that had been marketed under the name of ‘pen’ at the time, all found their way to Mejo-rani.

The house began to fill up. She had no difficulty with it, for it could almost be said that she had no connection with studies or writing. The accounts of the washerman’s house could be managed with the help of a neighbor’s tally stick. Yet, I see that in her writing box there still lies that old ivory pen from bygone days; whenever the rare urge to write comes upon her, her hand inevitably reaches for that very pen.

The real point is, she would do this only to answer my refusal to indulge my husband’s whims. Yet, she could never bring herself to confess this little deception to my husband. If she ever tried, he would fall silent with such a look on his face that I would understand the effect had been quite the opposite. Sometimes, in trying to save such people from being deceived, one ends up deceiving them all the more.

Mejo-rani loves to sew; one day, as she was sewing, I said to her quite plainly, “What is this you’re doing! On the one hand, your mouth waters at the very mention of a native pair of scissors in front of your nephew, and on the other, when it comes to sewing, you can’t go a moment without your foreign scissors!”

Mejo-rani replied, “And what’s wrong with that? Tell me, how happy it makes him! Since childhood, I’ve grown up with him, I can’t bear to give him pain with a smiling face as you do. He’s a man—he has no other passion.”
—One, this game with the swadeshi shop, and two, his all-consuming obsession with you—he will get stuck right here!”
I said, “Whatever you say, it’s not right to speak one way and act another.”

Mejo-rani laughed and said, “Oh Sarala, I see you’re much too straightforward, just like the stick of the guru—women are not so simple. It is because they are soft that they bend a little here and there—there’s no harm in that.”
I will never forget what Mejo-rani said, “His all-consuming obsession is you—he will get stuck right here?”
Today it keeps coming to my mind, a man needs some kind of intoxication, but that intoxication should not be a woman.

Our Shukhsayorer Hat is the biggest market in this district. On this side of the canal, there is a daily bazaar, and across the canal, every Saturday, the big market takes place. From the end of the monsoon, this market becomes especially lively. Then, with the river connecting to the canal, travel becomes easier. At that time, the import of thread and warm clothes for the coming winter increases greatly.
During that period, there was fierce turmoil in the markets all over Bengal over the conflict between swadeshi cloth and salt and sugar from abroad. All of us had become quite stubborn about it.
Sandip came to me and said, “Such a big market and bazaar—”
“It is in our hands to make this place thoroughly Swadeshi from beginning to end. We must drive away the foreign misfortune from this area with the sweep of our winnowing fan.”
I girded myself and said, “Of course we must.”
Sandip said, “I have had many arguments with Nikhil about this, but I could not prevail. He says, speeches are all right, but force is not.”
With a touch of pride, I replied, “Well, let me see to that!”

I know how deep my husband’s love for me is. If my mind had been steady that day, I would have felt mortified to go and make demands upon that love with my burnt face on such a day. But I had to show Sandip my strength! To him, I am the embodiment of power! By his marvelous explanations, he has made me understand again and again that the Supreme Power reveals Herself in a special form to each special person. He says, “We are so eager to behold the Vaishnava doctrine’s Hladini Shakti in person; whenever we see Her, we immediately understand what the flute, played in the threefold bend, means in the depths of our hearts.” Sometimes, in a dreamy mood, he would break into song—

When you had not yet appeared, Radha, the flute was playing! Now, as our eyes meet, my melody has drifted away! Then, through many tunes and tricks, The call echoed over water and water, But now, all my tears have blossomed into Radha’s smile.

Listening to all this, I had forgotten that I am Bimala. I am Shakti-tattva, I am Rasa-tattva, I have no bonds, within me everything is possible, whatever I touch I create anew:—I have created this world of mine anew, before my heart’s philosopher’s stone touched it, there was not so much gold in the autumn sky, and moment by moment I am recreating that hero, that ascetic, that devotee of mine— that extraordinary genius, radiant in knowledge, blazing with energy, anointed with the nectar of feeling;—I distinctly feel, at every instant I am pouring new life into him, he is my own creation.

One day, after much entreaty, Sandip brought to me his special devotee, the young boy Amulya Charan. After a moment, I saw in his eyes a new brilliance had kindled; I understood he had seen the primordial Shakti, I realized the work of my creation had begun in his blood. The next day Sandip came to me and said, “What is this mantra of yours? That boy is no longer the same, in a single moment his wick—”
The flame has caught. Who can hide this fire within the home? One by one, all will come. As each lamp is lit, one after another, one day the whole land will be ablaze with the festival of Diwali!
Intoxicated by the glory of this thought, I resolved inwardly that I would grant the devotee his boon. And I also believed that whatever I desired, no one would be able to prevent me.

That day, returning from Sandip, I let down my hair and then tied it up anew. My mem had taught me a particular way to twist my hair—pulling it up from the nape and coiling it high on my head. My husband loved that style dearly. He used to say, “Who could have imagined how beautiful a neck could be? The Creator revealed it not to Kalidas, the poet, but to an unpoetic soul like me. A poet might have called it the stalk of a lotus, but to me, it seems a torch, and above it, your dark hair burns like a black flame, rising upward.”
Saying this, he would—ah, why recall those words now, over my hair-gathered neck?
Afterwards, I called for him. Before, on little pretexts, true or false, I would summon him often—but for some days now, all such occasions had ceased; even the strength to invent them was gone.
Nikhilesh’s Narrative
Panchu’s wife has died, wasting away with consumption. Panchu must perform penance. The community, after due calculation, has declared the cost will be twenty-three and a half rupees.
I said to him, irritated, “Suppose you don’t perform the penance—what are you afraid of?”
He lifted his patient, burdened eyes, like those of a weary ox, and replied, “There’s the girl—I have to get her married. And my wife’s soul too—she must find peace.”
I said, “If it was a sin, hasn’t all this time been penance enough?”
He replied, “Enough penance, you say! The doctor’s fees alone forced me to sell off some land, and the rest is mortgaged. But unless I give alms and feed the Brahmins, I won’t be absolved.”
What use is argument? Inwardly I thought, “When will the Brahmins who eat these feasts atone for their own sins?”

Panchu has always lived on the edge of starvation, and now, with his wife’s illness and funeral, he has sunk completely beneath the surface. At such a time, desperate for any kind of solace, he turned to a wandering ascetic.

He began a life of asceticism. The result was this: he became immersed in a kind of intoxication that made him forget his children were starving. He convinced himself that the world was nothing—just as there was no happiness, so too was sorrow but a dream. At last, one night, leaving his four children behind in a broken hut, he set out, becoming a wandering ascetic.

I knew nothing of all this! Within my own mind, a churning of gods and demons was taking place. Mastermoshai did not tell me either that he had taken Panchu’s children into his own home and was raising them. At that time, his own son had gone off to Rangoon with his wife; he was alone at home, and all day at school.

In this way, about a month passed, and then one morning Panchu appeared. The spell of his renunciation had broken. When his eldest son and daughter sat on the ground beside him and asked, “Father, where did you go?”—when the youngest boy climbed into his lap, and the second daughter fell upon his back and clung to his neck—then came wave after wave of tears; nothing could stop his weeping. He began to say, “Master Babu, I have not the strength to feed them two full meals a day, and yet I cannot find freedom by running away and leaving them behind. Why am I bound like this? What sin have I committed?”

Meanwhile, the little business that he had somehow managed to keep going had now lost its last thread. For the first few days, when he found shelter at Mastermoshai’s house, he clung to that, refusing to even mention moving back to his own home. At last, Mastermoshai said to him, “Panchu, you must go home, or your house and hearth will fall to ruin. I will lend you some money; start a small cloth business and repay me little by little.” At first, Panchu felt a pang—when he thought about it, he realized there is no such thing as pure charity in this world. Then, when Mastermoshai made him sign a promissory note before giving him the money, he thought, “I must repay it, after all—so what is the value of such kindness?” Mastermoshai was utterly unwilling to make anyone indebted within by giving charity outwardly. He would say, “When a man’s self-respect is lost, his very humanity is destroyed.” After taking the money on a promissory note, Panchu could no longer bring himself to bow so deeply to Mastermoshai; he even omitted touching his feet. Mastermoshai smiled inwardly—he was relieved whenever he could lessen the burden of such reverence. He said, “I will give respect and I will receive respect; that is the truest relationship I know between people. Devotion is more than my due.” Panchu bought some dhotis and saris, some winter clothes...

The peasants began to go from house to house, selling their wares. True, they did not receive ready cash; instead, they would bring home some paddy, some jute, or some other crop as payment, but these could not be valued at their proper price. Within two months, Panchu managed to repay a portion of the master's loan—both some interest and a bit of the principal—and this repayment had to be deducted from his wages. Panchu now began to feel certain that he had been mistaken in once regarding the master as a guru; the man had an eye for gold.

Thus Panchu's days went on. At this time, the tide of Swadeshi swept in with great force. The boys from our village and neighboring villages, who studied in schools and colleges in Calcutta, returned home during the holidays; many of them left their schools and colleges altogether. All of them, with Sandip as their leader, threw themselves into the propagation of Swadeshi. Many among them had once passed the entrance examination from my free school; I had given scholarships to many to study in Calcutta. One day, a group of them came to me together. They said, “We must completely remove all foreign cloth, thread, and goods from the market at Shuksayer.”
I replied, “That I cannot do!”
They asked, “Why not? Will it cause you a loss?”
I realized that their words were meant to slight me a little.
I was about to say, “It is not my loss, it is the loss of the poor.”
Mastermoshai was present; he interjected, “Yes, his loss, indeed! But is that loss yours?”
They replied, “For the sake of the country—”

Mastermoshai cut them off, saying, “The country is not just soil; it is all these people. Have you ever, even once, glanced at them from the corner of your eye? And now, suddenly, you come and torment them over what salt they will eat, what cloth they will wear—why should they endure it, and why should we let them?”
They said, “We ourselves have taken up country-made salt and sugar, country-made cloth!”

He replied, “You are angry, obstinate, and in that intoxication you are doing whatever pleases you. You have money; you can pay a little extra to buy swadeshi goods, and in that satisfaction, they do not stand in your way! But what you are trying to force upon them is only by strength. Every day, they are caught in the struggle between life and death, fighting to their last breath simply to survive—do you have any idea what two paisa means to them? How can you compare yourselves to them? In the mansion of life, always—”

You have spent your lives in one room, and they in another—and now you want to shift your burden onto their shoulders, to vent your anger through them? I call this nothing but cowardice. Go as far as you can yourselves, even to the point of death—I am an old man, and as your leader, I am ready to salute you and follow behind. But when you trample upon the freedom of those poor people and then go about flaunting the victory flag of freedom, I will stand against you—even if it means I must die for it, I accept that!”

Almost all of them were Mastermoshai’s students; they could not utter any harsh words openly, but their blood boiled with rage within their chests. Looking at me, they said, “Look, the whole country has taken up this vow today—will you alone stand in its way?”
I replied, “What power do I have to stand in its way! Rather, I will support it with all my might.”
The MA class student gave a crooked smile and said, “And what support are you giving?”
I said, “From the Swadeshi mill I have brought Swadeshi cloth and Swadeshi thread and kept them in our market—even in other regions’ markets I send my thread—”
The student spoke up, “But we have gone to your market and seen for ourselves—no one is buying your native thread.”
I replied, “That is not my fault, nor is it the fault of my market; the sole reason is that the whole country has not taken up your vow.”

Mastermoshai said, “Not only that, those who have taken up the vow seem to have vowed only to create confusion. You want to have cloth woven by weavers who have not taken the vow, and you want to have this cloth bought by people who have not taken the vow. How? By force, by the threats of the landlord’s men! In other words, the vow is yours, but the fasting will be theirs, and you will be the ones to break the fast!”
The student from the science class said, “All right, then—let us hear, which part of the fasting have you yourself undertaken?”

Mastermoshai said, “You want to hear? From the native mill, it is Nikhilesh who has to buy that thread, Nikhilesh who has to get the weavers to make cloth from it, who has opened a school for weaving, and then, with Babaji’s business acumen, when the towels are finally made from that thread, their price will be like that of a piece of Kincob; so he himself will have to buy those towels and hang them as curtains in his storeroom, but those curtains will not preserve the honor of his house. By the time your vow is over, you will be able to look at the samples of native craftsmanship—”
“You will all laugh the loudest; and if, somewhere, that order for the colorful gamchha and the affection it brings is found, it will be with the Englishman.”

All these days I have been with him, but I have never seen Mastermoshai so disturbed. I could clearly sense that, for some time now, a silent pain had been accumulating in his heart—only because he loves me. That very pain had, from within, eroded the dam of his patience.
A student from the Medical College spoke up, “You are our elders; we will not argue with you. Then tell us in one word—will you remove foreign goods from your market or not?”
I said, “No, I will not remove them, because those goods are not mine.”
The MA class student smiled slightly and said, “Because you would incur a loss?”
Mastermoshai said, “Yes, he would incur a loss, so he alone will decide.”
Then all the students loudly shouted, “Bande Mataram!” and stormed out.
A few days later, Mastermoshai brought Panchu to me. What was the matter?
Their landlord, Harishkundu, fined Panchu one hundred rupees.
Why, what was his crime?

He sold foreign cloth. He went to the landlord and, clasping his hands and feet, said, “I bought a few pieces of cloth on borrowed money from others. If these are sold, I will never do such a thing again.” The landlord replied, “That will not do. Burn the cloth in front of me, then you will be released.”

Unable to bear it, Panchu suddenly said, “I do not have the means for that, I am poor; you have enough—buy them from me and burn them yourself.” Hearing this, the landlord flushed red and said, “Scoundrel, you have learned to talk back, have you? Give him a beating!” With this, not only was he thoroughly humiliated, but then fined a hundred rupees! These are the very people who run after Sandip shouting, “Bande Mataram!” These are the servants of the nation!
What happened to the cloth?
It was burned.
Who else was there?

There was no shortage of people; they all began shouting, “Bande Mataram!” Sandip was there—he took a handful of ashes and said, “Brothers, for the first time in your village, the funeral pyre has been lit for the last rites of foreign trade.”
"Burn it—this ash is sacred—smear this ash on your bodies, cut away Manchester’s nets, and, like naked ascetics, you must go forth in your quest!"
I said to Panchu, "Panchu, you must file a criminal case."
Panchu replied, "No one will bear witness."
No one will bear witness? Sandip! Sandip!
Sandip came out of his room and said, "What is it, what’s the matter?"
Your landlord has burned this man’s bundle of clothes before your very eyes, and you won’t bear witness?
Sandip laughed and said, "Why wouldn’t I? Of course I will. But I shall bear witness for his landlord."
I said, "How can a witness be for the landlord? A witness must be for the truth!"
Sandip said, "Is what happened the only truth?"
I asked, "What is the other truth?"

Sandip said, "What needs to happen. We must shape that truth, and for that truth, we need many lies, just as this world is shaped by illusion. Those who come into this world to create do not accept truth—they make truth."
Therefore—

Therefore, the testimony you call false, I shall give that very false testimony. Those who have expanded empires, built kingdoms, formed societies, established religious orders—they have all stood proudly in the courts of your so-called bound truth and given false testimony. Those who rule are not afraid of falsehood; it is only for those who are ruled that the iron chains of truth exist. Have you not read history? Do you not know that in the great kitchens of the world, where the state-sacrifice of politics is being cooked, all the spices are lies?

Many a khichuri has been cooked in this world—no, you will not be the ones to cook it; your throats will be seized and the khichuri will be forced down. They will partition Bengal, and say it is for your own benefit; they will close the doors to education, and claim it is with the noble intention of raising your ideals to the highest; you will remain virtuous and weep, and we, being unvirtuous, will fortify the citadel of falsehood. Your tears will not endure, but our fortress will.

Mastermoshai said, “These are not matters to be debated, Nikhil. Within us, and at the root of all things, there is a vast truth—one who cannot realize this from within himself, how will he ever believe that it is this innermost truth that, when all coverings are removed—”
“To express oneself is the ultimate aim of man, not to amass heaps of external things.”

Sandip burst out laughing and said, “That sounds just like something a schoolmaster would say! All this is found only on the pages of books; in the blink of an eye, I see that the true aim of man is to heap up external things, and those who have achieved this on a grand scale—they lie in bold letters in business advertisements every day, they write false accounts in the ledgers of statecraft with thick pens, their newspapers are ships loaded with lies, and just as flies carry the seeds of typhoid fever, so too do their preachers of religion go about spreading falsehood everywhere. I am their disciple—when I was in the Congress party, I never felt the least bit ashamed to mix fifteen and a half seers of water with half a seer of truth, according to the demands of the market. Now I have left that party—yet even now, I hold to this same principle: that truth is not man’s aim, the aim is to achieve results.”
The schoolmaster said, “The fruit of truth.”

Sandip replied, “Yes, but that crop only ripens in the fields of falsehood. The ground beneath one’s feet must be split, crushed, and reduced to dust before that harvest will grow. And whatever truth may spring up on its own—that is nothing but weeds, thorny bushes; those who expect fruit from them are but a swarm of insects and pests.”

Saying this, Sandip strode out in haste. Mastermoshai looked at me with a slight smile and said, “You know, Nikhil, Sandip is not irreligious, he is heterodox. He is like the moon on an amavasya night—still the moon, but by the turn of fate, he has found himself on the side opposite to the full moon.”
I replied, “That is why I have never been able to agree with him, yet I am naturally drawn to him. He has done me much harm, and will do more, but I cannot bring myself to disrespect him.”

He said, “I am gradually beginning to understand that. For a long time, I have wondered in amazement how you have been able to tolerate Sandip for so long. At times, I even suspected that there was some weakness in you. Now I see that while your thoughts do not match, your rhythms do.”
With a touch of humor, I said, “Friends in discord, yet united in meter! Perhaps our poet of fate has resolved to write an epic like Paradise Lost.”
Mastermoshai said, “Now, what can be done about Panchu?”
I replied, “You were saying that Panchu’s house stands on a few bighas of land over which he has long held hereditary rights. To extinguish those rights…”
The landlord tried hard—he wanted me to buy that piece of land and keep him there as my tenant.”
And the hundred-rupee fine? From what will that fine be collected? The land will be mine.
And his bundle of cloth? I will have it brought for him. Let him, as my tenant, sell it however he wishes—let me see who dares to stop him.

Panchu, joining his hands, said, “Sahib, it is a battle between kings— from the police inspector to the lawyers and barristers, a whole flock of vultures will gather, everyone will watch and be entertained, but in the end, it is I who will die.
Why, what can they do to you? They will set fire to my house; I, along with my children, will be burned.

Mastermoshai said, “Well, your children will stay in my house for a few days, do not be afraid—sit in your own house and conduct your business as you wish, no one will be able to lay a hand on you. I will not let you surrender to injustice and flee. The more you endure, the heavier the burden will become.”
That very day, I bought Panchu’s land, registered it, and took possession. From then on, the struggle continued.

Panchu’s property belonged to his maternal grandfather. Everyone knew that Panchu was the sole heir; there was no one else. Suddenly, out of nowhere, an aunt appeared, claiming rights to a share of the estate. She arrived at Panchu’s house with her bundle, her pots and pans, her pouch for chanting the name of Hari, and an adult widowed niece in tow.
Panchu, astonished, said, “But my aunt died long ago.”
She replied, “The first wife, your aunt, indeed passed away, but there was no lack of a second wife.”
“But the aunt who died did so long after my uncle’s death—there was no time for a second marriage after that.”

The woman admitted that the second wife was not after, but before, the death. Out of fear of living with a co-wife, she had stayed at her father’s house; after her husband’s death, in a fit of deep renunciation, she had gone to Vrindavan. Some of the officials of the Kundu zamindar knew these things, perhaps even some of the tenants were aware. And if the landlord were to make a strong inquiry, those who had been invited to the wedding might also come forward.
That day, at noon, while I was deeply occupied with Panchu’s misfortune, Bimala sent for me from the inner quarters.
I was startled and asked, “Who is calling?”
The reply came, “Ranima.”
The elder Rani-ma?
No, the younger Rani-ma.
The younger Rani? It felt as though a hundred years had passed since the younger Rani last called for me.

Leaving everyone seated in the drawing room, I went into the inner quarters. Entering the bedroom and seeing Bimala, I was even more surprised; for I noticed, upon her whole person, not much, but a distinct hint of adornment. For some days now, I had not seen any sign of care in this room either; everything had become so disordered that it seemed as if even the room itself had grown absent-minded. But today, amidst it all, I could see a touch of the old neatness.

Without saying anything, I stood looking at Bimala’s face. Bimala’s cheeks flushed a little; rapidly spinning the bangle on her left wrist with her right hand, she said, “Look, in all of Bengal, only in our market here is foreign cloth still being sold—do you think that is right?”
I asked, “What would be the right thing to do?”
“Tell them to remove those goods!”
“But those things are not mine!”
“But the market is yours, isn’t it?”
“The market belongs far more to those who come there to buy than it does to me.”

Let them buy indigenous goods or not. If they do, I shall be glad; but if they do not? What is that to say? Will they dare so much? If you were— My time is short; what is the use of arguing about this? I cannot commit oppression. The oppression is not for yourself, but for the sake of the country,— To oppress for the sake of the country is to oppress the country itself. You will not be able to understand that. Saying this, I walked away. Suddenly, it was as if the whole world before my eyes became radiant. The weight of the earthly world seemed to have vanished; even as it carries out all its tasks of sustaining life, and passes through all the endless stages of its own development, it rushes through the ages in the sky, turning day and night like a rosary with a strange force of energy—this I felt within my blood. There is no limit to the burden of action, yet there is no limit to the urge for freedom! No one will bind me—no one will bind me, nothing will bind me. Suddenly, from the depths of my mind, a vast joy, like a pillar of water from the sea, seemed to touch the clouds in the sky.
Again and again I asked myself, suddenly, this—

What happened? At first, I could not get a clear answer, but then I understood plainly: the bond that, these past few days, had caused such torment within my heart now revealed a great rift. I was deeply astonished—there was no confusion in my mind. Just as an image is imprinted on a photographic plate, so too was every detail of Bimala etched before my eyes. I could clearly see that Bimala had adorned herself in a particular way to extract some work from me. Until today, I had never distinguished between Bimala and her adornments. Today, the foreign-style knot of her hair appeared to me as nothing more than a coil of hair—not only that, once this knot had been priceless to me, now I saw it was ready to be sold at a cheap price.

With Sandip, my disagreements about the country are frequent, but they are genuine disagreements. But the things Bimala says in the name of the country are merely shadows cast by Sandip, not formed by her own ideas—if that shadow were to change, her words would change as well. All this I saw with perfect clarity, not a trace of mist anywhere.
When I emerged from that broken cage of my bedroom into the open light of that autumn noon, a flock of starlings was gathered beneath the trees in my garden.

Suddenly, for some reason, a strange excitement has seized me; in front of the veranda, to the south, on either side of the gravelled road, rows upon rows of kanchan trees have overwhelmed the sky with the exuberance of their countless pink blossoms; not far off, at the edge of the country path, an empty bullock cart lies toppled, its shafts raised to the sky like a tail, its face pressed to the earth. Of the pair of bullocks freed from their yoke, one is grazing, the other lies stretched out in the sun, and on its back a crow pecks and pecks, extracting insects—the bullock’s eyes are closing in comfort. Today it seemed to me that I have come very close to the throbbing breast of all that is simple yet immense in this world, that the warm breath of it, mingled with the scent of kanchan flowers, is falling upon my heart. It seemed to me: I exist, and all else exists too; and together, the music that resounds across the sky from this union—how generous, how profound, how ineffably beautiful it is!

Then I remembered Panchu, ensnared in the traps of poverty and cunning; I seemed to see Panchu today, sprawled across all the desolate fields and paths of Bengal in this autumn sunlight, like that bullock, eyes closed—not in comfort, but in exhaustion, in sickness, in hunger. He seemed the very image of all the poor raiyats of Bengal. I saw before me the supremely orthodox, pious, and diminutive schoolmaster Harishkundu. He too is no small man, he too is immense, he seems—
Under the bamboo grove, upon the stagnant, long-festering pond, a thick green scum stretches from one bank to the other, like an unbroken sheet, every now and then sending up poisonous bubbles.

That immense tamasik force—on one side, emaciated by fasting, blind in ignorance, worn out in exhaustion; on the other, swollen by sucking the blood of the dying—lies oppressing the earth beneath its immovable inertia. In the end, we must fight it—this task has been postponed for hundreds and hundreds of years.

Let my delusion be dispelled, let my coverings be torn away, let my manhood not remain entangled and futile in the webs of dreams spun within the inner chambers! We are men; freedom is our pursuit. Hearing the call of the ideal, we shall rush forward, scaling the walls of the demon’s city to rescue the captive Lakshmi. She who, with her skilled hands, prepares the victory banner for our campaign—she is our true companion in dharma. And she who, in the corner of the home, weaves the web of illusion—may we tear away her disguise and find her true, unbewitched self. Let us not, by coloring her with the hues of our own desire, fashion her into an apsara and thus send her to break our own tapasya!
Today, I feel I shall be victorious—I stand upon the path of simplicity, I see all with unclouded eyes—I am free, I have granted freedom. Where my duty lies, there lies my deliverance.

I know that, in pain, the nerves of my heart will throb again, one by one, on some days. But now I have come to recognize that pain—I can no longer revere it. I know it belongs to me alone—what is its worth, then? Only that sorrow which belongs to the world can become the necklace around my throat. O Truth, save me, save me—do not let me, by any means, return to the false paradise of deception. If you make me a solitary traveler on the road, let that road be yours alone—today, within my heart, the victory-drum of your triumph resounds!
chapters.summary: Bimala describes a sudden, passionate awakening sweeping across Bengal and within herself, as she, Nikhil, and Sandip debate the meaning of devotion, sacrifice.

chapters.title: Sandip: Wounded Pride, Burning Tears
paragraphs: That day, the dam of tears truly burst. Bimala called me in, but for a while, not a word escaped her lips; her eyes flashed and sparkled. I understood she had gained nothing from Nikhil. She had harbored the pride that, by whatever means, she would succeed—but I had no such hope. Where men are weak, women know them all too well; but where men are truly men, women cannot quite penetrate the mystery of that place. The real truth is, man is a mystery to woman, and woman is a mystery to man—if this were not so, then the distinction between these two kinds would be nothing but a pointless extravagance of nature!

Wounded pride! Why did what was necessary not happen—that, she does not remember; but what I asked for openly, why did that not come to pass—this alone is her grievance. Around this claim of “I am,” how many colors, how many gestures, how many tears, how much deceit, how many moods—there is no end to it; and in this lies their sweetness. They are far more patient than we are, each in their own way. When the Creator was fashioning us,

He had once been a schoolmaster, then his satchel held only books and theories; but for them, after leaving his teaching behind, he became an artist—then it was brush and paint-box! So, when Bimala, in the crimson flush of wounded pride and tears, stood silently at the horizon of sunset like a cloud ablaze with water and fire, she looked to me exceedingly sweet. I went very close and clasped her hand; she did not withdraw it, but it trembled violently. I said, “Makhi, we are companions, our goal is one. Sit down.”
Saying this, I seated Bimala on a chair.

Strange! All that momentum seemed to halt at just this point. The Padma in the monsoon, which swells and threatens to devour everything in its path, suddenly, for no apparent reason, abandons its straight line of destruction and veers from one bank to the other. What hidden obstacle lay beneath its surface, even the river itself does not know. I pressed Bimala’s hand in mine, and within me, every string of my bodily vina quivered and resonated; yet why did it stop at that unstable note, why did it not reach the refrain? I realized that the deepest bed of life’s current has been shaped by the flow of many years; when the flood of desire surges strong, then that...

The path below is broken in places, and elsewhere it comes to a halt! Somewhere inside, a certain hesitation remains—what is it? It is not just one thing, but entangled in many! That is why its form is not clearly discernible; I only sense that it is an obstacle. I realize that what I truly am can never be proved conclusively by the testimony of any court, sealed in any document. I am a mystery to myself; that is why I feel such a powerful pull toward myself. If I could fully know myself from beginning to end, perhaps I could cast myself off entirely and attain a state of transcendence.

As I sat on the couch watching, Bimala’s face grew utterly pale. She felt inwardly that a crisis had passed. The comet had swept by, but in the wake of its fiery tail, her heart and soul seemed, for a moment, to have fainted away. To dispel this confusion, I said, “There is an obstacle, but I shall not grieve over it—I shall fight! What do you say, Rani?”
Bimala cleared her throat a little, making her constrained voice somewhat clearer, and only said, “Yes.”
I said, “Let us make the plan for how to begin the work a little clearer and more definite.”
Saying this, I took out pencil and paper from my pocket and said, “From Calcutta, the members of our group who—”

All the boys had gathered, and we were discussing how to divide the work among them—when suddenly, in the midst of it, Bimala said, “Let it be for now, Sandip Babu. I will come at five o’clock, and then we can talk about everything.” With these words, she quickly left the room.

I understood that all this while, despite her efforts, Bimala had not been able to give her mind to what I was saying; she needed some time alone with her own thoughts. Perhaps she would have to lie down on her bed and weep.

After Bimala left, the air within the room seemed to grow even more intoxicated. Just as the clouds in the sky become tinged with color for a while after the sun has set, so too did my mind become suffused with hues after Bimala’s departure. It seemed to me that I had let the right moment slip by. Was this cowardice? Perhaps, in my strange hesitation, Bimala had left me with a sense of contempt! Perhaps she could.

While I was still dazed by this intoxicating state, my blood humming within me, the attendant came and announced that Amulya wished to see me. For a moment, I felt inclined to send him away—but before I could make up my mind, he entered the room.

Then came the news of the struggle over salt, sugar, and cloth. In that instant, the intoxication from the air of the home vanished. It felt as though I had awakened from a dream. I girded myself and stood firm. Then, onward to the battlefield! Har har byom byom!

The news is this: the tenants of the Kundus who bring goods to the market have submitted. Almost all the officials on Nikhil’s side are secretly in our camp. They are applying covert pressure! The Marwaris say, “Let us sell English cloth after paying you a small fine, otherwise we will be ruined.” The Muslims, however, refuse to yield in any way.

A peasant was taking home some cheap German shawls for his children; one of our local boys seized those shawls and burned them. This has caused a commotion. We are telling him, “We will buy you native warm clothes,” but where are such cheap native warm clothes to be found? I have not seen any colored cloth. We cannot buy him a Kashmiri shawl. He has gone to Nikhil in tears. Nikhil has ordered a complaint to be filed against that boy. The officials have taken it upon themselves to ensure that the complaint is not properly pursued; even the attorney is in our camp.
Now the question arises: if we must buy native cloth for the person whose clothes we burn, and then face a lawsuit afterward—

Then where will he get the money? And as for the burning of foreign cloth, the trade in it will only grow hotter. When the Nawab, enchanted by the sound of breaking chandeliers, went about smashing them in every house, the business of the chandelier-sellers flourished greatly.
The second question is this: cheap yet indigenous warm cloth is not to be found in the market. Winter has set in—should we keep or banish the foreign shawls, wrappers, and merino?

I said, “It will not do to reward with native cloth the man who buys foreign cloth. The punishment must fall on him, not on us. If anyone goes to file a lawsuit, we shall set fire to the straw of his harvest—stroking his back will do nothing. Oh Amulya, you must not be so startled. I have no fondness for cooking my food by burning a peasant’s straw. But this is war. If you fear to cause pain, then drown yourself in honeyed sweetness, and at dawn, like Radha, collapse to the ground in a swoon.

And what of foreign warm cloth? No matter how great the inconvenience, that cannot be allowed under any circumstances. On no account, for no reason, can we compromise with the foreign. When there were no foreign colored wrappers, the peasant’s son would wrap a coarse cloth over his head and pass the winter—he will do so again. I know their fancy will not be satisfied by this, but now is not the time to indulge in fancy.

Among those who bring boats to the market, many have been brought over, by trick or persuasion, to our side! The most prominent among them is Mirjan—he would not yield in any way. I asked Kulada, the local manager, “Can you manage to sink that boat of his?” He replied, “Is that so difficult? I can do it, but in the end, won’t the blame fall on me?”—I said, “One should not leave blame lying about in such a way that it falls on someone’s neck; still—if it absolutely must fall, I myself will bear it.”

After the market was over, Mirjan’s empty boat was tied at the ghat. The boatman was not there either. The manager, with some cunning, had invited them to a theatrical performance that night. That night, the boat was untied, taken to the middle of the current, a hole was made in it, sacks of rubbish were loaded into it, and it was sunk.
Mirjan understood everything. He came straight to me, weeping, hands folded, and said, “Huzur, I have committed an offense, now—”
I said, “How is it that now you understand it so clearly?”
Without answering that, he said, “That boat is worth no less than two thousand rupees, Huzur! Now I have come to my senses—if you could forgive my fault this time—”

Saying this, he clung to my feet. I told him to come to me again after ten days. If I can give this man two thousand rupees now, I can secure his loyalty. If I can bring people like him into the fold, then the work will truly progress. If I cannot manage to raise a little more money, there will be no result.
In the afternoon, as soon as Bimala entered the room, I rose from the couch and said to her, “Rani, everything is ready, there is no more delay, now I need money.”
Bimala asked, “Money? How much money?”
I said, “Not too much, but I need it, from wherever it may be!”
Bimala inquired, “Tell me how much you need!”
I replied, “For now, only fifty thousand.”
Hearing the amount, Bimala was startled within, but outwardly she concealed it. Again and again, she hesitated to say that she could not manage it.

I said, “Rani, you can make the impossible possible! You have done so. If only I could show you what you have accomplished! But now is not the time; perhaps one day that time will come. For now, I need money.”
Bimala said, “I will give it.”
I understood that Bimala had made up her mind.
She will sell her jewelry and give the money. I said, "You must keep your jewelry for now; one never knows when it might be needed."
Bimala looked at my face.
I said, "You must take this money from your husband's funds."
Bimala became even more stunned. After a while, she said, "How can I take his money?"
I said, "Is his money not your money as well?"
With deep hurt, she replied, "No!"
I said, "Then that money is not his either. That money belongs to the country. When the country is in need, Nikhil is keeping this money stolen from the nation."
Bimala said, "But how will I get that money?"

Somehow or other—you will manage. You will bring the money from him to whom it belongs. Today, in the name of 'Bande Mataram,' the doors of iron safes will open, the walls of storerooms will crumble, and those who invoke the name of Dharma yet do not honor that great power—their hearts will be rent asunder! Mokshi, say it—'Bande Mataram!'
'Bande Mataram.'
Sandip’s Soliloquy

We are men, we are kings, we are the collectors of tribute. Since our arrival on this earth, we have been plundering it. The more we have demanded from her, the more she has yielded to us. From the very beginning, we men have plucked fruits, felled trees, dug the earth, slain beasts, killed birds, caught fish. From the depths of the sea, from beneath the soil, from the jaws of death itself—demand, demand, always demand— we have only ever exacted, we are that race of men. Not a single iron chest in the treasury of the Creator have we spared—we have broken them open and seized their contents.

To satisfy the demands of these men is the earth’s own delight. In meeting these endless demands day and night, the world has become fertile, beautiful, and fulfilled; otherwise, hidden in the jungle, she would never have known herself. Otherwise, every door of her heart would have remained shut; her diamonds would have stayed buried in their mines, and the pearls in their shells would never have seen the light.
It is only by the force of our demands that we men have awakened women and brought them forth. Always before us, always for us—

By giving themselves, they have gradually, more and more, found themselves enlarged. They have only discovered the true worth of their diamonds of happiness and pearls of sorrow by depositing them in our royal treasury. In this way, for men, taking becomes the truest form of giving, and for women, giving becomes the truest form of gain.

I have made a very great demand of Bimala. Is it not the nature of the mind to quarrel without cause with itself? That is why, at first, there was a hesitation. It seemed to me, this is too difficult. For a moment I thought of calling her and saying, No, you need not get involved in all this turmoil; why should I bring such unrest into your life? For a brief while, I forgot that it is precisely for this reason that men are active, that we, by stirring up trouble and unrest among the inactive, make their existence meaningful. If we had not made women weep till now, then the doors to their treasury of sorrow’s wealth would have remained forever shut. Is it not the destiny of men to make the three worlds weep and thus be blessed? Otherwise, why would his hand be so strong, his grip so powerful?

Bimala’s innermost soul desires that I, Sandip, should make a great claim upon her, should summon her to die. Otherwise, why would she be happy? All these days she has not been able to weep freely—only for that reason had she been waiting for my path.

All this time, it was only because she had lived in happiness that, at the mere sight of me, the horizon of her heart suddenly darkened with the blue storm-clouds of sorrow. If I were to take pity and try to stop her tears, then what need would the world have for me!

In truth, the main reason for the slight unease in my mind was that this was a matter of money. Money is, after all, a man’s affair. To go and ask for it always carries a hint of beggary. That is why I had to make the sum large! If it were just a thousand or two, it would have the strong scent of theft, but fifty thousand—now that is robbery. Besides, I ought to be very wealthy.

All these days, so many of my desires have been thwarted at every step simply for lack of money; this, above all, does not suit me in the least. For my destiny, it would have been unjust—had it been so, I might have forgiven it—but it is distasteful, and therefore unforgivable. If I were to rent a house and, month after month, wring my hands over the rent, or, when boarding a train, press my purse anxiously and buy an intermediate-class ticket after much deliberation—such things are not tragic for a man like me, but laughable. I can clearly see that, for a man like Nikhilesh, ‘ancestral property is superfluous.’ If he were poor, nothing would be out of place for him. Then—
He could have easily become the match of his Chandramaster in the sacramental carriage of destitution.

At least once in my life, I want to hold fifty thousand rupees in my hand and squander it in two days, for my own pleasure and for the needs of the country. I am an Amir; for just two days, I wish to cast off this disguise of poverty and see myself in the mirror as I truly am—this is a desire I hold.

But I do not believe that Bimala will easily find her hands on fifty thousand. In the end, perhaps, it will come down to just two or four thousand. So be it. “The wise man sacrifices half,” it is said, but when the sacrifice is not of one’s own will, then the unfortunate wise man gives up not only twelve annas, but even fifteen.

Thus far have I written—so much for my personal affairs. These matters can be elaborated upon when I have more leisure. Now, there is no leisure. The estate manager has sent word; I must go to him at once. I hear some trouble has arisen.

The manager said that the man by whom the boat was sunk has been suspected by the police; the man is an old offender—there is a tug-of-war over him. He is clever, and it will be difficult to extract the truth from him. But who can say! Especially since Nikhil is angry, the manager clearly...

—you will not be able to do anything. The manager said to me— “Look, if I am to get into trouble, I will not spare you.” I asked, “Where is the noose that will entangle me?” The manager replied, “I have one letter written by you, and three letters written by Amulya Babu.” Now I understand, the letter that the manager had me write and from which he extracted a reply—he kept it for this very reason; it had no other purpose. I am learning these tricks anew. Just as I have sunk the enemy’s boat, I can just as easily sink an ally’s boat if need be. The manager had at least this much respect for me. His respect would have been even greater if the reply to the letter could have been given verbally rather than in writing. Now, the matter is this: the police must be bribed, and if things go any further, compensation must be paid to the man whose boat was sunk in the settlement. Now I can clearly see that a hefty portion of the profit from this net that is being cast will fall to the manager’s share as well. But I must keep that thought hidden in my mind. Outwardly, I too say, “Bande Mataram,” and so does he—“Bande Mataram.” The implements with which these affairs are managed are already showing cracks.

Much—much more melts away than the substance that remains. The sense of righteousness, it seems, hides deep within the marrow; that is why, at first, I felt great anger towards the manager, and I was on the verge of writing some very harsh words in this diary about the hypocrisy of our countrymen. But if God exists, I must acknowledge this much gratitude to Him—He has cleared my mind; there can be no room for obscurity, either within myself or outside. I may deceive others, but never myself. That is why I could not remain angry for long. What is true is neither good nor bad; it is simply true—this is science. The water that remains after the earth has absorbed as much as it can—that is what forms a reservoir. The soil beneath 'Bande Mataram' will absorb some water—I will absorb some, so will the manager—and whatever remains after that, that alone is 'Bande Mataram.' I may call this hypocrisy, but it is the truth—I must accept it! Beneath every great work in the world, a layer settles that is nothing but mire; even beneath the vast ocean, it is there.
Therefore, when undertaking great work, one must account for the claim of this mire. Thus, the manager will take something, and I too have some needs. That need is great.
It is part of necessity—for it is not only the horse that must be fed grain, the wheels too must be oiled.

Be that as it may, money is needed. We cannot afford to wait for fifty thousand; whatever can be gathered now must be collected at once. I know, in times of urgency, when necessity presses, one must be prepared to let go of the harvest. Today's five thousand devours the seed of tomorrow's fifty thousand. That is why I tell Nikhil: those who walk the path of renunciation do not need to conquer greed; it is those who walk the path of desire who must renounce their greed at every step. I have renounced fifty thousand; Nikhil's master, Chandrababu, does not have to renounce it.

Of the six enemies that exist, the first two and the last two belong to the brave, and the two in the middle belong to the coward. I will desire, but there shall be no greed, no delusion. If those remain, desire turns to dust. Delusion is that which binds itself to the past and the future. It is the master of leading the present astray. Those who cannot give their mind to what is needed now, those who listen to the flute of another time, are like the pining Shakuntala; they cannot hear the call of the guest at hand, and in that curse, the distant guest whom they long for with enchantment—

...is lost. For those who are ascetics of desire, there is the hammer of delusion— ‘Who is your beloved, who is your son?’ That day, I had clasped Bimala’s hand tightly; the resonance of that moment is still echoing in her mind. Its vibration has not ceased in mine, either. I must keep this resonance alive and fresh. If I let it become habitual and coarse, then what now glides upon the melody will descend into argument. At present, Bimala finds no opportunity to ask “why” to anything I say. What is the use of withholding the allocation of delusion from those who need it? Now, I am overwhelmed with work—so, for now, let the flavor of the cup remain only at its surface; if it reaches the dregs, confusion will arise. When the proper time comes, I shall not disdain it.
