O lover, renounce greed, and master delusion as an expert musician does his veena—let your fingers glide over its finest strings.

Meanwhile, the assembly of our work has gathered momentum. Our group has spread quietly within. After much shouting about brotherhood, at last we have realized that, no matter how much we stroke their backs, we will never be able to bring the Muslims into our fold. They must be utterly pressed down, made to know that the power rests in our hands.
These days, they pay no heed to our summons; they bare their teeth and howl in defiance. One day, we shall make them dance like performing bears.
Nikhil says, “If Bharatvarsha is a true entity, then within it there are Muslims as well.”
I say, “That may be so, but we must know exactly where they are, and it is in that very place that we must firmly seat them—otherwise, they will inevitably oppose us.”
Nikhil says, “Do you think that by increasing opposition, you will somehow resolve it?”
I say, “What is your plan, then?”
Nikhil says, “There is only one way to resolve opposition.”

I know that, like the tales written by holy men, all of Nikhil’s arguments inevitably end in some moral lesson. What is astonishing is that, after all this time handling these precepts, he still believes in them himself! No wonder I say, Nikhil is a born schoolboy! Among his virtues, he is pure, unadulterated stuff. Like Chand Sadagar, he has taken up the mantra of the unreal Shiva, and even when bitten by the snake of reality, he refuses to acknowledge it, even in death. The difficulty is, for people like him, dying is not the final proof; with eyes shut tight, they have decided there is something beyond even that.
For a long time now, I have had a plan in mind; if I ever get the chance to put it into action, then, in no time at all—

The whole country will be set ablaze. Unless our people see the country with their own eyes, they will not awaken. The country needs a goddess-image. This idea struck a chord with my friends; they said, “Alright, let’s make an idol.” I replied, “It won’t do if we make it ourselves; we must elevate the image that is already coming forth and make it the emblem of our motherland. The path of worship is deeply carved in our land; through that very path, we must draw the current of our devotion towards the country.”
Not long ago, I had a heated argument with Nikhil about this. Nikhil said, “It is not right to draw in delusion to accomplish a task we hold as truth and revere.”

I said, “Mṛṣṭānnamitarajanāḥ—without delusion, ordinary people cannot function; and twelve annas out of sixteen in this world are ordinary. It is to preserve that delusion that gods have been created in every land—man knows himself.”
Nikhil replied, “Gods exist to break delusion. To preserve it, there are demons.”

Very well then, let it be demons—otherwise, nothing moves forward. The unfortunate thing is, in our country, this delusion stands upright; we keep feeding it, yet we do not extract any work from it. See here, we call Rāma a god,

We take the dust of their feet, there is no end to our gifts and offerings, yet we are letting such a vast, constructed thing go to waste, not putting it to use. If only their power could be placed wholly in their own hands, then with that power we could today accomplish the impossible. For, in this world, there is a class of beings who are earth-bound; they are the majority; they cannot do any work unless they regularly receive the dust of feet—be it on their backs or on their heads. To set them to work, delusion is a mighty force. All this while, we have been sharpening those missiles in our armory, and now the day has come to strike—can we now cast them aside?

But it is exceedingly difficult to make Nikhil understand these things. The idea of truth has become, in his mind, a mere prejudice. As if there is some particular substance called truth. I have told him countless times: where falsehood reigns, there falsehood itself is the truth. Our country understood this, and so could say without hesitation that for the ignorant, falsehood is truth. If one strays from that falsehood, he will stray from truth itself. For the man who can accept the idol of the nation as truth, that idol will work within him as truth itself. By our nature or by our traditions, we cannot easily accept the nation, but the nation’s...
I can easily accept the idol. Since this is a known fact, those who wish to accomplish work must act with this understanding.

Nikhil suddenly became quite agitated and said, "It is because you have lost the strength to pursue the path of truth that you now wish to pluck a great fruit suddenly from the sky. That is why, for hundreds and hundreds of years, when all the tasks of the country have remained unfinished, you have turned the nation into a deity and sit with outstretched hands, waiting for a boon."
I said, "We must attempt the impossible; that is why it is necessary to make the nation a deity."
Nikhil replied, "In other words, your minds do not rise to the pursuit of what is possible. Everything that exists must remain as it is, and only its result will be something fantastic!"

I said, "Nikhil, what you are saying is advice. At a certain age, that may be necessary, but when a man’s teeth have come in, that will not do. I can see clearly before my eyes, the harvest is ripening in abundance, though we have never even dreamed of cultivating it—by what power? Because today I can see the nation as a deity within my mind. To give this form, to make it eternal through an image, is the task of the present genius. Genius does not argue, it creates! Today, what the nation feels, I will give it shape. I will go from house to house and say—"

We shall roam, the Devi has appeared to me in a dream, she desires worship. We shall go to the Brahmins and say, “You are the worshippers of the Devi—her worship is suspended, and that is why you sit idle.” You will say that I am lying! No, this is the truth—millions of people in our country are waiting for these words to come from my lips, and that is why I say this is true! If I can proclaim my message, then you will see its astonishing results!”
Nikhil said, “How many days do I have left to live, after all? The fruit you will place in the hands of the country will bear further fruit, which perhaps cannot be seen now.”
I said, “I want the fruit of today, that fruit is mine.”
Nikhil said, “I want the fruit of tomorrow, that fruit belongs to all.”

The real matter is this: one of the great riches of the Bengali is his faculty of imagination—perhaps Nikhil possessed it, but from outside, a great tree of religious impulse grew up and smothered it within its own shade! In India, the Durga and Jagaddhatri pujas that the Bengali has invented are a marvelous testament to his character. I can say with certainty—this Devi is a political goddess. During the rule of the Muslims, the Bengali prayed to the power of the land for boons against his enemies—
...had done so, these two goddesses are but two different forms of Herself. In what other nation of India has such a wondrous outward manifestation of spiritual striving been shaped?

Nikhilesh’s visionary imagination has become utterly blind, that is why he could so easily tell me: under Muslim rule, or under the Marathas, or the Sikhs—whoever it was—when they sought results by taking up arms themselves, the Bengali placed weapons in the hands of his goddess and, chanting mantras, desired the fruits of action. But the country is not a goddess, and so, the only result was the slaughter of goats and buffaloes. The day we work for the country along the path of true welfare, on that day He who is greater than the country, who is the true deity, will grant us the true fruit.

The difficulty is, Nikhilesh’s words sound good on paper—but my words are not meant to be written on paper, they are to be inscribed upon the breast of the country, cleaving it open with an iron spade. Not as the scholar writes about agriculture in printer’s ink, but as the farmer engraves his desires upon the earth’s bosom with the blade of his plough.

When I met Bimala, I said, “The deity for whose worship I have come to this earth after countless ages—until she reveals herself to me directly, can I truly believe in her with all my body and soul? If I had not seen you, could I ever have...”

I could never see the country as a single whole; I have told you this so many times, though I do not know if you truly understand what I mean. It is very difficult to explain that, just as in the realm of the gods the deities remain invisible, but reveal themselves only in the mortal world.
Bimala looked at me in a certain way and said, “I understand your words very clearly.” For the first time, Bimala addressed me as “tumi” instead of “apni.”

I said, “Just as Arjuna always saw Krishna as his mere charioteer, yet Krishna too had a vast, cosmic form, which Arjuna beheld one day—then he saw the whole truth. Among all the lands of my country, I have seen that vast form in you. Around your neck is the seven-stranded necklace of the Ganga and the Brahmaputra; in the kohl-darkened lashes of your black eyes I have seen the distant forest-lines across the blue waters of the river; and your sari, streaked with the play of shadow and light, trails and ripples over the young paddy fields; and I have seen your fierce radiance in the summer sun of Jaishtha, when the whole sky, like a lion of the desert, pants with its red tongue lolling out! When the goddess has revealed herself to her devotee in such a wondrous way, then it is her worship that I will spread throughout my land, so that the people of my country may find life. I will fashion your image in the temple
“In the temple!” But not everyone understood those words clearly.

So my resolve is this: I will call the whole country, and with my own hands I will shape the image of my goddess, and worship her in such a way that no one will ever be able to doubt her again. Grant me that boon, grant me that strength!

Bimala’s eyes closed. She seemed to merge with the seat on which she sat, becoming as motionless as a stone image. Had I spoken a little more, she would have fainted away. After a while, she opened her eyes and cried out, “O traveler on the path of destruction, you have set out on your way, and there is no one who can stand in your path. I see today that no one can withstand the force of your will. Kings will come, and lay their scepters at your feet; the wealthy will come, and pour out their treasures before you; those who have nothing left will come to you, begging only for the right to die. All rules of good and evil, all codes and customs, will be swept away, swept away!

My king, my god, I do not know what you see in me, but upon the lotus of my heart I have seen your cosmic form. Where am I before that? Destruction, utter destruction—what terrible power it is! Until it utterly destroys me, I cannot live, I cannot bear it—my heart is breaking.”
As she spoke, she slipped from the chair onto the floor and clung to my feet. Then came a flood of tears—sobbing, sobbing, sobbing!

This is hypnotism! This is the power that conquers the world. No means, no implements—only this enchantment! Who says “Satyameva Jayate”—Truth alone triumphs? It is illusion that will win. The Bengali understood this, and so the Bengali brought forth the worship of the ten-armed goddess, the Bengali fashioned the image of the lion-riding Mother. That same Bengali will again shape an image, will conquer the world with nothing but enchantment—Bande Mataram!

Gently, I took Bimala by the hand and helped her back onto the chair. Before the exhaustion could set in after such excitement, I said to her, “The task of establishing the Mother’s worship in Bengal has been entrusted to me, but I am poor.”

Bimala’s face was still flushed, her eyes still veiled with tears; in a choked voice she said, “In what way are you poor? Whatever anyone has is yours. Why should my jewels lie locked away in a box? Take all my gold and gems for your worship—I have no need of any of it.”

Once before, Bimala had wanted to give her jewelry—nothing else ever troubled me, but there I hesitated. I have thought about the source of this reluctance. All through the ages, it has been the man who gives ornaments to the woman—
...has come adorned, but to take ornaments from a woman's hand somehow wounds one's manhood.

But here, I must forget myself. I am untroubled. This is the worship of the Mother; I will pour everything into that worship. It must be performed with such grandeur that no one in this land has ever witnessed such a puja! This worship will be enshrined at the very heart of the history of the new Bengal for all time. This puja I shall offer to the country as the greatest gift of my life. The ignorant worship the deity; Sandip will create the deity.

That is the grand idea. But the smaller matters must also be addressed. For now, unless I have at least three thousand rupees, it will not do; with five thousand, things would proceed most handsomely. But can one speak of money at the height of such fervor? Yet there is no time left.
Stepping over my hesitation, I said, “Rani, the treasury has run dry here; the work will have to stop!”

At once, a shadow of pain crossed Bimala’s face. I understood—Bimala thinks I am already demanding that fifty thousand. This has lain heavy on her heart—perhaps she has thought of it all night, but found no way out. She has no other offering left for this worship of love; she cannot clearly pour her heart at my feet, and so her mind yearns to give this great sum of money...

...to bring to me the reflection of her pent-up affection. But, finding no outlet, her heart is suffocating. That pain of hers touches my own heart. Now that she is entirely mine, there is no longer any need for the sorrow of uprooting her; now I must cherish her with utmost care.
I said, “Rani, there is no special need for that fifty thousand now. I have calculated, and even five thousand—or even three thousand—will suffice.”
Suddenly, all the tension melted away, and Bimala’s heart overflowed with joy. As if singing a song, she exclaimed, “I will bring you five thousand!”
In the very tune that Radhika once sang—

“For my beloved’s sake, I will wear such a flower in my hair Whose root is not to be found in heaven, earth, or the three worlds. The sound of the flute floats on the breeze, Not everyone’s ears will hear it, But look—Yamuna, gazing, has overflowed her banks!”

It was just that melody, that song, and that very sentiment—“I will bring you five thousand!” “For my beloved’s sake, I will wear such a flower in my hair!” Because the hollow of the flute is so narrow, because it is bound all around, such a tune is born—if, under the pressure of too much greed, I were to crush and flatten the flute today, then what would be heard?—Why, what need have you for so much money?

What? And I, a woman, where would I ever get so much money? And so on, and so forth. Radhika’s song did not match even a single syllable with hers. That’s why I say, it is the illusion that is the truth—that is the flute, and if you take away the illusion, what remains is the hollow inside a broken flute—that utterly pure emptiness, what it is, Nikhil has lately tasted a little of it, you can see it just by looking at his face. My heart aches as well. But Nikhil’s pride is that he wants the truth, and my pride is that I will not, if I can help it, let go of the illusion. As one’s thoughts are, so is one’s fulfillment—so what is the use of grieving over it?

To keep Bimala’s mind soaring in that upper air, I quickly settled the matter of the five thousand rupees, and once again sat down to recite the mantras for the worship of the Mahishamardini. When and where would the worship take place? In Nikhil’s estate, after the end of the Rui-mari famine, there is a fair at Hosengazi where lakhs of people gather; if the worship could be held there, it would be a grand event. Bimala became excited. She thought, this is not burning foreign cloth, not setting people’s houses on fire—surely Nikhil would have no objection to such a noble proposal. I smiled inwardly—those who have spent nine years together, day and night, how little they truly know each other! They know only the matters of household management, only the affairs of the home:

When the subject of the outside world suddenly arises, they lose all footing. For nine years, they have sat and steadfastly believed that the inside and the outside are perfectly in harmony, as if the two are naturally one. Only now do they realize that these two have never truly been reconciled—so how can they suddenly be united now?

Let it be. Those who misunderstood may learn the truth through their own stumbles; I need not worry too much about that. It is not possible to keep Bimala buoyed for long by this wave of excitement, like a balloon in the air. Therefore, I must finish this business at hand as soon as possible. When Bimala rose from her seat and walked to the door, I said, rather offhandedly, “Rani, then when will you—about the money—?”
Bimala turned and replied, “At the end of this month, when the monthly accounts are settled—”
I said, “No, it cannot be delayed.”
“When do you need it?”
“Tomorrow.”
“Very well, I will bring it tomorrow.”
chapters.summary: Sandip grapples with his wounded pride as Bimala struggles with hesitation and emotion, while the Swadeshi movement's tensions escalate, forcing difficult choices about loyalty.

chapters.title: Nikhilesh: Mockery and Muddy Roads
paragraphs: Paragraphs and letters about me have begun to appear in the newspapers—I hear that even a satirical rhyme and a caricature are in preparation. The wellspring of mockery has been opened, and with the incessant downpour of countless falsehoods, the entire country seems utterly delighted. They know that in this muddy festival of ridicule, the syringe is in their own hands—while I, a gentleman, walk quietly along one side of the road, with no way to keep my white garment unsoiled.

It is written that in my estate, the common people are all intensely eager for Swadeshi, but only my fear prevents them from doing anything—those few brave souls who wish to use indigenous goods, I, with my landlord’s authority, oppress them according to the rules. Secretly, I am in league with the police, and I correspond covertly with the magistrate; and, according to reliable sources, the newspapers have learned that my efforts to add a self-earned title to my ancestral one will not go unrewarded.

They have written, “Renowned are you, sir, but the people of the country have given you a title of their own—we are aware of that too!”—My name has not been stated explicitly, but from within the vagueness of the outside, it stands out all the more clearly.

Meanwhile, the newspapers are publishing letter after letter, singing the praises of the mother-loving Harishkundu. They write, if only there were more such devoted sons of the Mother in our land, by now even the chimneys of the Manchester factories would be resounding in unison with the tune of Bande Mataram played on the ramshinga.

On the other hand, a letter written in red ink has arrived in my name, reporting which offices of which salt-loyal landlords of Liverpool have been set on fire. It says, from now on, the Lord of Fire will devote himself to this purifying work; arrangements are being made so that those who are not the Mother’s children cannot remain nestled in her lap.
The signature reads, “The humblest dust at the Mother’s feet, Shri Ambikacharan Gupta.”

I know well that all of this is the handiwork of my students here. I called two or three of them and showed them the letter. The B.A., with a grave face, said, “We have also heard that there is a group in the country who are desperate, who will stop at nothing to remove the obstacles to Swadeshi.”
I said, “If even a single person in the country is forced to yield to their unjust violence, then it is the defeat of the entire nation.”
The M.A. in history said, “I cannot quite understand.”

I said, “Our country, from the gods down to the petty officials, has been half-dead with fear. Now, if in the name of freedom, you wish to bring back that same old terror under a new guise, if you wish to plant the flag of your country’s victory upon cowardice through oppression, then those who truly love the country will never bow their heads, not by a hair’s breadth, to such a reign of fear.”
The M.A. in History said, “Is there any country where the rule of the state is not a rule of fear?”

I replied, “The extent of this rule of fear determines how much freedom the people of a country possess. If the rule of fear is limited to suppressing theft, robbery, and injustice against others, then it is clear that this rule exists to protect every person from the attacks of others. But if the rule of fear dictates what clothes a person will wear, from which shop he will buy, what he will eat, with whom he will sit and eat—if even these are bound by fear—then it is a denial of human will at its very root. That is nothing less than depriving a person of his humanity.”
The M.A. in History said, “But is there no arrangement anywhere in other societies to cut off the will at its root?”
I replied, “Who says there isn’t? Taking men and—”
Trade exists in a country only to the extent that people have corrupted themselves.”
The M.A. said, “Then that slave trade is truly the religion of man, that is what constitutes humanity.”

The B.A. remarked, “The example Sandipbabu gave the other day on this subject struck us deeply! Take Harishkundu, the landlord across the river, or the Chakrabartis of Sankibhanga—sweep through their entire domain and you won’t find a pinch of foreign salt today. Why? Because they have always ruled by force; for those who are slaves by nature, the greatest calamity is to be without a master.”

The F.A., that Pluck fellow, said, “I know of an incident. The Chakrabartis had a Kayastha tenant. He wouldn’t submit to them over a market he owned. After endless lawsuits, he was reduced to such a state that he could no longer afford to eat. When there was no food in his house for two days, his wife went out to sell her silver ornaments—her last possession. But under the landlord’s tyranny, no one in the village dared buy her jewelry. The landlord’s manager said, ‘I’ll buy it for five rupees.’ Its value was at least thirty rupees. Driven by desperation, when he agreed to the five rupees, the manager took the bundle of jewelry and said, ‘These five rupees I am crediting towards your arrears of rent.’—When we heard this story...
I told Sandipbabu that we would boycott Chakravarti.

Sandipbabu said, “If you exclude all these living men, then will you work for the country with the corpses from the ghat? These are the ones who know how to will with all their might, they are the masters. Those who do not know how to will with their whole being, they will either follow the will of these men, or perish by it. Comparing him with you, he said, ‘Today, in Chakravarti’s area, there isn’t a single person who dares utter a word about Swadeshi—yet, even if Nikhilesh wills a thousand times, he will not be able to run the Swadeshi movement.’”
I said, “I want to lead something greater than Swadeshi, that is why it is difficult for me to lead Swadeshi. I do not want dead posts, I want living trees. My work will take time.”

The historian laughed and said, “You will get neither dead posts nor living trees. Because I agree with Sandipbabu—getting means snatching. It has taken us time to learn this, because this is the opposite of what we were taught in school. I have seen with my own eyes, Kundu’s agent, Gurucharan Bhaduri, went out to collect money—there was nothing that a certain Muslim tenant could sell to pay. He had a young wife. The agent struck him and said, ‘You will have to pay your debt by giving away your wife in marriage.’ For the marriage—”

The agent was found, and the money was repaid. Let me tell you, seeing my husband’s tears, I could not sleep at night. But no matter how much it pains me, I have learned this much: when money must be collected, the person who can raise it by selling the debtor’s wife is, as a human being, greater than I am. I cannot do it; tears come to my eyes, and so everything gets tangled. If anyone is to save our country, it will be these gomostas, these Kundus, these Chakrabartis!”

I was stunned. I said, “If that is so, then my task is to save the country from the hands of these gomostas, these Kundus, these Chakrabartis! Look, the poison of servitude that lies deep within our marrow—when it finds the chance to rise to the surface, it takes on a terrible, tyrannical form. The daughter-in-law who is beaten becomes, as a mother-in-law, the greatest beater of all. The person who bows his head in society, when he emerges as the leader of a wedding procession, becomes such a nuisance that it is impossible for respectable householders to preserve their honor. Out of fear, you have blindly accepted everything from everyone, and you have learned to call that religion; that is why today, by oppressing others, you think forcing everyone to conform is religion. My fight is with the cruelty of that weakness!”
These words of mine are very simple—if you say them to a straightforward person, it takes but a moment to understand. But among us—
Those M.A.s, who twist the logic of history only to defeat the truth—their twists are for that alone.

Meanwhile, I am thinking about Panchu’s net, about Mami. It is difficult to disprove her. The number of witnesses to a true event is limited; sometimes, there may be no witness at all. But if one can fabricate an event that never happened, there is never any shortage of witnesses. This is the scheme to deprive me of the hereditary rights I bought from Panchu.
Seeing me helpless, I was considering giving Panchu some land in my own area and building him a house. But Mastermoshai said, “We cannot so easily yield to injustice. I will try myself.”
“You will try?”
“Yes, I will.”

All these are matters of lawsuits and litigation—I could not understand what Mastermoshai could possibly do. That evening, at the hour when he usually meets me, he did not come. Upon inquiry, I learned that he had left, taking his box of clothes and bedding, telling the servants only that he would be delayed by two or four days. I thought perhaps he had gone to Panchu’s uncle’s house to gather witnesses. If that is so, I know it will be a futile effort on his part. Jagaddhatri Puja, Muharram, and Sundays—
He had a few days’ leave from his school, so he could not be found there either.

In the afternoons of Hemanta, when the color of daylight grows turbid and dim, the hues within the mind too begin to change. There are many in this world whose minds dwell securely within the walls of their houses. They can afford to disregard the “outside” altogether, as though it were of no consequence. But my mind seems to reside beneath a tree. Every signal from the outside wind falls directly upon me; all the chords of light and shadow resound within my breast. When the day’s light is sharp and bright, the world crowds around me with its countless tasks, and it seems as if nothing else in life is needed. But when the sky grows pale, when the curtain descends from heaven’s window upon the earth, then my mind whispers that evening comes to shroud the entire world of household affairs—now only the companionship of one can fill the infinite darkness, this alone was the sole consolation of earth, water, and sky. The life that blooms among many during the day folds itself into the solitude of one at dusk; this was the true meaning hidden between light and darkness. I cannot deny this and harden myself against it—so, as soon as evening, like the beloved’s dark veil studded with stars, falls upon the world...

At such moments, my entire body and mind rise up, whispering— —It is not true, this can never be true, that only work is the beginning and end of man;—man is not merely a laborer, even if it be the labor of truth, the labor of religion,—in the light of those stars, the man who, released from work, is something beyond, the man who plunges into the nectarous darkness—have you lost him forever, Nikhilesh? In that place where the countless multitude of the world cannot give a man the slightest company, the one who is left alone there—how terribly alone he is.

That afternoon, just as the enchantment of dusk was settling in, I had no work, nor was my mind on work, nor was Mastermoshai present; when my empty heart was yearning to clutch at something in the sky, I went into the inner garden of the house. I have a great fondness for chrysanthemum flowers. I had arranged pots of chrysanthemums of many colors in the garden; when all the plants would burst into bloom, it seemed as if waves had risen in a green sea, frothing with color. I had not gone to the garden for some time; today, smiling to myself, I said, “Let me go and relieve my lonely chrysanthemums of their loneliness.”
When I entered the garden, the moon of Krishna Paksha had just appeared, peering over the top of our wall. Dense shadows lay at the foot of the wall—across them, crooked—

The moonlight had fallen over the western side of the garden. It seemed to me as if the moon had suddenly crept up from behind and was winking mischievously at the darkness with a sly smile. Along the edge of the wall, where it forms a sort of gallery—there, rows of tubs with blooming chrysanthemums were arranged. Going towards that side, I saw someone lying silently on the grass beneath those blossoming steps. My heart gave a sudden leap. As I drew nearer, that person too started in surprise and quickly sat up.

What was to be done then? I wondered whether I should turn back from there; Bimala too, no doubt, was wondering whether she should get up and leave. But to stay was as difficult as to go. Before I could make up my mind about anything, Bimala stood up, drew her sari over her head, and walked towards the house.
In that brief moment, Bimala’s unbearable sorrow seemed to take shape before me. In that instant, the grievances of my own life drifted far away! I called out to her, “Bimala!”

She started and stopped. But still she did not turn towards me. I came and stood in front of her. Her face was in shadow, while the moonlight fell upon mine. She stood with her hands clenched, eyes tightly shut. I
I said, "Bimala, within this cage of mine, all sides are closed. For what reason should I keep you confined here? You will not truly live like this!"
Bimala kept her eyes shut, not uttering a single word.
I said, "If I bind you with such force, then my entire life will become an iron chain. Is there any happiness for me in that?"
Bimala remained silent.
I said, "Listen, I speak the truth to you—I set you free. If I can be nothing else to you, at least I will not be the handcuffs on your wrists!"

Saying this, I walked towards the house. No, no, this is not my magnanimity, nor is it my indifference. If I cannot let go, I will never be free. The one whom I would make the ornament of my heart, I cannot keep as a lifelong burden upon it. To the Inner Witness, I pray with folded hands only this: let me not have happiness, let me not attain it; let me have sorrow, I accept that too—but do not keep me bound. To try to hold on to falsehood as truth is to strangle oneself. Save me from that self-destruction.
Entering the drawing room, I saw Mastermoshai sitting there. At that moment, within me, my mind was overflowing with emotion.
Seeing Mastermoshai, before I could ask him anything else, I exclaimed, “Mastermoshai, freedom is the greatest thing for man. Beside it, nothing else matters—nothing at all!”
Mastermoshai was astonished at my agitation. He looked at me in silence.

I said, “One understands nothing from reading books. In the scriptures I had read that desire itself is bondage—it binds itself and binds others. But those are only empty words, terrifyingly hollow. Only when one truly sets the bird free from its cage does one realize that the bird, in turn, sets me free. The one whom I confine in the cage binds me with my own desire; and the bonds of that desire are stronger than the chains of iron. I tell you, I do not think anyone in this world understands this. Everyone believes that reform must be made somewhere else. But nowhere else, nowhere—except within desire itself!”
Mastermoshai said, “We think that to obtain what we desire, to hold it in our hands, is freedom—but in truth, to renounce what we desire within our hearts, that is freedom.”
I replied, “Mastermoshai, when you say it like that, it sounds like some bald, worn-out advice; but the moment I even glimpse it with my own eyes, I see—yes, I see that this is the very thing—”

Amrita. The gods drink this and become immortal. We cannot truly see beauty until we let it go. It is Buddha who conquered the world, not Alexander; but this statement becomes a lie when we utter it in a dry voice. When will I be able to sing this truth? When will the words of life in this universe overflow the printed pages of books, and pour forth like the spring at Gangotri, the very source of the Ganges?
Suddenly I remembered that Mastermoshai had not been here for a few days—I did not even know where he had been. Somewhat embarrassed, I asked, "Where have you been?"
Mastermoshai replied, "At Panchu's house."
At Panchu's house? You have been there these past four days?

Yes. I thought I would speak with the woman who has come pretending to be Panchu's aunt. When she first saw me, she was a little surprised; she could not have imagined that someone could be so strange, even though he is the son of a gentleman. She saw that I stayed on. After that, she began to feel embarrassed. I told her, "Mother, you cannot insult me and drive me away. And if I stay, I will keep Panchu here as well; his motherless little children—I cannot bear to see them turned out onto the street." For two days, I spoke to her gently. She listened—neither agreeing nor refusing; finally...

Today I see bundles being tied up. She said, "We are going to Vrindavan, give us some money for the journey." — Whether they will actually go to Vrindavan, I do not know, but I will have to give a rather generous amount for their travel expenses. That is why I have come to you."
Very well, I shall give whatever is necessary.

The old woman is not a bad person. Panchu does not allow her to touch the water pitcher; whenever she enters the house, there is a great commotion over it, and so there have been constant petty quarrels between them. But when she heard that I had no objection to eating food cooked by her hands, she lavished me with care and attention. She cooks excellently. Whatever little devotion and respect Panchu had for me has now completely vanished. Earlier, he believed that at least I was a simple man, but now he thinks that my eating food cooked by the old woman was merely a ploy to win her over. One does need some cunning in this world, but does that mean one must altogether lose one’s sense of righteousness? If I could outdo the old woman in giving false testimony, then it would be something to reckon with.

Anyway, even after the old woman leaves, I shall have to guard Panchu’s house for a few days—otherwise, Harishkundu will surely do something drastic. Apparently, he has told his followers, "I got him a fake aunt, and now that fellow has outdone me by producing a fake father from somewhere; let us see how his father manages to save him now!"

I said, "He may live or he may die, but these people are forging a thousand kinds of traps for the countrymen—in religion, in society, in trade. Even if we are defeated fighting against these, still, we shall be able to die in peace."
chapters.summary: Nikhilesh faces public ridicule and false accusations as satirical attacks and rumors spread.

chapters.title: Bimala: The Thunderbolt Fails
paragraphs: It is hard to believe that so much can happen in a single lifetime. It feels as though I have lived seven lives already. In these few months, a thousand years seem to have passed. Time was rushing by so swiftly that I did not even realize it was moving. Only when I was suddenly jolted did I come to understand.

When I went to my husband to speak about bidding farewell to foreign goods from the market, I expected there would be some argument over it. Yet I had a certain confidence that it was unnecessary for me to counter argument with argument. There is a kind of magic in the atmosphere that surrounds me. A man as great as Sandip, like a wave of the vast ocean, came crashing at my feet. I did not call him—he was summoned by the very air that surrounds me. And that day, I saw Amulya—ah, such a boy—innocent, fresh, as simple and sweet as a young bamboo flute. When he came to me, it was like the river at dawn, and as I watched, a new color blossomed from within the current of his life. That day, I realized how a goddess, gazing upon the face of her devotee, can be so utterly enchanted—Amulya’s...
Looking around, I understood it. I have now seen for myself what kind of work my golden wand of power can accomplish.
That is why, on that day, with unshakable faith in myself, I went to my husband like a thunderbolt wrapped in lightning.

But what happened? In these nine years, not once have I seen such a distant look in my husband's eyes. It was like the sky over a desert—no trace of moisture within himself, and in whomever he gazed upon, not a hint of color could be found. Had he even shown a little anger, I might have been saved. I could not touch him at all. I felt I was false. Like a dream—no sooner had the dream broken than there was nothing but the dark night!

All these years, I have envied my beautiful sisters-in-law for their beauty. In my heart, I knew the Creator had not given me strength—my husband’s love was my only strength. Today, I have drunk deep from the cup of power, and its intoxication has taken hold of me. Now, suddenly, the cup has shattered and fallen to the ground. How am I to survive now?

I sat down hurriedly to tie up my hair! Shame! Shame! Shame! As I was passing in front of the elder queen’s room, she called out, “What’s this, little queen? Your hair bun seems ready to leap over your head—are you sure your head is all right?”

That day, in the garden, my husband told me with utter ease, “I give you your freedom.” Is freedom so easily given, or taken? Is freedom a thing, a tangible object? Freedom is emptiness. Like a fish, I have always swum in the cherished waters of love— suddenly, when I am lifted up into the sky and told, “Here is your freedom”— then I see, here I can neither walk nor live.

Now, when I enter the bedroom, I see only the furniture, only the wardrobe—only the mirror—only the bed— but that all-pervading heart is no longer there. What remains is freedom, only freedom, a void. The stream has dried up completely, the stones and pebbles have emerged. There is no affection, only furniture.

In this world, where and how much truth remains for me— when suddenly such a great riddle arose about this, then once again I met Sandip. When soul collided with soul, that fire blazed up just as before. Where is the falsehood in this? This is overflowing truth— truth that floods over both banks. These people who wander about, who talk, who laugh— there, the elder queen is counting her prayer beads, the middle queen is laughing with her maid, singing the tales of Panchali— but this emergence within me— this is a thousand times truer than all of that!
Sandip said, “I need fifty thousand.” —my intoxicated...
My mind cried out—fifty thousand is nothing! I will bring it!

Where will I find it, how will I get it—are those even questions? Just now, from nothing, I have in a moment soared above everything—as if, with a single gesture, all things can be made to happen. I can do it, I can do it, I can do it—there is not the slightest doubt.

So I set out. Then, looking around, I see—where is the money? Where is the wish-fulfilling tree? Why does the outside world shame the mind so? But still, I will bring the money. However it may be done, there is no disgrace in it. Where there is poverty, there alone is crime; strength is never touched by guilt.

It is the thief who steals, but the victorious king seizes by force. Where is the treasury, in whose hands is the money kept, who stands guard—these are the things I am investigating. At midnight, I have gone to the outer house, stood on the veranda, and gazed fixedly toward the office room. How can I snatch fifty thousand from that bundle of iron bars? There was no pity in my heart—if those who are guarding it were to fall dead there by some magic, then at this very moment, I could, in frenzy, rush into that room. In the mind of the queen of this house, a band of robbers, swords in hand, began to dance, praying to the goddess for her blessing—but the sky outside remained silent, the guards changed at each watch, hour by hour...
The clock struck with a resonant clang, hour after hour, yet the great palace slept on, unafraid, in peace.
At last, one day, I called for Amulya. I said, “The country needs money—can you get this money out from the treasurer?”
He puffed out his chest and replied, “Why shouldn’t I be able to?”
Alas, I too had spoken to Sandip in just such a way—why shouldn’t I be able to? Seeing Amulya’s bravado, I felt not the least bit reassured.
I asked, “Tell me, what will you do?”
Amulya began to propose such outlandish plans that they were fit only for the short stories in monthly magazines, and nowhere else.
I said, “No, Amulya, put aside these childish ideas.”
He said, “All right, I’ll use money to win over those guards.”
“Where will you get the money?”
With an untroubled face he said, “By looting the market.”
I said, “That won’t be necessary, I have my jewelry, that will suffice.”
Amulya said, “But bribes won’t work on the treasurer. There’s a much simpler trick.”
“What kind?”
“That is not worth your hearing. It is very simple.”
“Still, let me hear it.”
Amulya took out first a pocket edition of the Gita from his pocket and placed it on the table, then drew out a small pistol and showed it to me—saying nothing more.

What a disaster! Not for a moment did he hesitate to think of killing our old cashier. His face is such that one would think even killing a crow would be hard for him, yet his words are of an entirely different kind. The real point is, he cannot at all see how real the old cashier is in this world—there, it is as if there is only empty sky. In that sky, there is no life, no pain, only verses:
“Na hanyate hanyamane sharire.” (It is not slain when the body is slain.)
I said, “What are you saying, Amulya! Our Rai-Moshai has a wife, has children—he—”

Where would you find a man in this country who does not have a wife and children? See, what we call compassion is only compassion for ourselves—lest our own weak hearts feel pain, we cannot bring ourselves to hurt another—that is the height of cowardice!
To hear Sandip’s words coming from the mouth of a boy made my heart tremble. He is so utterly raw, believes good to be good simply because—

It is his time to act. Ah, he is at the age to live, to grow. The mother within me awoke. For myself, there was neither good nor evil—there was only death, wearing a sweet form; but when this eighteen-year-old boy could so easily think that killing an old man without fault was dharma, my whole body shuddered. When I saw that there was no sin in his heart, then the sin of his words appeared to me all the more dreadful. It was as if I saw the crime of father and mother reflected in the innocent child.

Looking into those two large, simple eyes, full of faith and enthusiasm, something stirred deep within my soul. He is about to walk into the jaws of a python—who will save him? Why does my country not rise up as a true mother and clasp this boy to her breast? Why does she not say, “O my child, what will you do to save me if I cannot save you?”

I know, I know, the great powers of the world have grown by making pacts with the devil, but the mother stands alone, ready to scorn the devil’s prosperity. The mother does not seek success in action, no matter how great that success may be—she only wants to save! Today, my whole being longs to pull this boy back with both hands and save him.

Just a short while ago, I had told him to commit robbery; now, no matter how contradictory my words may be, he will dismiss it as a woman’s weakness. They only indulge a woman’s weakness when it suits their own pleasure.
I said to Amulya, “Go, you need do nothing—let the responsibility of collecting the money rest with me.”

When he had reached the door, I called him back and said, “Amulya, I am your sister. Today is not the date marked for Bhai Phonta in the almanac, but the true day of Bhai Phonta comes three hundred and sixty-five days a year. I bless you—may God protect you.”

Hearing these words suddenly from my lips, Amulya paused for a moment. Then, bowing down, he touched my feet and took the dust from them. When he stood up, his eyes were brimming with tears. My brother, I am ready to die—may I die bearing all your misfortunes—may you never be guilty of any wrong because of me.
I said to Amulya, “You must give me your pistol as an offering.”
“What will you do with it, Didi?”
“I will practise dying.”
“That’s what I want, Didi, women too must learn to die, to kill.” Saying this, Amulya placed the pistol in my hand.

Amulya, with the radiant lines of his youthful face, left upon my life the first crimson streak of a new dawn. Taking the pistol and tucking it inside the folds of my bodice, I said, “Here lies my last hope of deliverance, my offering for the brotherhood of Rakhi.”
In that place within a woman’s heart where the mother’s seat resides, the window suddenly opened for me, just this once. Then I thought, perhaps from now on it would remain open forever.
But the path of the noble was soon closed again; the beloved woman came and locked the door to the mother’s sanctuary.
The next day, I met with Sandip. Once more, a naked frenzy began to dance upon my heart. But what is this! Is this truly my nature? Never.

Never before have I seen such shamelessness, such cruelty. It was as if a snake-charmer had come and drawn out this serpent from beneath my sari to show me—but this serpent was never within my sari; it was always a thing hidden in the charmer’s own basket. Some evil spirit seems to have possessed me—today, whatever I do is not my own, it is all his play.
That evil spirit, one day, came to me with a flaming torch in hand and said, “I am your country, I am your—”

Sandip, you have nothing greater than me— Bande Mataram." I folded my hands and said, "You are my religion, you are my heaven; whatever I have, I will let it flow in the stream of your love—Bande Mataram."

You want five thousand? Very well, I will bring you five thousand. You want it tomorrow? Very well, you shall have it tomorrow! In the infamy and recklessness of it, that gift of five thousand rupees will foam up like wine—then the festival of the drunkard—ruin. The earth will sway beneath my feet, flames will dart before my eyes, the roar of a storm will rise in my ears, I will not know what lies ahead or behind—then, reeling, I will fall into death—all the fire will be extinguished in an instant, all the ashes will scatter in the wind—nothing will remain.
Until now, I could not think of any way to get the money. That day, in the fierce light of excitement, I suddenly saw the money clearly before my eyes.

Every year, during the Puja, my husband gives his eldest and second eldest sisters a gift of three thousand rupees each. That money, year after year, is deposited in the bank in their names, and grows with interest. This year too, as usual, the gifts have been given, but I know the money has not yet been sent to the bank. I also know where it is. In our bedroom...

In the small dressing room adjoining the inner quarters, in a corner, there is an iron safe; the money is kept inside it. Every year, my husband takes this money to deposit it in the bank in Calcutta. This year, he could not go. That is why I believe in fate. The money is being held back because the country will take it—who has the power to take this money to the bank now? And what power do I have not to take this money myself?

The cataclysmic destroyer has stretched out his claws—he says, “I am hungry, give it to me”—I have given the blood of my own heart, these five thousand rupees! Mother, the one who loses this money will suffer little—but you have made me utterly destitute this time!

How many times before have I, in my heart, called the elder and the middle queens thieves—I accused them of deceiving my trusting husband and taking money by trickery. After their husbands' deaths, they hid and took away many government things; I have told my husband this many times. He would not answer, only remain silent. Then I would get angry and say, “If you must give, give with your own hand, but why allow theft?” The Creator must have laughed at my complaints that day—today, I am about to steal the elder and middle queens’ money from my husband's safe.

At night, my husband undressed in that very room; his keys always remained in the pocket of his coat. I took out those keys and opened the iron safe. The faint noise I made seemed to awaken the entire world. Suddenly, a chill ran through me—my hands and feet turned cold, and my heart began to tremble violently in my chest.

Inside the iron safe, there was a long drawer. I opened it and saw there were no notes, only guineas divided and wrapped in paper packets. How many guineas were in each packet, how many I needed—this was not the time for such calculations. There were twenty packets; I took them all and tied them up in my sari’s end.
It was not light. The weight of theft pressed my spirit to the ground. Perhaps, if it had been a bundle of notes, it would not have felt so much like stealing. But this was all gold.

From the moment I entered my own room as a thief that night, it ceased to be mine. In this room, I once had such great rights, but with this theft, I lost them all. In my mind, I began to chant, “Bande Mataram—Bande Mataram.” Country, my country, my land of gold. All this gold belongs to the country; it is no longer anyone else’s.
But in the darkness of night, the mind grows weak. My husband was sleeping in the next room; with closed eyes, within his own room...

I left the room—went out onto the open terrace of the inner quarters, and, pressing my chest against the bundle of bangles tied in my sari, I lay down on the ground—the parcels throbbed against my heart. The silent night stood by my pillow, raising a finger in warning. I could never see the home as separate from the country. Today, I have plundered the home, I have plundered the country itself—in this sin, at once, my home is no longer my own, and the country too has become alien. If I had served my country through begging, and died before that service was complete, then that unfinished service would have been worship, and the deity would have accepted it. But theft is not worship—how can I offer such a thing to my country? I have come to fill my country’s sacred pond with stolen goods! I am ready to perish myself, but why should I defile my country by clinging to it?

There is no way back for this money to the iron safe. I do not have the strength, in this night, to return to that room, take that key, and open that safe again. If I tried, I would collapse unconscious at the threshold of my husband’s room. Now, before me, there is no path but the road ahead.
I could not bring myself, out of shame, to sit and count how much money I had taken. Let it remain hidden as it is; I will not keep an account of this theft.
On that cold, dark winter night, there was not a trace of mist in the sky;

All the stars are glittering. Lying on the roof, I was thinking—if, in the name of the country, I had to steal those stars one by one, like gold coins—those stars stored in the bosom of darkness—then from the next day, night would be forever widowed—the midnight sky utterly blind—then such a theft would be a theft from the whole world. Today, what I have stolen—this is not the theft of money, it is like stealing the eternal light of the sky—this theft is a theft from the entire world—a theft of trust, a theft of dharma!

The night passed as I lay on the roof. In the morning, when I realized that my husband had already risen and gone, I slowly wrapped my shawl tightly around me and made my way toward the room. At that moment, Mejo-rani was watering the plants in her veranda pots with a pitcher. As soon as she saw me, she exclaimed—
“Oh Choto-rani, have you heard the news?”

I stood still and silent, trembling inside—feeling as if the coins tied in the end of my sari were bulging too high from within the shawl, as if at any moment my clothes would tear and the coins would spill out, jingling, all over the veranda. Having stolen my own wealth and become destitute, such a thief would now be caught even by the servants and maids of this house.
Mejo-rani said, “Your Debi Chowdhurani’s gang has threatened to loot Thakurpo’s funds—they’ve sent an anonymous letter.”

I stood there like a thief, utterly silent! I had been telling Thakurpo to seek your protection. O gracious Devi, be pleased—hold back your followers! We are offering you the sweetmeats of ‘Bande Mataram’. So much has happened before our eyes already; now, for your mercy’s sake, do not let a burglar’s hole be dug in our home.
Without saying a word, I hurried off to my bedroom. I have stepped into quicksand—there is no way to climb out—now, the more I struggle, the deeper I shall sink.
If only I could rid myself of this money at once—slip it from my anchal and hand it over to Sandip—I would be saved. I can bear this burden no longer—my ribs feel as if they are breaking.
Early in the morning, I heard that Sandip was waiting for me. Today, I made no effort to dress or adorn myself—throwing a shawl over my shoulders, I hurried outside.

As soon as I entered the room, I saw Amulya sitting with Sandip. It felt as if whatever little honor and dignity I had left was numbed, draining down my body, slipping through my feet, and sinking deep into the earth.
Today, before that boy, I must lay bare the ultimate dignity of woman! Are they now sitting together, discussing my theft within their group? They have not left even a shred of covering over it!

We shall never understand men. When they set about paving the way for the chariot of their purpose, they do not hesitate for a moment to break the world’s heart into pieces and scatter it as gravel on their path. When they are intoxicated with the urge to create with their own hands, they find joy only in shattering the creations of the Creator himself. My excruciating shame will not even touch the corners of their eyes—there is no tenderness in them for the soul—every bit of their eagerness is directed toward their goal!
Alas, what am I to them! Like a wildflower before the mouth of the flood.

But what did Sandip gain by extinguishing me in this way? These five thousand rupees? But was there not something in me greater than five thousand rupees? Of course there was. I heard of it from Sandip himself—and it was upon hearing that, that I was able to scorn all the world. I would give light, I would give life, I would give strength, I would give nectar: in that faith—in that joy—I had overflowed my banks and rushed out. If only someone could have fulfilled that joy of mine,
Then even if I had died, I would have lived on; even if I had let my whole world drift away, I would not have suffered any loss.

Are they now trying to say that all this was a lie? That the goddess within me does not have the power to grant boons and protection to her devotee? The hymn I heard, the song that drew me down from heaven to dust—was that not to make this dust a heaven, but only to drag heaven down into the dirt?
Sandip fixed his piercing gaze on my face and said,
"Money, Rani! I need money!"

Amulya kept looking at my face—that boy—he was not born from my womb, it is true, but he was born from his mother’s womb, and that mother, is she not the same mother? Ah, that tender face, those gentle eyes, that youthful age! I am a woman, of a mother’s race—yet he asks me to place poison in his hand, and I—am I to give him poison?

"Money, Rani!"—in anger and shame, I wanted to fling that bundle of gold at Sandip’s head. I could not seem to untie the knot of my sari; my fingers began to tremble violently. Then, when those paper-wrapped bundles fell upon the table, Sandip’s face darkened. Surely he thought that inside those wrappings there were only half-rupees.
What contempt! What cruel disdain for helplessness!
It seemed as though he could strike me. Sandip must have thought that I was here to bargain with him—that I wanted to settle his demand for five thousand rupees with just two or three hundred.
For a moment, I thought he might take these bundles and fling them out the window. Was he a beggar? He was a king.
Amulya asked, “Is there no more, Ranididi?”
His voice was full of compassion. I felt as if I might cry out and burst into tears. With all my strength, I pressed down on my heart and only managed to shake my head a little.
Sandip remained silent—he did not even touch the bundles, nor did he say a word.
I thought of leaving, but my feet simply would not move—as if the earth might split open and draw me in, only then would this lump of clay find shelter in the soil and be saved.
My humiliation struck the heart of that boy. Suddenly, pretending great joy, he exclaimed, “Is this not enough! This will do more than plenty! You have saved us, Ranididi!”
With that, he tore open one of the bundles—the coins inside gleamed and glittered.
In a single moment, it was as if a dark covering was lifted from Sandip’s face. His eyes and face began to shine with joy as well. In the depths of the mind, this sudden reversal of wind—

Unable to contain the gust of emotion, he leapt up from the chair and rushed to me. What blessing he sought, I do not know. Like lightning, I glanced once at Amulya’s face—suddenly, as if struck by a whip, his face had turned pale. With all my strength, I pushed Sandip away. His head struck the stone table with a sharp sound, and then he fell to the ground—he lay motionless for a while. After this tremendous effort, there was not an ounce of strength left in my body—I collapsed onto the chair.

Amulya’s face lit up with joy—he did not even glance at Sandip—he sat at my feet, taking the dust from them. Oh, my child, my dear, this little act of reverence of yours is today the last drop of nectar in the empty vessel of my world. I could bear no more—my tears broke forth. Covering my face with both hands and the end of my sari, I began to sob. The more I felt Amulya’s gentle, sorrowful touch upon my feet, the more my tears threatened to overflow.

After a while, regaining some composure, I opened my eyes to see Sandip sitting by the table as if nothing at all had happened, tying up the coins in his handkerchief. Amulya rose from my feet—his eyes were brimming with tears.
Sandip, without hesitation, looked up at our faces and said, “Six thousand rupees.”
Amulya said, “But we don’t need that much money, Sandip Babu. I’ve calculated—three and a half thousand rupees will be enough for our present needs.”
Sandip replied, “Our work is not just for the present. Is there any limit to what we need?”
Amulya said, “That may be, but for what we’ll need in the future, I’ll take responsibility—please return those extra two and a half thousand rupees to Ranididi.”
Sandip looked at my face, and I spoke up, “No, no, I don’t want to touch that money anymore. Do whatever you wish with it.”
Sandip, turning to Amulya, said, “Can men ever give as women do?”
Amulya, his voice full of emotion, said, “Women are goddesses.”

Sandip said, “At best, we men can give our strength, but women—they give themselves. From the depths of their being, they give birth to the child, nurture it—not from the outside, but from within. That is the true gift, the real giving.”
Saying this, Sandip looked at me and said, “Rani, what you gave today—if it were only money, then I—”
I did not touch it; you have given me something greater than your own life.”

Perhaps man has two kinds of intelligence. One part of my mind understands that Sandip is deceiving me, but another part is beguiled. Sandip has no character, but Sandip has power. That is why, in the very moment he awakens life, he also strikes with the arrow of death. In his hand is the inexhaustible quiver of the gods, yet among the blades of grass lie the weapons of demons.

All the gold coins would not fit in Sandip’s handkerchief, so he said, “Rani, could you give me one of your handkerchiefs?” As soon as I took out a handkerchief and handed it to him, he touched it to his head. Then, sitting down at my feet, he bowed before me and said, “Devi, I came running only to offer you this salutation, and you pushed me away. That push is my blessing. I have placed that push upon my head.” Saying this, he showed me the very spot on his head where my hand had struck.

Did I truly misunderstand? Had Sandip really come to bow before me with outstretched hands, and the sudden frenzy that flared in his face and eyes—surely Amulya saw it too? But in his hymns of praise, Sandip knows how to weave such wondrous melodies that I cannot argue; it is as if some opium intoxication clouds the eyes with which I see the truth.

The wound I inflicted upon Sandip, he returned to me twofold; the injury on his head began to bleed within my own breast. When I received Sandip’s salutation, my theft was suddenly exalted. The gold coins upon the table, disregarding all public censure, scorning every pang of moral conscience, began to gleam and laugh aloud. Even Amulya, like myself, lost his senses. For a brief moment, the reverence he had withheld from Sandip surged forth unimpeded; the vessel of his heart overflowed with flowers for my worship and for Sandip’s as well. What gentle nectar of simple faith, like the light of the morning star at dawn, began to radiate from his eyes!
I offered worship, I received worship, and my sin became luminous. Amulya, gazing at my face with folded hands, said, “Bande Mataram.”

But the words of praise are not always to be heard. I have nothing within myself to preserve my own reverence for myself, nothing to sustain it from within. I cannot enter my own bedchamber. That iron safe frowns at me; our bed seems to extend a forbidding hand toward me. I long to flee from this humiliation within myself—again and again I feel as if I must go to Sandip and listen to his hymn of praise. My

From the abyss of unfathomable shame, there remains in this world only that one altar of worship—if I step away from it, there is emptiness everywhere. That is why, day and night, I wish to cling to that altar. I long for praise, I long for praise, day and night I crave praise—if that single cup of wine is ever emptied, I cannot survive. That is why, all day long, my heart aches to go to Sandip and listen to his words—for today, to realize the worth of my own existence, I need Sandip in this world so much!

When my husband comes for lunch at noon, I cannot sit before him—yet, not sitting is so much more embarrassing that I cannot do that either—so I sit a little behind him in such a way that our faces do not meet.

That day, I was sitting just so, while he was eating, when Mejhorani came in and said, “Thakurpo, you laugh off all those threatening letters from the dacoits, but I am afraid. Haven’t you yet sent this year’s offering money to the bank?”
My husband replied, “No, I haven’t had the time.”
Mejhorani said, “Look, brother, you are so careless, that money—”
My husband laughed and said, “Why, it’s in the iron safe in the room next to my bedroom!”
“If it’s taken from there, can you say anything about it?”
“If a thief enters my house as well, then someday you too might be stolen!”
“Oh, no one will take me, you needn’t worry. What’s worth taking is right here in your own house. No, brother, I’m not joking—don’t keep money at home.”
“The payment for the main rent is due in about five days. I’ll send that money to the bank in Calcutta along with it.”
“Look, brother, don’t forget. With your absent-minded nature, anything could happen.”
“If money is stolen from this house, it will be my money that is stolen, not yours, Baurani.”

“Oh, brother-in-law, when I hear you talk like that, I get a fever. Am I speaking in terms of mine and yours? If yours is stolen, will it not affect me? The cruel fate has taken everything from me, and left me only my precious brother-in-law—do you think I don’t understand his value? I can’t, like your elder wife, spend my days and nights lost in worship. What the gods have given me is more precious than the gods themselves. What do you say, Chotorani, why are you sitting there so silently, like a wooden doll? You know, brother-in-law, Chotorani thinks I flatter you. Well, if the need arises, flattery it must be—”

But are you that kind of brother-in-law who waits for flattery? If you were like that Madhab Chakraborty, then even our elder queen would have given up her worship of the gods by now, and would spend her days begging you, hands and feet together, for the sake of a half-paisa. Still, I say, that would have been better for her—she wouldn’t have so much time to make up stories and slander you.”
Thus the middle queen went on chattering endlessly, and in between, she kept drawing Thakurpo’s attention to the fried fritters, the bell-shaped sweets, and even the prawn heads.

My head was spinning by then. There was no time left; I had to find a way out immediately—what could be done, what was possible—these questions kept circling in my mind, and at that moment, the middle queen’s incessant scolding became utterly unbearable to me. Especially since I knew nothing escaped her eyes—she kept glancing at my face every now and then. I do not know what she saw, but it felt to me as if every thought was plainly written on my face.
There is no end to audacity—I forced a casual, easy laugh and said, “The real truth is, it’s only me whom the middle queen distrusts so much—thieves, robbers, all sorts of nonsense!”
The middle queen smiled slyly and said, “That’s exactly right, you know—”
Ah, a woman's theft is truly ruinous. But you will surely be caught by me, for I am not a man! With what will you try to deceive me?”
I said, “If you are so afraid, then let me leave whatever I have with you as security. If I cause any loss, you may deduct it from that.”
Mejorani laughed and said, “Listen, just listen to what Chotorani says! There are losses in this world that no security, in this life or the next, can redeem.”
During this conversation, my husband did not say a single word. As soon as he finished eating, he went outside. These days, he no longer sits inside the house to rest.

Most of my precious jewelry was kept in the treasurer’s storeroom. Still, what I had with me was worth no less than thirty or thirty-five thousand rupees. I took that jewelry box and opened it before Mejorani, saying, “Mejorani, I am leaving this jewelry with you. Now you can be at ease.”
Mejorani rested her cheek on her hand and said, “Oh my, you have astonished me! Do you really think I am losing sleep at night out of fear that you will steal my money?”
I said, “But what is wrong with being afraid, Mejo-rani? Tell me, who truly knows whom in this world?”

Mejo-rani replied, “So, you have come to teach me a lesson by asking me to trust you, have you? I don’t even have a fixed place to keep my own jewelry—am I to spend my life guarding ornaments? The maids and servants are always moving about; you’d better take your jewelry with you, my dear.”

As soon as I left Mejo-rani, I went to the outer drawing room and sent for Amulya. Along with Amulya, I saw Sandip arrive as well. I had no time to delay then, so I said to Sandip, “I have something special to discuss with Amulya—if you would just—”
Sandip gave a wooden smile and said, “Do you see Amulya as someone separate from me? If you wish to win him away from me, I won’t be able to hold him back.”

I did not answer this and stood there in silence. Sandip said, “All right then, finish your special conversation with Amulya, but after that you must also give me a chance to speak with you privately. Otherwise, I shall be defeated; I can accept anything, but not defeat. My share is always greater than everyone else’s. I have been fighting with Providence over this all my life. I shall defeat Providence, but I shall not be defeated myself.”
With a sharp, biting remark, Sandip struck Amulya and left the room. I said to Amulya, “My dear brother Lakshmi, you must do something for me.”
He replied, “Whatever you ask, I will do it with my life, Didi.”

From inside the shaal tree chest, I took out the jewelry box and placed it before him. I said, “By pawning or selling this jewelry—however it may be—you must bring me six thousand rupees as soon as possible.”
Amulya, pained, exclaimed, “No, Didi, no—not by selling or pawning your jewelry! I will bring you six thousand rupees myself.”
I said irritably, “Keep such talk to yourself—I have not a moment to lose. Take this jewelry box—go to Calcutta by tonight’s train, and by tomorrow, you must bring me six thousand rupees in cash.”

Amulya lifted a diamond choker from the box, its brilliance flashing in the light, then set it down again with a sorrowful face. I said, “These diamond ornaments will not easily fetch their proper price; that is why I am giving you jewelry worth more than thirty thousand. Even if it all goes, so be it—but I must have six thousand rupees, without fail.”
Amulya said, “Listen, Didi, this taking from you—”

Sandipbabu has taken six thousand rupees; I quarreled with him over this. What shame it is to speak of! Sandipbabu says, for the sake of the country, one must cast aside all shame. That may well be so. But this feels somehow different— I have gained the strength not to fear death for the country, not to hesitate to kill for it, but I cannot, by any means, rid my heart of the disgrace of taking this money from your hands. Here, Sandipbabu is much stronger than I—he bears not a trace of regret. He says, “The one whose box held the money, the one who truly owned it—this illusion must be broken; otherwise, what meaning has the mantra ‘Bande Mataram’?”

As he spoke, Amulya grew more and more animated. When he finds a listener in me, his enthusiasm for such talk increases all the more. He continued, “In the Gita, Lord Sri Krishna has said, the soul cannot be slain by anyone. To kill someone is but a manner of speaking. Taking money is just the same! Whose is the money? No one creates it, no one takes it with them, it is not a part of anyone’s soul. Today it is mine, tomorrow it belongs to my son, another day to my creditor. That restless money, when in truth it belongs to no one, if instead of falling into the hands of your idle son it is used in the service of the country by patriots, then if you condemn it, does it truly become blameworthy?”

When I hear Sandip’s words coming from the mouth of this boy, my heart trembles with fear. Let the snake-charmers play with snakes to the sound of their flutes—if they must die, let them die knowingly. But alas, these boys are so naïve, the blessings of the whole world seem always intent on protecting them, and yet, laughing, they reach out to play with the snake without knowing it for what it is. Then I understand clearly how dreadful a curse this snake is! Sandip has understood it exactly—I could die at his hands myself, but I will save this boy by snatching him away from Sandip’s grasp.
I smiled a little and said to Amulya, “So, even you patriots need money for your service to the country?”

Amulya lifted his head proudly and replied, “Of course we do. They are our kings—if they are poor, their strength wanes. You know, I never let Sandip Babu travel in anything but first class. He never feels the slightest hesitation in enjoying royal fare—he must maintain this dignity—not for himself, but for all of us. Sandip Babu says that those who are gods in this world, their greatest weapon is the enchantment of wealth. For them, to take a vow of poverty is not to embrace suffering, but self-destruction.”
At that moment, Sandip entered the room silently and suddenly. I hurriedly placed my hand over my jewelry box.
I put on my shawl. Sandip asked, with a crooked smile,
"Your special conversation with Amulya isn’t over yet, is it?"
Amulya, a little embarrassed, said, "No, our talk is done. Nothing special."
I said, "No, Amulya, it isn’t finished yet."
Sandip said, "Then, is this Sandip’s second exit?"
I replied, "Yes."
"Then, Sandip Kumar’s re-entry—"
"Not today—I won’t have the time."
Sandip’s eyes flared up—he said, "So, there is time only for special work, and none to waste?"
Jealousy! Where the weak is overpowered, can the helpless refrain from sounding the trumpet of victory? That is why I said, very firmly, "No, I don’t have the time."
Sandip left, his face darkened. Amulya, a little anxious, said, "Ranididi, Sandipbabu is annoyed."
With some force, I said, "He has neither reason nor right to be annoyed. Let me tell you one thing, Amulya—you must never, under any circumstances, tell Sandipbabu about my selling the jewelry."
Amulya said, "No, I won’t tell him."
"Then don't delay any longer, leave tonight by the night train."

Saying this, I immediately left the room with Amulya. Coming outside, I saw Sandip standing on the veranda. I realized at once that he would try to catch Amulya now. To prevent that, I had to call out to him—"Sandipbabu, what was it you wanted to say?"
"My words are nothing important, just idle talk, and when there is no time—"
I said, "There is time."
Amulya left. As soon as we entered the room, Sandip said, "You gave something, a box, into Amulya's hands—what kind of box is that?"
The box had not escaped Sandip's notice. I replied a little firmly, "If it were something I needed to tell you, I would have given it to him in your presence."
"Do you think Amulya won't tell me?"
"No, he won't!"

Sandip could no longer contain his anger; he flared up completely and said, "You think you can exercise authority over me—you cannot. That Amulya, if I were to trample him under my feet, that would be his blissful death. You want to subdue him to your will, but as long as I am here, that will not happen."
Weak, weak! After all this time, Sandip has realized that he is weak before me. That is why this sudden, uncontrolled anger. He—

He has understood that he cannot force me, that I possess a strength against which coercion will not work;—with a single glance of mine I can shatter the walls of his fortress. That is why today he blusters so. I did not reply, only smiled a little.
After so long, I have come to stand on the upper floor above him—let me not lose this place, let me not descend. Even in my misfortune, let me retain a little of my dignity!
Sandip said, “I know that box of yours is the jewel box.”
I replied, “You may guess as you please, but I will not tell.”
“You trust Amulya more than you trust me? Do you know, that boy is but the shadow of my shadow, the echo of my echo; if he were to leave my side, he would be nothing!”
“Where he is not your echo, there he is Amulya, and there I trust him more than I trust your echo.”
“For the consecration of the Mother’s worship, you have promised to give me all your jewels—do not forget that. That is already as good as given.”
“If the deity leaves any of my jewels remaining, then I shall give those to the deity. How can I give away jewels that are stolen from me?”

"Look, don’t try to slip away from me like that. I have work to do now; let me finish that first. After that, there will be plenty of time for all your feminine wiles and subterfuge. Then I too shall join in that play."

From the very moment I stole my husband’s money and handed it to Sandip, the inner harmony of our relationship vanished. Not only have I lost all my worth, become as cheap as a mere trifle—since then, even Sandip finds no real ground to wield his power over me. Once something falls into the fist, there’s no more use for arrows. That is why Sandip no longer has the heroic aura about him. In his words now, there is a harsh, base note of discord!

Sandip sat looking at me, his bright eyes raised to my face; as I watched, his gaze seemed to burn with the thirst of the midday sky. His feet stirred restlessly once or twice—I could sense he was about to rise—at any moment he might get up and seize me. My heart began to tremble within me—the veins in my whole body throbbed, blood roared in my ears; I realized that if I sat there a moment longer, I would not be able to get up at all. With all the strength I could muster, I tore myself away from the chair and stood up.
I rushed towards the door. From Sandip’s almost strangled throat came a muffled cry—“Where are you running, Rani?”

The next moment, he sprang up and came towards me to catch hold of me. Just then, the sound of footsteps and shoes was heard outside. Sandip quickly returned to the couch and sat down. I turned my face towards the bookshelf and stood gazing at the names of the books.

As soon as my husband entered the room, Sandip exclaimed, “Oh, Nikhil, don’t you have Browning on your shelf? I was just telling the Queen Bee about our old college club—do you remember that poem by Browning, the one we all fought over, trying to translate? Come now, don’t say you’ve forgotten! You know, the one that goes—

She should never have looked at me. If she meant I should not love her! There are plenty...men you call such, I suppose...she may discover All her soul to, if she pleases, And yet leave much as she found them; But I'm not so, and she knew it When she fixed me, glancing round them.
I had tried to fumble out a Bengali version of it, but it didn’t turn out like “Those who are wise will joyfully…”

Pan is an endless nectar.” At one time I thought, perhaps I have become a poet, it won’t be long now—Providence, in His mercy, saved me from that fate. But our Dakshinacharan, if he were not today an inspector of the salt monopoly, would surely have become a poet. He did a splendid translation—reading it, one feels as if it is pure Bengali, not the language of some country that exists only in geography and nowhere else.
“If she knew she would not love me, Then should she have cast her glance at me?”
There are many such people in this world (though I hesitate to call them people at all)—if she had bared her soul to them, still they would have remained as empty and unmoved as before.
I am not like them—she knew this in her heart, when she bound me fast, piercing me with the corner of her eye.

No, Queen of the Bees, you are searching in vain—since her marriage, Nikhil has completely given up reading poetry. Perhaps he no longer needs it. I gave it up out of the press of work, but now it seems as if “the fever of poetry in men” is about to seize me!
My husband said, “I have come to warn you, Sandip.”
Sandip replied, “About the fever of poetry?”
