My husband, instead of joining in the banter, said, “For some days now, Maulvis have been coming and going from Dhaka—there is an effort underway to incite the Muslims of this region from within. They are displeased with you, and might suddenly cause some disturbance.”
“Are you advising me to flee?”
“I have come to inform you, not to advise.”

“If I were the landlord here, then it would be the Muslims who should be worried, not I. Instead of making me anxious, if you would direct a little of your concern towards them, that would be more fitting for both you and me. Do you know, through your weakness, you have made even the neighboring landlords weak?”

“Sandip, I have not given you advice, so if you would refrain from advising me, let us go. It is pointless. There is one more thing I must say. For some time now, you and your followers have been secretly causing trouble among my tenants. This cannot continue; now you must leave my estate.”
“Is it for fear of the Muslims, or is there some other fear?”
There is a kind of pride that makes the absence of fear itself a form of cowardice—I am speaking to you out of that very fear, Sandip. In another five days, I am going to Calcutta; at that time...
“You want to come with me too! You can stay at our house in Kolkata, there is no objection to that!”

“Well then, five days to think it over. Meanwhile, O Queen Bee, let us sing the farewell song as you leave your hive! O poet of modern Bengal, open your doors, let me plunder your words—this theft is yours—for you have made my song your own—so be it, your name is known, but the song is mine.”
With this, in his coarse, broken voice, just off-key, he began to sing in the Bhairavi raga—

“Season of honey lingers ever in your land of sweetness. Tears and laughter of coming and going drift in the wind there. Those who depart, only they leave, but alas, the blooming of flowers never ends, The flowers that must fall, only they drop at the end of the day. When I was near, how many songs I gave; Now that I am gone, is there nothing left as a gift? Shaded by the garden’s blossoms, I leave behind this hope, That the fire-filled spring may find your mud when the monsoon comes.”

There is no end to his courage—nor any covering for it—it is as naked as fire itself. There is never time to stop him—trying to forbid him is like forbidding thunder, the lightning laughs at such commands and sweeps them away.
I stepped outside. When I turned to the inner part of the house...
As I was about to leave, suddenly I saw Amulya appear from somewhere and stand before me. He said, “Ranididi, don’t worry about anything. I am going, and I will not return defeated, no matter what.”
Looking at his earnest, youthful face, I said, “Amulya, let me not think for myself, but let me be able to think for all of you.”
Amulya was about to go, but I called him back and asked, “Amulya, is your mother alive?”
“She is.”
“A sister?”
“No, I am my mother’s only son. My father died when I was very young.”
“Then go, Amulya, go back to your mother.”
“Didi, here I see both my mother and my sister.”
I said, “Amulya, before you leave tonight, eat here before you go.”
He replied, “There won’t be time, Didirani. Give me your prasad to take with me, and I’ll carry it along.”
“What do you like to eat, Amulya?”
“When I was with my mother, in the month of Poush, I would eat my fill of pitha. When I return, I will eat pitha made by your hands, Didirani!”
chapters.summary: Bimala, struggling with her sense of power and loss, tries to obtain money for Sandip.

chapters.title: Nikhilesh: Ghosts in My Home
paragraphs: Waking up at three in the night, I suddenly feel that the world in which I once lived has died, become a ghost, and now sits here occupying my bed, my room, all my belongings. I can well understand now why people are afraid even of the ghosts of those they once knew. When the familiar becomes unknown in a single moment, it is a terror. All the habits of life that once flowed in an easy stream—now, when I must guide them into a channel that has not yet been dug, a strange confusion arises; it becomes hard to preserve my own nature; looking at myself, I wonder if I too have become someone else.

For some days now, I have sensed that Sandip and his followers have begun to stir up trouble in our region. If I were still my usual self, I would have told Sandip firmly, “Leave this place.” But in this turmoil, I have become unnatural. My path is no longer straightforward. There is a certain shame in telling Sandip to go. Another thought intrudes alongside it; in my own eyes, I become diminished.
Marriage was something internal to me—it was not merely

My household life, or my journey through the world, is not merely a domestic institution. It is the unfolding of my life itself. That is why I could never exert the slightest force upon it from the outside—if I ever tried, it felt as though I were insulting my own deity. I will never be able to make anyone understand this. Perhaps I am strange. Perhaps that is why I have been defeated. But how can I save the outer world from being deceived, if in doing so I must deceive my own inner self?

I have taken initiation into that truth which, from within, creates the outer world. That is why today I have had to tear apart the web of the external so completely. My deity will grant me freedom from the slavery of the outside. I shall win that freedom at the cost of my heart’s own blood. But when I do win it, then the kingdom of the inner self will be mine.

Already I am tasting the flavor of that liberation. Again and again, from within the darkness, the dawn-bird of my soul bursts into song. Even if the Bimala fashioned by illusion, that dream, should fly away, it will not matter; my inner being, my true self, keeps reassuring me with this message.

From Mastermoshai I have heard that Sandip, joining with Harishkundu, is making grand preparations for the worship of Mahishamardini. The expenses for this festival are being extracted from Harishkundu and from the tenants. Our poet and the learned Vidyabagish Mosai have been set to composing a hymn...

...is being done, which has two meanings. Sandip even had a bit of an argument with Mastermoshai about this. Sandip says, “There is an evolution of the gods; if the grandsons do not remake the gods created by their grandfathers in their own image, then they will become atheists. My mission is to modernize the ancient gods, to liberate them from the shackles of the past—this is why I was born. I am the savior of the gods.”

Since childhood I have seen that Sandip is a magician of ideas—he has no need to discover the truth; his delight lies in conjuring illusions of truth. Had he been born in Central Africa, he would have been thrilled to prove, with new arguments, that the greatest spiritual practice for bringing people closer together is to offer human sacrifices and feast on human flesh. Deception is his craft; he cannot live without deceiving even himself. I believe that every time Sandip creates a new enchantment with his words, he himself feels he has found the truth—no matter how much one creation contradicts the next.

In any case, I cannot in the least assist in brewing this intoxicating liquor of illusion for the country. From the very beginning, I feel I cannot take part in the effort to habituate the young men, who wish to serve the country, to this intoxication.

If there are no hands. Those who wish to accomplish work by beguiling with mantras, they value only the deed itself, but the mind they bewitch means nothing to them. If I cannot save the country from frenzy, then the worship of the nation will become its own poison-offering; the work done for the country will strike at its heart like a hostile Brahmastra.

I have told Sandip, right in front of Bimala, that he must leave my house. Perhaps both Bimala and Sandip will misunderstand my intention in this. But I wish to be free from the fear of being misunderstood. Let Bimala misunderstand me as well.

From Dhaka, the visits of Maulvi preachers have begun. The Muslims in our area used to abhor cow-slaughter almost as much as the Hindus. But now, in one or two places, the slaughter of cows has started to appear. I first heard of it from my own Muslim tenants, and I also heard their protests. Now I realize, it will be difficult to prevent. At the root of this affair is an artificial obstinacy. If we try to oppose it, that obstinacy will gradually become genuine. That is precisely the strategy of our adversaries.

I summoned my principal Hindu tenants and tried hard to explain to them. I said, “We can keep to our own religion. We have no right over the religion of others. Because I am a Vaishnava, does that mean the Shakta will refrain from bloodshed?”
What can be done? The Muslims must be allowed to follow their own religion. You must not create any disturbance.”
They said, “Maharaj, all these troubles never existed before.”
I replied, “They did not, because they did not wish it. Now see to it that, by their own will, they desist again. That is not the path of quarrel.”
They said, “No, Maharaj, those days are gone. If we do not enforce discipline, nothing will stop.”
I said, “Discipline through violence will never bring an end to this; rather, it will only increase man’s cruelty towards man.”
Among them was one who had studied English; he had learned to repeat the phrases of the day. He said, “Look, this is not just a matter of custom, our country is agrarian—here, cattle—”

I interrupted, “Here, buffaloes also give milk, buffaloes also plough the fields, but when, with their severed heads smeared with blood, we dance about the courtyard, and then, invoking religion, quarrel with the Muslims, religion itself laughs in secret; only the quarrel grows fierce. If only the cow is sacred and the buffalo is not, then that is not religion, that is blind superstition.”
The English-educated one said, “But do you know who is behind all this—”
Can’t you see? The Muslims have come to know that they will be punished—haven’t you heard what a commotion they caused in Panchur?”

I said, “This very weapon, with which the Muslims can now strike at us—this weapon is one we have forged with our own hands—such is the justice of dharma. What we have accumulated for so long will now be spent upon ourselves.”

The English-educated one said, “All right, let it be spent then. But there is a certain satisfaction for us in this—this time, it is our victory—the law, which was always their greatest strength, today we have trampled it into dust. All this time they were the rulers, but now we will make them taste banditry. No one will write this in history, but it will remain forever in our hearts.”

Meanwhile, in paper after paper, I became notorious in infamy. I hear that, in the Chakrabartis’ area, by the riverside cremation ground, a group of patriots made an effigy of me out of straw and burned it with great ceremony—there were many other arrangements for my humiliation! These people had come to me, wanting to set up a joint business by opening a cloth mill, and tried to persuade me to buy a large share. I had said, “If only it were just my money that would be lost, I would have had no regret, but—”
“If you open a factory, many poor people will lose their money—that is why I will not buy shares.”
Why, sir? Do you not care for the welfare of the country?

Business may bring benefit to the country, but simply declaring that we will serve the country does not make it business. When we were calm, our business did not flourish—and now, just because we are fired up, will our business suddenly soar?
In short, tell me plainly—you will not buy shares.
I will buy them when I am convinced your business is truly business. Just because your fire is burning does not mean your pot will boil—there is no direct evidence of that.

They think I am very calculating, that I am miserly. Sometimes I feel like opening my Swadeshi business ledger and showing it to them! And do they even know the story of that time when I sat down to improve the crops of my motherland? For years I imported sugarcane from Java and Mauritius and had it cultivated; on the advice of the government’s agricultural department, I left no method of plowing or irrigation untried. And what was the final harvest? It was the suppressed laughter of the farmers in my area. That laughter is still suppressed to this day. Later, when I translated government agricultural journals and tried to introduce them to Japanese beans or foreign cotton cultivation...

Whenever I have tried to speak, I have seen that old, suppressed smile can no longer remain hidden. In those days, there was no sign or sound of patriots in the country; the mantra of 'Bande Mataram' was silent. And as for that steamship of mine—let those distant matters remain unspoken, what is the use of bringing them up? If, in the fire these men kindle for the good of the country, my own straw effigy is burnt and the flames subside, then perhaps there will be some respite!

What news is this! There has been a robbery at our Chakwa office! Last night, an installment of seven and a half thousand rupees from the main revenue was deposited there, and at dawn today it was to be sent by boat to our headquarters. For convenience, the manager had exchanged the money at the treasury for ten and twenty rupee notes and had sealed them in packets. In the middle of the night, a gang of robbers, armed with guns and pistols, looted the treasury. Kasem Sardar was wounded by a pistol shot.

What is astonishing is that the robbers took only six thousand rupees, leaving the remaining fifteen hundred rupees scattered about the room. They could easily have taken all the money. In any case, the robbers have had their turn; now it will be the police’s turn. The money is gone, and now there will be no peace either.
When I went inside the house, I saw that the news had already spread. The second queen came and said, “Brother-in-law, what a disaster this is!”
To dispel her worries, I said, “There is still much calamity left to come. For now, we can manage to live for some time, eating and drinking as usual.”
No, brother, I am not joking—why are they so angry with you? Dear brother-in-law, couldn’t you try to keep them a little pleased? For the sake of the whole country’s people—
For the sake of the whole country’s people, I cannot let the country itself be ruined.

Just the other day, I heard what they did with you by the riverside. Shame, shame! I am terrified! The younger queen has been reading English books—she has no fear at all— As for me, I only find relief after calling the priest Kenaram and arranging for rites of peace and well-being. Scold me if you will, brother-in-law, but you should go to Calcutta—if you stay here, who knows what they might do to you someday!
Today, the elder queen’s worries have poured nectar into my heart! Annapurna, the doors of your hearts will never close to our pleas for alms.
Brother-in-law, that money you have kept beside your bedroom—it's not good, you know. What if they get wind of it from somewhere, and in the end— It’s not the money I worry about, brother—who knows—
To calm the elder queen, I said, “All right,
I took out the money and sent it at once to our accounts office! "The day after tomorrow, I will deposit it in the Calcutta bank and return."
Saying this, I entered the bedroom and saw that the adjoining room was closed. As I pushed the door, Bimala called from inside, "I am changing my clothes."
Mejorani said, "So early in the morning, Chotorani is dressing up! How surprising! Perhaps today they have their Bande Mataram meeting! Oh, Devi Chowdhurani, are you loading up the spoils of loot?"
Thinking I could settle everything a little later, I stepped outside and found the police inspector present!
I asked, "Did you find any clue?"
"I do have my suspicions."
"Whom do you suspect?"
"That Kasem Sardar."
"What are you saying? He is injured!"
"The injury is nothing—just a scratch on his leg, a little blood—he did it himself."
I could not, in any way, suspect Kasem—he is trustworthy.
"Trustworthy, I agree, but that alone does not mean he cannot steal. I have seen this too."
A man who has kept his trust for twenty-five years—if one day, suddenly—
Even if that happens, I cannot send him to jail.
Why should you be the one to do it? The responsibility of punishment lies with those whose duty it is!
Why did Kasem take six thousand rupees and leave the rest behind?

That very doubt is born in the mind to give rise to suspicion. Say what you will, the man is clever. He guards your estate office, and surely, all the thefts and robberies that have occurred in this area recently have him at their root.

The inspector gave many examples of how the lathiyals, after committing robberies twenty-five or thirty miles away, could return in a single night and have their attendance marked in the landlord’s office.
I asked, “Have you brought Kasem here?”
He said, “No, he is at the police station—the Deputy Sahib will come soon to investigate.”
I said, “I want to see him.”
As soon as I met Kasem, he clung to my feet and wept, saying, “By God, Maharaj, I did not do this.”
I said, “Kasem, I do not suspect you. Do not be afraid—I will not let you be punished for a crime you did not commit.”

Kasem could not give a proper description of the dacoits—he only kept exaggerating—four or five hundred men, such enormous guns, swords, and so on. I realized all this was nonsense; either everything had grown larger in his eyes out of fear, or he was inflating the story to cover the shame of defeat. He suspects that my enmity with Harishkundu is at the root of all this—even claims he distinctly heard the voice of their leader, Ekram Sarddar.
I said, “Look here, Kasem, don’t you dare drag others’ names into this based on mere guesswork. Whether Harishkundu is involved or not is not for you to invent.”

Returning home, I sent for Mastermoshai. He shook his head and said, “There is no welfare left. We have set aside religion and enthroned the nation in its place—now all the sins of the nation will rise up, unashamed, and burst forth.”
What do you think, is this the work—
I do not know, but the wind of sin has begun to blow. Drive them out, drive them out from your area at once. I have given them one more day—these beasts must go.
Listen, let me tell you one thing: take Bimala to Calcutta. From here, she is seeing the outside world in a narrow way; she cannot rightly judge the measure of men and things.

He cannot. Show him the world once— Let him see humanity, the field of human action, from a broader vantage. I was thinking the same thing. But do not delay any longer. Listen, Nikhil, the history of mankind is being forged by all nations, all peoples of the world; therefore, even in politics, one cannot barter away religion to expand the nation. I know Europe does not accept this in its heart, but for that reason alone I will not accept Europe as our sole teacher. For the sake of truth, a man may die and become immortal; if a nation dies for truth, it too will become immortal in the history of mankind. May the feeling of that truth become pure in this very land of Bharat, amidst the unyielding, thunderous laughter of the Evil One! But what is this plague of sin that has entered our land from abroad? The whole day passed amidst such various tumults. Weary, I went to bed at night. I decided not to take out that money today but to do so tomorrow morning. At some point in the night, I awoke. The room was dark. I seemed to hear a sound—someone, perhaps, weeping. Now and then, like the gusts of a monsoon storm, I heard long sighs, heavy with tears. It seemed to me, this was the weeping from the very heart of my room.
There is no one else in my room. For some days now, Bimala has been sleeping in an adjoining room. I rose from my bed. Going out to the veranda, I saw Bimala lying face down on the ground.

Such things cannot be put into words. What this is, only He knows, who sits at the heart of the universe and receives all the sorrows of the world. The sky is mute, the stars are silent, the night is still—in the midst of all this, that one sleepless weeping!

We try to settle all these joys and sorrows by giving them some name, reconciling them with worldly life and with scripture, calling them good or bad, and thus making our peace! But this source of pain that wells up, flooding the breast of darkness—does it have any name? Standing there, in the dead of night, in the midst of the silence of millions of stars, when I looked at her, my heart cried out in fear, Who am I to judge this? O Life, O Infinite World, O Lord of the Infinite World, I bow with folded hands before the mystery that dwells among you.
For a moment I thought of returning. But I could not.

Silently, I sat down by Bimala’s head and placed my hand upon her hair. At first, her whole body became rigid as wood—then suddenly that hardness broke, and her tears began to flow in a thousand streams. Human
There is so much weeping in the heart that it is impossible to say where it might find a place to rest.

Gently, I began to stroke Bimala’s head with my hand. Then, at some moment, she groped for my feet and drew them towards her—pressing them to her breast so tightly that I felt, in that very pressure, her heart might break.
chapters.summary: Nikhilesh grapples with profound alienation and turmoil in his home as Sandip's influence grows, communal tensions rise.

chapters.title: Bimala: The Burden of Misfortune
paragraphs: This morning Amulya is supposed to return from Calcutta. I have told Behari to let me know as soon as he arrives. But I cannot remain still. I went and sat in the outer drawing room.

When I sent Amulya to Calcutta to sell my jewelry, I suppose I thought of nothing but myself. It never occurred to me, not even once, that he is just a boy; if he goes to sell such valuable jewelry, everyone will suspect him. We women are so helpless that we seem to have no way but to shift our own dangers onto others’ shoulders. When we are drowning, we drag five others down with us.

I had spoken with such pride, saying I would save Amulya. As if one who is herself sinking can save another! Alas, alas, am I the one who has doomed him? My brother, am I truly such a sister to you, that the day I gave you brother’s blessing in my heart, Yama, the god of death, smiled in his heart as well? What a burden of misfortune I am carrying today!
Today it seems to me that at certain times, a person—

The plague of misfortune strikes—its seeds come suddenly from nowhere, and in a single night, death draws near. At such times, can it not be kept far away from all household life? I can clearly see how dreadful its contagion is! Like a torch of disaster, it burns itself only to set the world aflame.

It is nine o’clock. I have a strange feeling that Amulya has fallen into grave danger, that the police have caught him. There has been some commotion at the police station over my jewelry box—whose box it is, where it was found, in the end I shall have to answer for it. What answer shall I give before all the people of the world?

Mejorani, all this time I have treated you with such disdain! Today your day has come! Today you will exact your due, assuming the form of the whole world. O Lord, save me now—let all my pride be swept away, let me lie at Mejorani’s feet!
I could bear it no longer—at once I went inside the house and presented myself before Mejorani. She was sitting on the veranda in the sunlight, preparing betel leaves, with Thako seated beside her.

At the sight of Thako, my heart shrank for a moment—but I quickly overcame it, and fell at Mejorani’s feet, touching the dust at her feet. She exclaimed, “What is this, Chotorani? What has happened to you? Why this sudden devotion?”
I said, "Didi, today is my birthday. I have committed many wrongs—please, Didi, bless me, so that I may never again bring you any sorrow! My heart feels so small!"

Saying this, I bowed to her once more and hurriedly left. She called after me, "Why, Chhutu, your birthday, and you didn’t tell me before? You must come here for lunch today. My dear sister, don’t forget!"
O Lord, do something so that today truly becomes my birthday. Can I not become entirely new? Wash me clean, let me be tested once more from the very beginning, O Lord!

As I was about to enter the drawing room outside, Sandip appeared there. My whole being seemed to fill with revulsion. In the light of this morning, the face I saw in him bore not a trace of the magic of genius. I exclaimed, "Please leave this place!"
Sandip laughed and said, "Amulya isn’t here, so now it’s my turn for a special conversation."
Ill fate! The right I myself had given him—how could I now deny it? I said, "I need to be alone."
Rani, even if there is another person in the room, to be alone—
There is no disturbance. Do not think of me as one of the crowd—I am Sandip, even among a hundred thousand people, I am alone.
Will you come another time? This morning I—
Are you waiting for Amulya?
Annoyed, I was about to leave the room when Sandip drew my jewelry box from within his shawl and placed it with a sharp sound on the stone table.
I started in surprise, “Then Amulya hasn’t gone?”
Hasn’t gone where?
To Calcutta?
Sandip smiled a little and said, “No.”
I was saved! My Bhai Phonta is saved! Let me be the thief, let the punishment of fate reach only so far—let Amulya be spared!

Seeing the expression on my face, Sandip said mockingly, “So happy, Rani? Is this jewelry box so precious? Then with what heart did you wish to offer these ornaments to the goddess? You have already given them—do you now wish to take them back from the hands of the deity?”
Pride does not die even in the throes of death—I wanted to show that after giving away this jewelry, I have no attachment even for a quarter-anna.
I said, “If you desire these ornaments, please take them.”

Sandip says, “Today, in Bengal, wherever there is wealth, my greed is for all of it. Is there any pursuit as great and noble as greed? Those who are Indra on this earth, greed is their Airavata. So, then, are all these ornaments mine?”

Saying this, Sandip picked up the box and, covering it with a shawl, was about to hide it when Amulya entered the room. There were dark circles under his eyes, his face was pale, his hair disheveled—as if, in a single day, the youthful radiance of his age had withered away. The moment I saw him, a pang twisted within my chest.
Without even glancing at me, Amulya went straight to Sandip and said, “Did you take the jewelry box out of my trunk?”
Is the jewelry box yours?
No, but the trunk is mine.
Sandip burst out laughing. He said, “Your sense of ‘mine’ and ‘yours’ regarding the trunk is so very subtle, Amulya! I see you too will die a preacher before you die.”
Amulya sat down on a chair, buried his face in his hands, and rested his head on the table. I went to him, placed my hand on his head, and said, “Amulya, what has happened?”
At once he stood up and said, “Didi, this jewelry box—”
It was my own cherished wish to bring you here with my own hands—Sandip Babu knew this—so he hurried—
I said, “What will happen with that jewelry box of mine—let it go, what does it matter?”
Amulya, astonished, said, “Where will it go?”
Sandip said, “This jewelry is mine—this is the offering given to me by my queen.”
Amulya, like a madman, cried out, “No, no, no, never! Didi, I have brought this back and returned it to you, you cannot give it to anyone else!”
I said, “Brother, your gift will remain in my heart forever, but if someone covets the jewels, let them take it!”
Then Amulya, glaring at Sandip like a wild beast, said in a choked voice, “Listen, Sandip Babu, you know, I am not afraid of the gallows. If you take this jewelry box—”

Sandip, trying to smile mockingly, said, “Amulya, by now you should know that I am not afraid of your threats. Queen of the Bees, I did not come today to take this jewelry—I came to give it to you. But to prevent the injustice that you would take what is mine from Amulya’s hands, I first made you take this box from me with your own clear words. Now my—”

“I am giving this thing to you—here it is! Now, settle matters with that boy yourself, I am leaving. For some days, there have been special discussions between the two of you, I am not involved in them. If anything particular happens, you cannot blame me. Amulya, all your things—trunks, books, and whatever else was in my room—I have sent them all to your lodgings in the bazaar. Nothing of yours can remain in my room.”
Saying this, Sandip hurriedly left the room.
I said, “Amulya, ever since I gave you my jewelry to sell, my mind has not been at peace.”
“Why, Didi?”

“I was afraid that you might get into trouble with that box of jewelry—that someone might suspect you of being a thief and catch you. I have no need for that six thousand rupees. Now you must listen to me—go home at once—go to your mother.”
Amulya drew a small bundle from within his shawl and said, “Didi, I have brought the six thousand rupees.”
I asked, “Where did you get it?”
Without answering, he said, “I tried very hard to get gold coins, but that was not possible, so I have brought notes instead.”
Amulya, for heaven’s sake, tell me the truth—where did you get this money?
He replied, “I won’t tell you.”
It was as if darkness clouded my vision. I said, “What have you done, Amulya? This money—”
Amulya burst out, “I know you’ll say I’ve brought this money by wrongful means—well, I admit it. But the greater the wrong, the higher the price; and I have paid that price. Now, this money is mine.”

I no longer wished to hear any more details about this money. My veins seemed to contract, drawing my whole body inward. I said, “Take it back, Amulya. Return this money to wherever you took it from. Go, right now, and put it back.”
“That’s very hard to do.”
“No, it’s not hard, brother. What an ill-fated moment it was when you came to me! Even Sandip could not have harmed you as much as I have!”

The mention of Sandip’s name seemed to sting him. He said, “Sandip! It’s only because I came to you that I have come to know him for what he is. Do you know, Didi, from you—on that day, the six thousand rupees in gold coins that he took—he hasn’t spent a single paisa of it. After leaving here, he went straight home, shut the door—”

He poured all the guineas from the handkerchief onto the table, gathered them into a heap, and gazed at them in rapt wonder. He said, “This is not mere money, this is the bounty of the celestial Parijat, hardened into gold as it dripped from the flute of Alakapuri—this cannot be exchanged for banknotes, for it longs to rest as a necklace on a beauty’s throat—O Amulya, do not look upon this with coarse eyes, this is Lakshmi’s smile, Indrani’s radiance—no, no, this was not created to fall into the hands of that unfeeling Naib. Look, Amulya, the Naib has told nothing but lies, the police have heard nothing of that boat theft—he only seeks to profit from this opportunity. Listen, Amulya, we must recover those three letters from the Naib—”
I asked, “How?”
Sandip replied, “By force, by intimidation!”
I said, “I agree, but these guineas must be returned.”
Sandip said, “Very well, that shall be done.”

How we frightened the Naib and recovered those letters from him to burn—that is a long story. That very night, I went to Sandip and said, “There is no more fear, give me the guineas, tomorrow morning I shall return them to Didi.”
Sandip said, “What enchantment has come over you! Has the country now been veiled in Didi’s sari? Say ‘Bande Mataram’—let the spell be broken! You know, Didi, what magic Sandip wields—”

The gold coins remained with him. In the dark of night, I sat on the stone steps by the pond, chanting "Bande Mataram." Yesterday, when you sent the jewelry to be sold, I went to him again at dusk. I could clearly see that he was burning with anger towards me. Yet he did not express that anger; he said, "See if those gold coins are in any of my boxes, then take them." Saying this, he threw the bunch of keys onto my lap. Nowhere could I find them. I asked, "Please tell me where you have kept them."

Sandip replied, "First, let go of your attachment, then I will tell you. Not now." I saw that I could not move him by any means, so I had to find another way. Even after this, I tried many times to get those gold coins from him by showing him these six-thousand-rupee notes. He kept deceiving me, saying he would bring the coins, and meanwhile, from his bedroom, he broke open my trunk, took the jewelry box, and brought it to you—yet you did not let me bring this box to you myself! And then he claims—this jewelry is his gift! Whom can I tell how much he has deprived me? This I shall never be able to forgive. Sister, his spell has been completely broken. It is you who have broken it."
I said, "My dear brother, my life has found its fulfillment. But, Amulya, there is still something left. Only attachment—"
It will not do simply to cut it off; the blackness I have smeared must be washed away.
Do not delay, Amulya, go now—return this money to the very place from where you brought it. Can you do it, dear brother?
By your blessing, I will be able to, sister.

It is not only your own strength that will carry you through. There is my strength in this as well. I am a woman; the road outside is closed to me, otherwise I would not have let you go—I would have gone myself. For me, this is the hardest punishment of all: that you must bear the burden of my sin.

Do not say such things, sister! The path I was treading was not yours. It was its very difficulty that drew my mind to it. Sister, now I have been called to your path—let this path be a thousand times more arduous for me, but I shall return victorious, bearing the dust of your feet—there is no fear!
Then, it is your command that I must return the money to the place from where I brought it?
Not my command, brother, it is the command from above.

I do not know about that. That command from above has come through your lips—that is enough for me. But, sister, I have an invitation at your house. I must claim it today before I go. You must give me prasad. After that, if I can, I will finish my task and return before evening.
As I tried to laugh, tears welled up in my eyes— I said, “All right!”

As Amulya left, my heart sank. Which mother’s child have I sent adrift into danger! Lord, why must the atonement for my sin come in such a ruinous form? So many people invited? Was I alone not enough? Must you make so many bear the weight of my burden? Alas, why must that innocent boy be sacrificed?
I called him back, “Amulya!”—my voice came out so faint, he could not hear. I went to the door and called again, “Amulya!” But by then he was gone.
“Behara, Behara!”
“Yes, Rani Ma!”
“Call Amulyababu!”

Who knows, perhaps the behara does not know Amulya’s name, so after a moment he brought Sandip instead. Entering the room, Sandip said, “When you drove me away, I knew at once you would call me back. The same moon that draws the ebb also draws the tide. I was certain you would call; that’s why I waited by the door. The moment I saw your behara, before he could say anything, I quickly said—‘All right, all right, I’m coming, coming right now.’ The Bhojpuri fellow stood there, mouth agape in astonishment. He must have thought—”

The man is a master of spells. Queen of the bees, the greatest battle in this world is the battle of enchantment. It is a duel of hypnosis against hypnosis. His arrows are words that pierce the soul—yet he also has arrows that pierce in silence! After so long, at last, Sandip has found his equal in this struggle. You, warrior queen, have many arrows in your quiver! In this world, I see, only you have been able to turn Sandip as you wish, to draw him in or send him away at your will. The prey has fallen into the trap. Now, tell me, what will you do with him? Will you utterly destroy him, or will you keep him caged for yourself? But let me warn you in advance, O queen, it is as difficult to slay this creature as it is to imprison him! Therefore, do not delay in testing the divine weapon you possess. A shadow of defeat has entered Sandip’s mind—that is why he spoke so incessantly today. I believe he thought I had called for Amulya—the servant must have mentioned his name, and Sandip, deceiving him, came himself. He did not give me a chance to say that I had not called for him, but for Amulya. But his bravado is false—now I have seen his weakness. Now, I cannot yield even a hair’s breadth of the ground I have won. I said, “Sandipbabu, how do you manage to talk on and on like this? Do you prepare yourself in advance before coming?”
In a moment, Sandip’s face flushed red with anger.
I said, “I have heard that storytellers keep all sorts of lengthy descriptions written down in their notebooks, ready to use whichever suits the occasion. Do you have such a notebook, perhaps?”

Sandip began to speak, chewing his words, “By the grace of Providence, you people have no end of airs and artifices, and on top of that, you have the tailor’s shop and the confectioner’s shop to aid you. And—has Providence left us so utterly defenseless that—”

I interrupted, “Sandipbabu, please check your notebook—these things you are saying are not quite right. I see that, every now and then, you contradict yourself—such is the great flaw of reciting by rote from a notebook!”
Sandip could bear it no longer—he roared out,
“You! You will insult me! What have you discovered about me, tell me? That you—”

No more words came from his lips. Sandip, the magician of words, the very moment his spell fails, loses all his power—he falls from king to mere herdsman! Weak! Weak! The harsher and more abrasive his words became, the more my heart filled with joy. The serpent’s noose with which he tried to bind me had run its course—I was free. I was saved, I was saved. Insult me, insult me—this is your truth; do not praise me, for that is false.

At that moment, my husband entered the room. On other days, Sandip would have composed himself in an instant, but today he lacked that strength. My husband looked at his face with a hint of surprise. In the past, I would have felt ashamed at this, but whatever my husband might think, today I was glad. I wanted to see this weakened man for myself.
Both of us remained silent, and seeing this, my husband hesitated a little before sitting down on the couch. He said, "Sandip, I was looking for you. I heard you were in this room."

Sandip, putting a particular emphasis on his words, replied, "Yes, the queen of the hive summoned me this morning. I am but a worker bee, so at her command, I had to leave all other work and come at once!"
My husband said, "Tomorrow I am going to Calcutta. You must go as well."
Sandip said, "Why, tell me? Am I your attendant or what? All right, you go to Calcutta, and I will be your attendant. I have no business in Calcutta."
"That is precisely why you need to go to Calcutta. Here, you have too much business."
"I am not going to budge."
Then you must be stirred.
By force?
Yes, by force.
All right, very well—I shall be stirred. But the world is not divided into just two parts—Calcutta and your domain. There are other places on the map.
From your attitude, it seemed as if there was no place in the world outside my domain.

Sandip then stood up and said, "There comes a time in a person's life when the entire world seems to be compressed into a tiny space. Within this very drawing room of yours, I have seen my whole universe face to face—that is why I cannot move from here. Queen of the bees, none of them will understand what I say—perhaps you will not either. I worship you. I am about to begin your worship. Since the moment I saw you, my mantra has changed. No longer 'Bande Mataram'—but 'Bande Priyam, Bande Mohinim.' The Mother protects us—the Beloved destroys us—how beautiful is that destruction! You have set the anklets of the dance of death ringing in my heart! The gentle, fertile, beautiful, soft-breezed, cool land of Bengal—its form you have transformed in an instant before the eyes of your devotee. Mercy and compassion, you have none—Mohini, you have come with your cup of poison—those...

Drinking poison, and being ravaged by that very poison, I shall either perish or become immortal! The days of the mother are over—Beloved, beloved, beloved, you have cast aside god, heaven, religion, truth, all as trifles; all other ties of the world today are but shadows, all bonds of rule and restraint are severed! Beloved, beloved, beloved, on the land where you have set your two feet, I could set fire to the rest of the world outside, and dance in wild joy upon its ashes!

These people are good, exceedingly good—they wish well for all—as if everything were truth. Never! Nowhere else in the world is there such a truth; this is my only truth. I worship you—my devotion to you has made me ruthless, my reverence for you has kindled the fire of destruction within me—I am not good, I am not righteous, I acknowledge nothing in this world, I recognize only that which I have been able to perceive above all!

Strange! Strange! Only a little while ago I hated her with all my heart! The one I saw as ashes, from within her the fire has flared up. This is pure fire, there is no doubt of it. Why does the Creator thus mingle such elements when making man? Is it only to display His miraculous magic? Half an hour ago I was thinking to myself about this person—

One day, I was indeed deceived into thinking of a king, but the king of this traveling troupe—no, no, not that—the king sometimes hides even within the costumes of the troupe. Within this, there is much greed, many tricks, much deceit, layer upon layer, hidden within the flesh, and yet—we do not know, we do not know the final word, it is better to admit this, we do not even know ourselves. Man is a great wonder—what tremendous mystery is being wrought with him, only that fierce deity knows—meanwhile, I am consumed! Catastrophe! Shiva is the god of destruction, he alone is blissful, he alone will break these bonds.

For some days now, I have felt as if I have two minds. One part of me perceives the dreadful, catastrophic form of Sandip—another mind says, but this is sweet. When a ship sinks, those who swim all around are dragged under—Sandip seems like that very embodiment of death—before fear can seize you, his overwhelming pull takes hold—he wants, in the blink of an eye, to sweep away from all light, all goodness, from the freedom of the sky, from the breath of air, from the hoarded treasures of eternity, from the daily cares, into a dense, utter ruin. As if he has come as the messenger of some great plague—reciting unholy mantras as he walks the road, and all the boys of the country, all the youths, are rushing after him. Upon the lotus-heart of Bengal, where the Mother sits enthroned—

He broke down in tears—these people have shattered the doors of his vessel of nectar, and, bringing in their casks of wine, have set up a drunken revel there—they want to pour all the ambrosia onto the dust, to shatter forever the eternal chalice of sweetness! I understood it all, yet I could not restrain my infatuation! It is the work of Truth itself to test the austerity of Truth—drunkenness, adorned in the garb of heaven, comes to dance before the ascetics, saying, “You fools, perfection is not attained through penance; its path is long, its pace slow—therefore the wielder of the thunderbolt has sent me—I shall welcome you—I am beauty, I am intoxication, in my embrace, in a single instant, all perfection is yours.”

After a brief pause, Sandip spoke to me again, “Now the time has come to go far away, Devi! It is for the best. My work of coming close to you is done. If I remain any longer, everything will be ruined, one by one. When we try to cheapen that which is greatest in the world by succumbing to greed, disaster is inevitable—when we try to stretch the infinite, which exists in a moment, across the expanse of time, we only confine it. We were about to destroy that infinity—at just such a moment, your thunderbolt was raised, you protected your worship, and also your ‘worshipper’. Today, in the midst of my departure, your veneration has become greater than all else. Devi, I too—

Today I set you free—my earthen temple could not contain you— This temple trembled with every touch— It was breaking, breaking—today I go to worship your greater image in a greater temple— I shall find you truly only by being far from you— Here, I would only receive boons from you!”
My jewelry box was on the table. I picked it up and said, “These ornaments of mine—I give them, through your hands, to her at whose feet you will lay them.”
My husband remained silent. Sandip went out and left.
chapters.summary: Bimala anxiously awaits Amulya’s return, burdened by guilt over involving him in her troubles, and confronts both Mejorani and Sandip before a tense.

chapters.title: Bimala: Fearless Amidst the Looters
paragraphs: I was sitting down to prepare food with my own hands for Amulya, when Mejo-rani came and said, “Well, little one, are you arranging to feed yourself on your own birthday?”
I replied, “Is there anyone else to feed except myself?”

Mejo-rani said, “Today it is not your turn to feed; we are supposed to feed you. I was making all the arrangements, when suddenly I heard some news that made my heart leap in fear—apparently, in one of our offices, five or six hundred dacoits attacked and looted six thousand rupees. People are saying that now they will come to loot our house next.”

Hearing this news, my heart felt strangely light. So, it is our own money! I will call Amulya right now and tell him: let him return this six thousand rupees here, in front of me, into my husband’s hands—then I will say to him all that I have to say!
Observing the expression on my face, Mejo-rani said, “You astonish me! Aren’t you the least bit afraid?”
I said, "I cannot believe that they will come to loot our house!"
You cannot believe it! Who could have believed that even the servants would turn into looters?

—Without replying, I lowered my head and began stuffing coconut filling into the rice cakes. After looking at my face for a moment, he said, "Let me go and call for Thakurpo. We must take out those six thousand rupees at once and send them off to Calcutta—there must be no more delay."

Saying this, he left, and I quickly left the rice cakes half-finished and hurried to the room with the iron safe, closing the door behind me. My husband is so absent-minded that the shirt with the safe key in its pocket was still hanging on the peg! I took the key to the iron safe off the ring and hid it inside my jacket.

Just then, there was a knock at the door from outside! I called out, "I am changing my clothes!"—I heard Mejo Rani say, "Just a little while ago I saw her preparing rice cakes, and now suddenly she is in a rush to dress up! How many of her little tricks must we witness! Perhaps today they are holding their 'Bande Mataram' meeting. Oh, Devi Chowdhurani, are you loading up the loot?"

On a sudden impulse, I slowly opened the iron safe. Perhaps I was thinking, what if it had all been a dream;—what if, as I pulled open that little drawer, I found the bundles of papers arranged just as before! Alas, like the empty faith of a traitor, everything was gone! I had to change my clothes for nothing. There was no need, yet I tied my hair anew. When I met Mejo-rani, she asked, “Why are you so dressed up today?”—I replied, “For my birthday.”
Mejo-rani laughed and said, “Any excuse for you to dress up! I’ve seen plenty, but never anyone as imaginative as you!”

I was searching for Behara to send for the doctor for Amulya, when he came and handed me a small note written in pencil. In it, Amulya had written, “Sister, you called me to eat, but I could not wait. Let me first carry out your command, then I shall take the offering. Perhaps I will return by evening.”

Amulya has gone off to return the money to someone, and again, into what web is he about to entangle himself! I can only hurl him like an arrow, but if he misses the mark, there is no way for me to call him back.
That I am steeped in the stain of this crime—this very thought, right now…

I should have confessed. But women live in the world sustained by trust—that is their universe. To reveal that I had deceived that trust, to admit it, would make it almost impossible for us to continue in this household. We must stand upon precisely what we have broken—the sharp edges of that broken thing would prick us at every moment, tormenting us endlessly. It is not difficult to commit a wrong, but for women, correcting that wrong is more difficult than for anyone else.

For some days now, the easy manner of conversation with my husband has ceased. So I could not, for the life of me, think how or when to tell him such a grave matter. Today he came to eat very late—it was already two o’clock. Distracted, he could barely eat anything. I have lost even the right to gently urge him to eat a little more. Turning my face away, I wiped my tears with the end of my sari.

Once, I thought I would overcome my hesitation and say, “Please, rest a little in the house, you look so tired!”—I was just about to clear my throat and broach the subject when the attendant came and informed us that the police inspector had brought Kasem Sardar.
With a worried face, my husband quickly got up and left. Shortly after he went outside, Mejo-rani came in.
She said, “Why didn’t you let me know when Thakurpo came to eat? Today, seeing that his meal was delayed, I went to bathe—and in the meantime, when—”
Why, what is it!

Shuchi, you are going to Calcutta tomorrow. Then I cannot stay here any longer. The elder Rani will not leave her Radhaballabh Thakur for anything. But I—I cannot bear to sit guarding this empty house of yours in these days of robbery, startled and frightened at every little sound, dying a thousand deaths. You are leaving tomorrow, aren’t you?

I said, “Yes, it’s decided.” In my mind I thought, in this little time before you leave, who knows how many stories will be born, how much history will unfold. After that, whether I go to Calcutta or stay here, it will all be the same. After that, what will this household be, what will life be—who knows! All smoke, all dream!

Now that my fate has become visible before me, and only a few hours remain—can no one stretch this time, pull it out, day by day, making it longer and longer? Then, within this, I could slowly, as best as I can, finish everything, set everything in order—at least prepare myself and the household for this blow. As long as the seeds of destruction remain buried beneath the earth—

It takes a long time—so long that it seems there is perhaps nothing to fear. But once the tiniest sprout appears above the earth, it grows before your very eyes, and then there is no time left to smother it with the edge of your sari, with your heart, with your very life.

I tell myself I will not think about it, I will lie inert and silent, and let whatever comes fall upon my head! In a few days, whatever is to happen will happen—knowing and unknowing, laughter and tears, questions and answers, all of it!

But I cannot, by any means, forget the face of Amulya, radiant with the beauty of self-sacrifice. He did not sit quietly, waiting for fate—he rushed into the very heart of danger. I, a woman and so much less than him, bow before him. He is my boy-god—he has come, as if in play, to snatch away the burden of my shame; he will take my death upon his own head and save me—how can I bear such terrible mercy from God? My child, I bow to you; my brother, I bow to you—pure you are, beautiful you are, brave you are, fearless you are, I bow to you—may you be born as my son in another life and come into my arms, this boon I pray for.
Meanwhile, rumors have begun to stir on all sides, the police are coming and going, and all the maids and servants in the house are anxious.

Kshema, the maid, came to me and said, “Chotoranima, please put my gold anklet and armlet away in your iron chest.” Who can I tell that it is the little queen of the house herself who has spun this web of worry across the land, only to find herself ensnared within it? Like a dutiful person, I had to accept Kshema’s jewelry and Thakur’s saved money! Our milkmaid brought a tin box and left a Benarasi sari and her other precious belongings with me—she said, “Ranima, I received this Benarasi sari at your wedding.”

Tomorrow, when the iron chest of my own house is opened, what will become of this Kshema, Thakur, the milkmaid—no, what use is it to imagine such things! Instead, I think, after tomorrow, another year will have passed, and once again the day of the third Magh will return. Will all the festering wounds of my household remain unhealed then as well? Amulya has written that he will return by evening today. Meanwhile, I cannot sit quietly alone in the house. Again, I went to prepare more pitha.

What has already been made is enough, but still, more must be done. Who will eat so much? I will feed all the maids and servants of the house. Tonight, they must be fed. My day’s boundary ends tonight. Tomorrow is no longer in my hands.

I am folding saris one after another, without rest. Now and then, it seems as if some commotion is going on upstairs, towards my husband's quarters. Perhaps my husband has come to open the iron safe and cannot find the key. Over this, Mejo-rani has summoned the maids and servants, causing an uproar. No, I will not listen—I will hear nothing; I will keep my door shut. Just as I am about to close the door, Thako comes rushing in—panting, she says, “Choto-ranima!”
I burst out, “Go, go, don’t bother me, I have no time now.” Thako says, “Mejo-ranima’s nephew, Nandababu, has brought a ‘kol’ from Kolkata that sings like a human, so Mejo-ranima has sent for you.”

I cannot decide whether to laugh or to cry! Even in the midst of all this—gramophone! Every time it is wound up, that nasal tune from the theater emerges—there is no sense or feeling in it! When a machine imitates life, it becomes such a cruel mockery!

Evening has fallen. I know, as soon as Amulya arrives, he will not delay in sending word to me—yet I cannot wait—so I call the behara and say, “Send word to Amulyababu.” The behara goes around for a while and returns to say, “Amulyababu is not here.”
It is nothing, really, just a simple statement, but suddenly my heart is thrown into turmoil. Amulyababu is not here—that very...

In the darkness of evening, this thought struck me like a cry of sorrow. He is gone, he is no more! He appeared for a moment, like the golden line of the setting sun—and then he was gone! All sorts of possible and impossible disasters began to gather in my mind. I am the one who sent him into the jaws of death; that he felt no fear was his greatness—but after this, how am I to go on living? I had no token of Amulya left with me—except for that gift he gave me at Bhai Phonta—the pistol. It seemed to me there was a hint of fate in this. The stain that had settled at the root of my life, my Narayan, disguised as a boy, had left the means to erase it in my hands before vanishing somewhere. What a gift of love! What a purifying mantra lies hidden within it! I opened the box, took out the pistol, and, raising it with both hands, pressed it to my head. At that very moment, the conch and bells of arati sounded from our thakur-bari. I prostrated myself in reverence. At night, the household was fed. Mejo-rani came and said, “So you went ahead and celebrated your birthday with such fanfare all by yourself, did you? Are you not going to let us do anything at all?”—Saying this, she set her gramophone to play, filling the air with the rapid, high-pitched, delicate notes of all the world’s nautch-girls.

It seemed as though, from the stables of the Gandharvas, the horses with their celestial music were neighing in high, clear tones. By the time the feeding was done, it was very late at night. I had wished, tonight, to take the dust of my husband’s feet.

When I entered the bedroom, I saw him sleeping soundly, utterly spent. The whole day he had been out and about, his mind burdened with many thoughts. Very carefully, I lifted a corner of the mosquito net and quietly placed my head near his feet. As soon as my hair brushed against him, even in his sleep, he gently nudged my head away with his foot.
I went out to the western verandah. In the distance, a shimul tree stood in the darkness like a skeleton—its leaves all shed. Behind it, the moon of Saptami slowly set.

Suddenly it seemed to me that all the stars in the sky were afraid of me—the vast world of the night was glancing at me askance. For I am alone! There is nothing in creation so forsaken as a solitary human being. Even one whose kin have all died, one by one, is not truly alone, for from beyond the veil of death, companionship lingers.
But one whose loved ones are all near, yet not truly with them, who has fallen away utterly from the fullness of household company—it seems as if, in the darkness, all faces turn away from her.

When I desire, it is as though the entire world of stars bristles with thorns. "I am not where I am—those who surround me, I remain distant from them. I move, I turn, I live upon a vast, universal separation—as if I were a drop of dew upon a lotus leaf.

But when a person changes, why does not every part of them change entirely? Looking into my heart, I see that all that was there remains, only it has been shaken and disturbed. What was once arranged is now in disarray—what was strung together in a garland now lies in the dust. That is why my heart feels as though it will burst. I wish to die, yet everything in my heart still lives—within death, I see no end. It seems to me that within death there is an even more terrible sorrow. Whatever must be settled, can only be settled through life—there is no other way.

Forgive me this once, O my Lord! All that you placed in my hands as the treasures of my life, I have turned into burdens. Now I can neither bear them nor relinquish them. Once more, play that flute which you played, standing at the edge of my dawn-red sky; let all problems become simple—without the melody of your flute, none can mend what is broken.
No, no one can make the impure pure. In the music of that flute, you recreate my world anew. Otherwise, I see no other way.

I lay face down upon the earth and began to weep—seeking some mercy from somewhere, a refuge, a hint of forgiveness, some assurance that perhaps all may yet be absolved. In my heart I said, I will lie here day and night in supplication, Lord—I will not eat, I will not touch water, until your blessing descends upon me!

At that moment, I heard footsteps. My heart leapt within my breast. Who says the gods do not appear! I did not lift my face, lest my gaze be too much for him to bear. Come, come, come—let your feet touch my head, come stand upon the trembling of my heart, Lord, let me die this very instant!

He came and stood by my pillow. Who? My husband! In my husband's heart, the very throne of my deity trembled, he who could no longer bear my tears. I felt I would faint. Then, as if the bonds of my veins were torn asunder, the pain in my heart surged forth in a flood of tears. I clasped his feet to my breast—will not the imprint of those feet be etched there for all eternity?

Now, at last, I could have revealed everything! But is there anything left to say after this? Let my words remain unsaid! He gently stroked my head with his hand. I have received his blessing. Tomorrow, the dishonor that awaits me—I shall bear that garland of shame upon my head before everyone, and, with a pure heart, bow at the feet of my deity.

Yet, as I think of this, my heart breaks within me. The music that played nine years ago will never sound again in this lifetime. The one who welcomed me into this home! Oh, in this world, at whose feet must a woman lay her head and die, so that she may once more stand, draped in bridal sandalwood silk, upon that seat of welcome? How many days will it take—how many ages, how many eternities—before I can return, even once, to that day nine years ago? The gods can create anew, but do they have the power to remake what has been broken?
chapters.summary: Bimala faces turmoil as rumors of looters swirl, Amulya disappears on a dangerous errand, and she wrestles with guilt, longing.

chapters.title: Nikhilesh: Parting with Attachments
paragraphs: Today we are going to Calcutta. If one keeps on accumulating happiness and sorrow, the burden grows heavy. For sitting still is an illusion, hoarding is an illusion. That I am the master of this house is a fabricated thing—the truth is that I am a traveler on the path of life. Therefore, the master of the house will be wounded again and again—until the final blow comes: death. The union between you and me is a union on the journey—as long as we walk the same path together. That much is good—as long as it lasts; but if we try to draw it out further, union becomes bondage. That bondage remains behind today—now I have stepped out—whatever glances meet, whatever hands touch in passing, that alone is good. And after that? After that lies the path of the infinite world, the rush of endless life—how much can you deprive me of, beloved? If I listen with my ears, I can hear the flute playing ahead; through all the cracks of separation, the fountain of its sweetness pours down. Because Lakshmi’s vessel of nectar is inexhaustible, she sometimes breaks our little pots, making us weep and laugh. I will not go to gather the broken pieces; I will carry my unfulfilled longing in my heart and move forward.
Mejoranididi came and said, “Thakurpo, what does it mean that you’re packing all your books into trunks and loading them onto a bullock cart to be taken away?”
I replied, “It means I still haven’t been able to detach myself from those books.”
It is only because a little attachment remains that I survive. But does that mean you won’t return here anymore?
I’ll come and go, but I won’t be able to stay as before.
Is that really so? Then come with me, let me show you how many things I’m still attached to.—Saying this, she took me by the hand and pulled me along.

When we entered her room, I saw all sorts of boxes and bundles, big and small. She opened one box and showed me, “Look, Thakurpo, these are my betel-nut arrangements. I’ve ground up the kewa and catechu and stored them in bottles—see, each tin contains a different spice. Here are playing cards, I haven’t forgotten even the tens and twenty-fives; if I can’t find you all, I’ll gather others to play with. This comb is your own swadeshi comb, and this—”
“But what is all this, Mejorani? Why have you packed everything into boxes?”
“Because I’m going to Calcutta with you all.”
“What are you saying?”
“Don’t worry, brother, don’t worry, I won’t intrude on your company—”

I will not go, nor will I quarrel with Chhoto Rani. Since I must die, it is better to seek refuge in the land by the banks of the Ganga while there is still time—when I think of being cremated under that bare banyan tree of yours, the very thought fills me with revulsion for death. That is why I have been troubling you all these days.

After so long, it is as if this house itself has found a voice and begun to speak. When I was six years old, Mejo Rani came to our house at the age of nine. On the terrace of this house, in the afternoons, I would sit with her in the shadowy corner by the high wall and play. In the garden, I would climb the hog plum tree and drop the unripe fruits from above, while she sat below, slicing them into tiny pieces and mixing them with salt, chili, and coriander leaves to concoct forbidden delicacies. For the feasts of our dolls’ weddings, whatever ingredients needed to be secretly gathered from the pantry, that responsibility fell to me—for, according to grandmother’s judgment, I was not subject to any punishment for wrongdoing.

Later, for all those little luxuries she desired after Dada, I was the messenger of her wishes—I would pester Dada relentlessly until, by one means or another, I managed to procure what she wanted. I also remember, in those days, whenever I had a fever, the strict regimen of the kaviraj allowed me only hot water and cardamom for three days—Mejo Rani could not bear my suffering, and so many times she secretly brought me food.

On certain days, she has even had to endure rebuke when caught. Later, as we grew older, the colors of happiness and sorrow deepened—so many quarrels have taken place, at times there has been much jealousy, suspicion, and conflict over matters of property and affairs, and sometimes even Bimala has been caught in the midst of it all. There have been times when it seemed that the rift would never be healed—but then it would be proven that the bond of the heart was stronger than any outward wound. Thus, from childhood until today, a true relationship has awakened, day by day, without interruption: the branches and offshoots of that relationship have spread their shadow through every room, courtyard, veranda, terrace, and garden of this great house, claiming everything as their own.

—When I saw Mejo-rani standing, all her little belongings packed into boxes, ready to leave our house, then it felt as if all the roots of that eternal relationship shuddered within my heart. I could well understand why Mejo-rani, who since the age of nine had never spent even a single day outside this house, was now cutting all the ties of her habits and floating away among strangers. Yet she would not utter a word about the real reason—she would raise all sorts of trivial excuses. This woman, deprived by fate, bereft of husband and son, had in this world only this one thing—

She has nurtured this relationship with all the nectar stored in her heart; how deep her pain is—I have never understood it as clearly as I do now, standing amidst these scattered boxes and trunks filling the house. I realize now that the frequent quarrels she had with Bimala and me over money, household matters, and trivial domestic details were not truly about material concerns. The real cause was that, in this one relationship of her life, she could never assert her claim with strength—Bimala had suddenly come in between and dimmed her presence; here, at every step, she was wounded, yet she had no power to complain. Bimala, too, in her own way, understood that the claim Mejo-rani held over me was not merely a matter of social convention, but something much deeper—that is why she felt such jealousy over our lifelong bond. Today, at the threshold of my heart, I felt a pounding ache. I sat down on a trunk and said, “Mejo-rani-didi, I wish we could both return, just once, to the day we first arrived in this house as strangers.”
Mejo-rani let out a long sigh and said, “No, brother, not again—not after being born a woman. What I have endured, let it remain with this one life; could I bear it all over again?”
I said, “The freedom that comes through sorrow is greater than the sorrow itself.”

She replied, “That may be so, dear nephew, you are men—freedom is for you. We women want to bind, and to be bound—you will not get away from us so easily. If you wish to spread your wings, you must fight us—you cannot simply cast us off. That is why we keep all these burdens ready—if we let you become completely light, what would become of us!”
I laughed and said, “That’s exactly what I see—the burden is quite clearly a burden. But since you pay us the wages for bearing it, we do not complain.”

Mejo-rani said, “Our burdens are of little things. Whoever you try to cast off will say, ‘How small my weight is, how insignificant’—in this way, with these light things, we make your total load heavy. When do you have to leave, dear nephew?”
At half past eleven at night—there’s still plenty of time.

“Listen, dear nephew, you must grant me one request—eat your meal early today, and take a little nap in the afternoon—at night you won’t get good sleep in the carriage. Just looking at your body, I feel as if a little more…”
If it happens, it will all come crashing down. Come, you must go bathe right now.
At that moment, Khema, pulling a large veil over herself, said in a honeyed voice, “Daroga-babu has brought someone along; he wishes to see Maharaj.”
Mejorani rose in anger and said, “Is Maharaj a thief or a bandit that the Daroga is always after him? Go tell him, Maharaj has gone to bathe now.”
I said, “Let me just go and see—perhaps there is some urgent matter.”

Mejorani said, “No, that will not do. Chotorani made a lot of pitha yesterday; I am sending the Daroga to eat that pitha and keeping his temper cool that way.” Saying this, she took me by the hand, dragged me into the bathing room, and shut the door from outside.
From inside, I said, “But my clean clothes are still—” She replied, “I will take care of that; in the meantime, you go and bathe.”
I have no power to disobey this reign of mischief—such a thing is rare in this world. Let it be, Daroga-babu will sit and eat pitha! If my work is neglected, so be it!
Meanwhile, about that robbery, the Daroga with a few others—

They have started their usual catching and tying up again. Every day, it seems, they drag in some innocent fellow, tie him up, and keep the gathering heated. Today, too, I suppose they have caught hold of some unfortunate soul in the same way. But is it only the daroga who will get a beating on his back? That would not be fair. I banged on the door loudly. From outside, Mejo-rani called out, “Pour water, pour water! Has your head started to heat up again?”
I replied, “Send out enough for two backs—whoever the daroga has caught as a thief, let him get his due on his back. Tell the bearer to make sure he gets the larger share.”
I finished my bath as quickly as possible and opened the door to step out. I saw Bimala sitting on the ground outside the door.

Is this my Bimala, the same proud woman, filled with fire and self-respect? What beggary does she harbor in her heart, sitting at my door like this? As I paused for a moment, she stood up, lowered her face a little, and said to me, “I have something to say to you.”
I said, “Then come to our room.”
“Are you going out for some important work?”
“Yes, but let that be for now—first, with you—”
“No, finish your work first—after you’ve eaten, we’ll talk.”
When I went outside, I saw that the daroga’s plate was empty. The man he had brought as a witness was still sitting there, eating pitha.
Astonished, I said, “What is this, Amulya!”

With his mouth full of pitha, he replied, “Yes, sir—I’ve eaten to my heart’s content. Now, if you don’t mind, I’ll tie up the few that are left in my handkerchief.” Saying this, he wrapped up all the remaining pithas in his handkerchief.
I looked at the daroga and asked, “What is the matter here?”
The daroga laughed and said, “Maharaj, the riddle of the thief remains a riddle, and now I’m dizzy with the riddle of the stolen goods as well.”
Saying this, he opened a bundle made of a torn rag and placed a stack of notes before me. He said, “Here are your six thousand rupees, Maharaj.”
Where did they come from?

For now, from Amulyababu’s bag. Last night, he went to your Chakua estate’s manager and said, ‘The stolen notes have been found!’ The manager was not as frightened by the theft as he was by the return of the stolen goods. He feared that everyone would suspect he had hidden the notes himself and, seeing the possibility of danger, concocted an improbable story. Under the pretense of feeding Amulyababu, he kept him seated and sent word to the police station. I rode over on horseback...

From early morning, I have been with him. He said, “I will not tell you where I got it from.” I replied, “You won’t get away without telling.” He said, “Then I will lie.” I said, “Very well, then say that.” He said, “I found it lying in a bush.” I said, “Telling a lie is not so easy. Where is the bush? For what reason did you go into that bush? You must tell everything.” He said, “I will have plenty of time to make up all that—don’t worry about it.”

I said, “Haricharan Babu, what is the point of dragging a gentleman’s son into this for no reason?” The inspector said, “He is not just a gentleman’s son, he is the son of Nibaran Ghoshal—he was my class friend. Maharaj, let me tell you what the matter is. Amulya has found out who committed the theft—he recognized him during this ‘Bande Mataram’ excitement. He wants to save him by taking the blame upon himself. All this is his heroism. My boy, we too were once your age—eighteen or nineteen—studying at Ripon College. One day, on the street, to save a bullock-cart driver from the oppression of a guard, I nearly ended up at the very gates of the jail—by chance, I escaped. Maharaj—
Now it has become difficult to catch the thief, but I am telling you who is at the root of it all.”
I asked, “Who?”
“Your manager, Tinkori Dutta, and that Kasem Sardar.”
The daroga, after presenting various arguments in support of his suspicion, left. I said to Amulya, “If you tell me who took the money, no harm will come to anyone.”
He said, “I did.”
“How? They say it was a gang of dacoits—”
“I was alone.”

What Amulya said was astonishing. The manager, after finishing his dinner at night, was sitting outside; the place was dark. Amulya had two pistols in his pockets—one loaded with blank cartridges, the other with real bullets. Half his face was covered with a black mask. Suddenly, a beam from a bull’s-eye lantern. As soon as the light fell on the manager’s face, he fired the blank pistol, and the manager began to scream in terror. As soon as two or four barkandazes came running, he fired the pistol above their heads; they ran wherever they could, locked themselves inside rooms and shut the doors. Kasem Sardar came running with a stick; aiming at his leg, Amulya fired a bullet, and Kasem fell down. Then, making the manager open the iron safe, Amulya took the six thousand rupees in notes and, with one of our office horses—
After galloping that horse five or six times, he left it in one place and arrived here the next morning.
I asked, "Amulya, why did you go to do this?"
He replied, "I had a special reason."
Then why did you return it?
Call the one at whose command I returned it; I will speak in her presence.
Who is she?
Chhoto-Ranididi.

I sent for Bimala. She entered the room slowly, covering herself with a white shawl draped over her head—she wore no shoes on her feet. Seeing her, it seemed to me I had never seen Bimala like this before—like the moon in the morning, as if she had veiled herself in the light of dawn.
Amulya prostrated himself at Bimala's feet and took the dust from her feet in reverence. Rising, he said, "I have fulfilled your command, Didi. I have returned the money."
Bimala said, "You have saved me, brother."
Amulya said, "Remembering you, I did not utter a single lie. My mantra of 'Bande Mataram' remains with you."
...underfoot. Returning and entering this house, I have received your grace as well.”

Bimala could not quite understand these words. Amulya took a handkerchief out of his pocket, untied its knot, and showed her the stored pithas. He said, “I haven’t eaten them all; I’ve kept some—these are saved so that you might serve them to me with your own hand.”

I realized that I was no longer needed here; I left the room. I thought to myself, I only waste away with my endless words, while they garland my straw effigy with a string of torn shoes and burn it by the riverbank. I cannot turn anyone back from the path of death—only those who can, do so with a mere gesture. Our words do not possess that inevitable sign.
We are not flame, we are cinders, we are the extinguished, we cannot light the lamp. The history of my life only proves this: the lamp I arranged did not burn.

Once more, slowly, I went to the inner quarters. Perhaps, once again, my mind was drawn toward the room of the second queen. Today, I feel an urgent need to sense that my life has struck a true and clear note on the veena of someone else’s existence in this world;—one cannot find proof of one’s own existence within oneself—one must search for it somewhere outside.

As soon as I came in front of Mejo-rani’s room, she came out and said, “Ah, Thakurpo, I was just thinking, perhaps your Devi is still at it today. No Devi now, your meal is ready and coming right up.”
I replied, “In the meantime, let me take out that money and set it aside properly.”
As I was heading towards my bedroom, Mejo-rani asked, “That Daboga who came—did he give any clue about the theft?”
I did not feel inclined to tell Mejo-rani about the recovery of those six thousand rupees, or even a part of it. I said, “That’s still going on.”

When I entered the room with the iron safe, I took the bunch of keys out of my pocket and found that the key to the safe was missing. Strange, my absent-mindedness! Since morning, I had opened so many boxes and cupboards with this bunch of keys, but not once did I notice that this particular key was gone.
Mejo-rani asked, “Where is the key?”

Without answering her, I futilely rummaged through this pocket and that—searched through all my belongings ten times over. There was no doubt left for us to understand: the key was not lost, someone had deliberately taken it out. Who could have taken it? In this room—
Mejo-rani said, “Don’t be anxious, eat first. I am sure, it’s only because you were careless that Chhoto-rani has especially put that key away in her box.”

I felt a great confusion. It is not in Bimala’s nature to take the key from the ring without telling me. During my meal today, Bimala was not there—she was then in the kitchen, having rice brought in and feeding Amulya herself. Mejo-rani was about to send her to call the doctor—I forbade it.

Just as I was finishing my meal, Bimala came in. I wished that the matter of the missing key would not be discussed in front of Mejo-rani. But that did not happen. As soon as Bimala entered, she asked, “Do you know where Thakurpo’s iron safe key is?”
Bimala replied, “It’s with me.”
Mejo-rani said, “Didn’t I say so! There are thefts and robberies everywhere these days. Chhoto-rani may appear unafraid outwardly, but inwardly she has not failed to be cautious.”
Looking at Bimala’s face, I felt a strange unease—I said, “All right, let the key remain with you for now, I’ll take out the money in the afternoon.”
Mejo-rani immediately said, “Why again in the afternoon—”
“Thakurpo, now is a good time—take that out and send it to the cashier.”
Bimala said, “I have already taken out the money.”
I was startled.
Mejo-rani asked, “Where did you put it after taking it out?”
Bimala replied, “I have spent it.”
Mejo-rani exclaimed, “Oh my! Listen to that! How did you manage to spend so much money?”

Bimala did not answer her. Nor did I ask her anything—I stood silently by the door, holding onto it. Mejo-rani was about to say something to Bimala, but she stopped; looking at my face, she said, “Well done, she took it. I used to steal and hide whatever money my husband kept in his pocket or in his box, knowing that otherwise it would be squandered by the five ghosts. Thakurpo, you are almost the same—you have a hundred ways to throw money away. If we women do not steal your money, it will never be safe. Now come, go and get some rest.”

Mejo-rani took me by the hand and led me to the bedroom. I hardly knew where I was going. She sat down cheerfully beside my bed and said, “Olo, O Chutu, bring me a paan, will you? You people are simply—”
