“You’ve become a bride! There’s no betel leaf in the house? Then have some brought from my room.”
I said, “Mejo-rani, you haven’t eaten yet, have you?”
She replied, “Long ago.”

That was an outright lie. She sat beside me and began to chatter, talking all sorts of nonsense from every corner of the world. A maid came and, standing outside the door, informed us that Bimala’s rice was getting cold. Bimala gave no response. Mejo-rani said, “What’s this, you haven’t eaten yet? It’s already so late.” Saying this, she forcefully took her away.
I understood there was some connection between the six-thousand-rupee robbery and the money being taken out of this iron safe. What kind of connection, I did not wish to know—nor would I ever ask.

Providence always draws the lines of our life’s picture a little blurred. It is His intention that we, with our own hands, erase, alter, and fill in those lines, and bring forth a clear image shaped by our own minds. With the Creator’s signal, we are to create our own lives, to express a great idea through all our being—this pain, this longing, has always been within me.

I have spent so many days in this pursuit! How much have I deprived my instincts, how much have I suppressed myself—only the indwelling Lord knows the history of that inner struggle. The hard truth is this: no one’s life belongs to themselves alone—one who seeks to create must create with all that surrounds them, or else they will fail. That is why, in my heart, there was always a fervent desire to draw Bimala into this creation as well. Since I loved her with all my soul, why should I not be able to do so—this was my confidence.

But then, I saw clearly: those who can effortlessly create not only themselves but also their surroundings are a different kind of people, and I am not of that kind. I have received the mantra, but I have not been able to give it to anyone else. Those to whom I have poured myself out completely have taken everything from me—except for this innermost thing of mine. My trial became severe. Where I needed support the most, there I found myself most alone. Even in this trial, I resolved to prevail. Until the last moment of life, my difficult path will be mine alone.

Today, I begin to suspect that there was a kind of tyranny within me. I wanted to mold my relationship with Bimala into a rigid form of goodness, to cast it perfectly in a flawless mold—within this desire of mine, there was a certain forcefulness. But a human life cannot be cast in a mold. And, to think of goodness as a lifeless object—
Whenever one tries to mold another, the spirit dies and takes its terrible revenge.

Because of this oppression, we have become inwardly estranged from each other without even realizing it. What Bimala herself could have become never surfaced under my pressure; and so, from the friction of a stifled life beneath the surface, the bonds have worn thin. Today, she has had to steal these six thousand rupees—she could not be open with me, because she sensed that in one vital place I am utterly, powerfully separate from her. Those who match with people like us, with our one-track ideas, do so; those who do not, deceive us. Even the simple-hearted, we turn into hypocrites. In trying to mold a companion of faith, we distort the wife.

Is it not possible to return to the beginning? Then let me once walk the path of simplicity. This time, I will not bind my companion with any chain of ideas—only play the flute of my love and say, “Love me. In the light of that love, let your nature unfold fully; let my commands be utterly suppressed—let the will of the Creator within you triumph, let my will return, abashed.”
But the estrangement that had been quietly growing between us has now burst forth through such a wound that—can the natural...

Will you be able to tend to the wound? That gentle touch behind which Nature silently works to heal—now that gentle touch has been utterly severed! A wound must be covered; I will cover this wound with my love—enfold the pain, coil after coil, within my heart, shielding it from the touch of the world. One day, perhaps, not even a trace of this wound will remain. But is there any time left? So many days were spent in misunderstanding, and now this day has come, steeped in error—how many more days will it take to set things right? And after that? After that, the wound may dry, but will there ever be any true compensation for what is lost?

Did I hear a faint sound? Turning, I see Bimala retreating from the doorway. Perhaps she had been standing there silently for some time—uncertain whether to enter or not—at last, she was turning away. I rose quickly and called, "Bimala!" She stopped, her back to me. I took her by the hand and brought her into the room.
No sooner had she entered than she collapsed onto the floor, clutching a pillow to her face, and wept! Without a word, I sat by her head, holding her hand.
When her sobs subsided and she sat up, I tried to draw her to my breast. She hesitated a little—

With force, he pulled his hand free from mine, knelt down, and began to bow his head repeatedly at my feet in reverence. When I tried to withdraw my feet, he clasped them tightly with both hands and, in a choked voice, said, “No, no, no, do not take your feet away—let me worship you.”
I remained silent then. Who am I to stand in the way of such worship? When the worship is true, so too is the deity of that worship—am I that deity, that I should feel any hesitation?
chapters.summary: Nikhilesh prepares to leave for Calcutta, reflecting on the burdens of attachment as Mejo-rani and Bimala confront their own sorrows, longing.

chapters.title: Bimala: Ashes and Awakening
paragraphs: Go, go, now step out—where all love has merged into the ocean of worship, at that sacred confluence. In that pure blue depth, the weight of all mud will dissolve. And now I am no longer afraid—neither of myself, nor of anyone else. I have passed through fire—what was meant to burn has turned to ashes, what remains now can never die. That self I offer at the feet of Him who has taken all my sins into His profound sorrow.

Tonight, I must leave for Kolkata. All this while, my mind, troubled by the turmoil inside and out, could not settle on the task of packing my things. Now, at last, I pulled the trunks close and began to arrange them. After a while, I saw my husband had come to stand beside me. I said, “No, that won’t do—you promised me you would take a little rest.”
My husband replied, “It seems I made the promise, but my sleep did not—it is nowhere to be found.”
I said, “No, that will not do—you must go and lie down.”
He said, “Why should you do everything alone?”

I may not be able to do it well. Even if I am not here, you may want to carry on this grandeur—do as you wish, but without you, I cannot manage. That is why, alone in my room, I could not fall asleep at all.
Saying this, he set about his work. Just then, the servant came and announced, "Sandip Babu has come; he asked me to inform you."
I did not have the courage to ask whom he had told to be informed. In that instant, it felt as if the daylight in my world shrank away like the shy touch-me-not plant.
My husband said, "Come, Bimala, let’s go and hear what Sandip has to say. He had taken his leave and gone, but now that he has returned, perhaps there is something important."

Not going would be more embarrassing than going, so I accompanied my husband outside. In the drawing room, Sandip was standing, looking at the pictures hanging on the wall. As soon as we entered, he said—
"You must be wondering—why does this fellow return? Unless the last rites are properly performed, the spirit does not depart."

Saying this, he drew a small bundle wrapped in a handkerchief from within his shawl and placed it open on the table. Those were the coins. He said, "Nikhil, do not misunderstand, do not think that suddenly, by coming into your company, I have turned into a saint. I am not here to shed tears of repentance and return these six thousand rupees—"
Sandeep is not the sort of petty fellow who would return the jewels.
But—

With this, Sandeep did not finish his sentence. After a brief pause, he looked at me and said, “Queen of the hive, after all these days, a ‘but’ has entered into the root of Sandeep’s life—every day, waking after three in the morning, I wrestle with it, and I see it is no mere illusion. Sandeep cannot escape without settling this debt. Into the hands of that ruinous Fate I have given my worship. I tried with all my might, but in this world, it is only this wealth of yours that I cannot accept—I must leave you empty-handed, O Goddess! Here—take it!”
Saying this, Sandeep took out the jewel box and placed it on the table, then made as if to leave quickly. My husband called out to him, “Listen before you go, Sandeep!”

Sandeep, standing by the door, said, “I have no time, Nikhil. I have received word that a band of Muslims is plotting to seize me like a precious gem and bury me in their graveyard. But I must stay alive. Only twenty-five minutes remain before the northbound train departs. So, for now, I must go—later, if I get a chance, I will settle all remaining matters with you. If you take my advice, you too should not—”
Don’t delay. Queen of the bees, “I bow to the Destructive One, garlanded with hearts!”

Saying this, Sandip almost ran out. I remained stunned! Never before had I seen, so starkly, how insignificant my jewels and ornaments truly were. Just a short while ago, I was wondering what things to take with me, where to put what—now it seemed that none of these things mattered at all—only leaving, only going out, was necessary.
My husband rose from his chair, came over, and gently took my hand. “There isn’t much time left now,” he said softly. “Let us get things in order.”

At that moment, Chandranath Babu entered the room and, seeing me, hesitated for a moment in embarrassment. “Forgive me, my child, I couldn’t send word before coming. Nikhil, the Muslim crowd has grown wild! Harishkundur’s office has been looted—there was no fear for that, but now they have begun to torment the women. That is something we cannot endure while life remains in us!”
My husband said, “Then I must go.”
I held his hand and said, “What can you do by going there? Mastermoshai, please stop him.”
Chandranath Babu said, “Child, there is no time to stop him now.”
My husband said, “Don’t worry about anything, Bimala.”
I went to the window and saw him riding away at full gallop. He had no weapon in his hand.
A little later, the second queen rushed into the room and exclaimed,

"What have you done, Chhutu, what a disaster! Why did you let Thakurpo go?"—She called to the servant, "Quick, quick, call the Dewan Sahib at once!" The second queen had never appeared before the Dewan Sahib before. That day, she had no shame. She said, "Send riders quickly to bring Maharaj back."
The Dewan Sahib replied, "We have tried hard to stop him, he will not return."
The second queen said, "Send word to him, tell him the second queen has been struck by cholera—her death is near."
When the Dewan left, the second queen began to scold me, "Demoness, destroyer! You survived, and sent Thakurpo to his death!"

The light of day faded away. In front of the window, beyond the blooming drumstick tree of Goalpaar, the sun set in the western sky. Even now, I can see every ray of that sunset before my eyes. Around the sinking sun, a mass of clouds spread north and south in two directions, like the outstretched wings of a giant bird—its fiery feathers arranged in layers.
chapters.summary: Bimala, feeling transformed after deep turmoil, prepares to leave for Kolkata, but is shaken when Sandip returns the stolen jewels and Nikhil rushes into danger.
